items.content:
—As VP Shettima directs relevant stakeholders, agencies to develop roadmap for NEC’s endorsement
By Johnbosco Agbakwuru
ABUJA— THE Federal Government on Tuesday, directed stakeholders and relevant agencies to design a comprehensive operational roadmap for the nationwide rollout of the 112 national emergency number.
Accordingly, it constituted a committee comprising the Nigeria Police Force (NPF), the Nigerian Communications Commission (NCC), the National Emergency Management Agency (NEMA), the Federal Road Safety Corps (FRSC), and other relevant agencies to finalise the roadmap and standard operating procedures for formal endorsement of the National Economic Council (NEC).
Recall that NEC had recently approved the 112 as Nigeria’s single universal toll-free emergency number to replace fragmented and slow response lines, with a view to eliminating bureaucratic red tape and allow citizens easy access to rapid help during fires, accidents, medical crises, or security breaches.
Speaking in Abuja during the National Emergency Number 112 Project stakeholders meeting, the Vice President who gave the directive, urged the committee to ensure their decisions are based on global best practises in order to have a clear roadmap.
Charging the committee to finalize the roadmap and standard operating procedures for formal NEC endorsement, Senator Shettima stressed the need to make significant progress, assuring that once it becomes visible, resources will be available to fund the process.
“Let’s make progress so that whatever time we have spent here is worth spending. And most importantly, the engine is finance. It is resources to drive the process. And I want to assure you that we will get the resources,” he stated.
On his part, the Inspector General of Police (IGP), Olatunji Rilwan Disu, said the Nigeria Police Force was fully in support of the adoption of 112 as Nigeria’s unified national emergency number.
From an operational perspective, he noted that it is “a significant step towards ensuring that citizens have a simple and reliable means of accessing emergency assistance.”
He explained that for a citizen facing an armed attack, accident, fire outbreak, medical emergency, kidnapping, or any other life-threatening situation, while the first challenge is to determine which agency to call, one number should provide access to the appropriate response.
Earlier in her presentation, the Personal Assistant to the President on e-Governance (Office of the Vice President), Mrs. Lydia Aina, noted that emergency response in Nigeria runs across many agencies, systems, and jurisdictions, creating fragmentation in how emergencies are received, coordinated, and responded to.
The goal, she said, is to move from the fragmented states through coordinated response to a fully integrated national framework, just as she explained that the meeting was about the system behind the process, including “the people, the agencies, the standards that make the number actually work when citizens dial it.
“Our job now is to turn it into an actual working programme with milestones. So, we have identified six immediate priorities. First, governance. We need a clear structure of who’s responsible for what,” she explained.
Other stakeholders who pledged the full support of their agencies at the meeting included the Director-General of NEMA, Mrs. Zubaida Umar; Corps Marshal of FRSC, Shehu Mohammed, and Director-General of the National Orientation Agency (NOA), Mallam Lanre Issa-Onilu, among others.

The company said it had commenced arrangements to mobilise the necessary personnel, equipment and other resources to the affected location to rehabilitate the collapsed tower and restore the transmission line to service as quickly as possible.
Meanwhile, TCN said it had successfully maintained electricity transmission to Sokoto by enabling the Talata Mafara-Sokoto corridor to receive supply through an alternative transmission path from the Kaduna-Mando axis.
The alternative route utilises the 132kV Zaria-Funtua-Gusau transmission line, it said.
TCN expressed regret over the inconvenience the incident could cause electricity consumers and other stakeholders affected by the development.
The company assured the public that every effort was being made to restore normal bulk power transmission service as quickly as possible.

items.content:
By Islamiyyah Adekanbi
The circulation of a fake notice claiming that fintech company OPay would suspend its operations has highlighted the need for members of the public to verify financial information before acting on or sharing it.
The notice, which circulated on WhatsApp and other social media platforms, urged OPay customers to withdraw their funds ahead of an alleged shutdown. OPay subsequently dismissed the notice as false and advised customers to rely on its verified communication channels.
The incident also triggered reactions among some users and point-of-sale (POS) operators, with some customers transferring funds from their OPay accounts to other banks after seeing the notice.
A POS operator, Adeyemi Samuel, who operates at Iyana School, LASU Road, said the notice caused some customers to rush to move their money from OPay.
“Many of them emptied their OPay accounts completely because they were afraid the platform might actually shut down,” Samuel said.
He said the development affected his business because customers wanted to withdraw their money as physical cash, leaving him with limited cash for other transactions.
Samuel said he became suspicious after noticing differences between the official OPay logo and the logo used on the alleged shutdown notice.
He advised customers to remain calm and verify financial information through official company channels before taking action.
For Kokumo Kafayat,a student who came across the notice on WhatsApp Status after receiving it from a relative, the situation produced a different response.
Kafayat said she did not act on the information but instead tried to verify it. She said she felt relieved after discovering that the information was false and subsequently tried to inform others about the fake notice.
Cybersecurity Analyst and Instructor at MiazTech Academy, Josiah Zion Mauton, said members of the public should pay attention to the source and content of financial messages circulating online.
According to him, messages that create unnecessary urgency or panic should be treated with caution, particularly when they pressure users to take immediate action.
Mauton identified suspicious links, unusual sender details, poor grammar and unprofessional formatting as some of the warning signs users should look out for.
He also warned against messages that instruct users to contact private numbers, download software or provide sensitive personal information.
He advised users to first “kill the panic and sense of urgency” before acting on suspicious messages and to contact financial institutions directly through their official customer-care channels.
A software engineer specialising in web and mobile development, Abdullahi Raji, also advised users to verify major announcements through the official website and verified social media accounts of the organisation involved.
Raji said screenshots and forwarded messages should not automatically be regarded as evidence because they can easily be manipulated.
He advised users not to click suspicious links or provide sensitive information such as passwords, PINs or one-time passwords (OTPs) based on unverified messages.
According to him, false financial information can trigger real financial actions, including unnecessary withdrawals, transfers and payments, while also exposing users to scams and other security risks.
Raji further advised anyone who had already interacted with a suspicious link to stop further activity and contact the affected financial institution through an official channel. He said anyone who had disclosed credentials should change them immediately, while unauthorised financial transactions should be reported without delay.
The experts urged members of the public to verify information from its original source, cross-check major claims through credible channels and avoid sharing messages that cannot be confirmed.
A data analyst, Afolayan Marvellous, advised members of the public to adopt a simple approach when dealing with information received online: “Pause, Check, Confirm.”
According to him, users should pause before reacting, check the original source and confirm the information through the organisation’s official channels and other credible sources. He advised that information that cannot be verified should not be shared.
The OPay incident serves as a reminder that the speed at which information spreads online can also make it easier for false financial claims to trigger unnecessary panic and financial decisions.

By Prince Osuagwu
More than 8,000 Nigerian youths have participated in the 18th edition of Aptech Career Quest, with over 200 aspiring technology and creative professionals receiving scholarships worth more than N701 million.
The initiative, organised by Aptech Nigeria in collaboration with Middlesex University London, is part of efforts to expose young Nigerians to career opportunities in technology, creative industries and international education.
Held from August 7 to 21, Career Quest featured physical sessions in Lagos, Abuja, Port Harcourt, Calabar, Enugu, Ibadan and Abeokuta, as well as two nationwide virtual sessions.
The programme provided participants with career guidance, practical learning opportunities, project showcases, scholarship opportunities and information on international education pathways.
This year’s edition also highlighted the progression pathway between Aptech and Middlesex University London through the Credit Transfer Facility, CTF, which enables eligible students to progress from selected Aptech programmes to undergraduate degree programmes in the UK.
Students enrolled in programmes including the Advanced Diploma in Software Engineering, Artificial Intelligence, ADSE AI, and Advanced Diploma in Multimedia & Animation, ADIM, can, subject to applicable requirements, progress to selected programmes such as BSc, Computer Networks, BSc, IT & Business Information Systems, BA Animation and BA Animation & Games.
Executive Vice President, International Business, Aptech Limited, Kallol Mukherjee, said the strong response to Career Quest reflected the growing interest among Nigerian youths in building careers in the digital economy.
He said: “Over the past 26 years, Aptech has remained committed to empowering students with practical, industry-relevant skills that prepare them for global opportunities.”
Mukherjee said the partnership with Middlesex University was further expanding international opportunities for Aptech students through access to globally recognised degree pathways.
According to him, Career Quest would continue to support the development of future-ready talent capable of contributing to Nigeria’s technology ecosystem while competing in the international labour market.
Aptech, which has operated in Nigeria for 26 years, currently has 72 centres nationwide and offers programmes in artificial intelligence, machine learning, data science, software development, cybersecurity, networking, cloud computing, Internet of Things, digital marketing, UI/UX, animation and 3D visualisation.
The company also offers fast-track technology courses and programmes for teenagers.
The 8,000-plus participation figure underscores the growing appetite among Nigerian youths for technology careers, but also highlights the challenge of converting such interest into practical, employable skills.
As demand rises for professionals in areas such as AI, software development, cybersecurity, data science and cloud computing, the focus is increasingly shifting from access to digital education to the acquisition of industry-relevant skills, recognised qualifications and practical experience.
Career Quest provides one avenue for bridging that gap by combining career guidance, technical training, scholarships and international progression opportunities for young Nigerians seeking a foothold in the digital economy.

*SMEs lament: Our livelihood goes with poor network connections
•Nigeria recorded over 5,000 fibre-optic cuts in six months – NCC
•Telcos blame fiber cuts, vandalism, power
By Juliet Umeh
For Nigeria’s growing army of internet-reliant entrepreneurs and workers, the network bars on a mobile phone can mean the difference between earning a living and going home empty-handed.
For an online seller, a lost connection can mean a missed order; for a ride-hailing driver, a missed trip; for a POS operator, a failed transaction; and for an online tutor, a disrupted class.
Increasingly, the internet is no longer just a tool for communication. For millions of workers and small businesses, it has become the marketplace, payment channel, classroom, dispatch system and customer-service desk.
But when the connection disappears, so does the livelihood built around it.
For Mrs Anna Nso, a small business centre owner in Aba, Abia State, a poor network has become a daily battle with frustrated customers, financial losses and mounting anxiety.
One day, a network glitch turned a routine electricity payment into a costly mistake.
“My husband wanted to recharge N1,900 electricity bill for a customer, but because of the network problem, he mistakenly recharged N19,000,” Nso told Vanguard.
“The network stressed him so much that he made the mistake.”
It was not an isolated incident.
“There are times we transfer money twice because we don’t know the first transfer has gone through. If you don’t check the transaction history before trying again, you can end up making a double transfer,” she said.
The pressure is compounded when customers crowd her shop waiting for transactions to go through.
“You discover that customers will line up in the shop, waiting for me to attend to them. In the process, I will be turning my phone up and down, moving from one corner to another in search of a network,” she said.
The stress has also begun to take a toll.
“I recently checked my BP because I was having constant headaches and feeling dizzy. My nurse told me it was 150 over 100. Honestly, I wasn’t surprised. The challenge I face in my shop every day is enough to give someone a headache,” she said.
‘If I’m unreachable, I can’t earn’
For e-hailing driver Polycarp Dawalere, poor network can mean the difference between receiving an order and going home empty-handed.
The Taraba State indigene, who formerly lived in Ikorodu, Lagos, said unstable connectivity had become a familiar frustration.
“We do have problems with the network, especially in some places in Ikorodu. The network is always very poor in so many areas,” he said.
Dawalere depends on digital platforms for his livelihood.
“If I am in a place where the network is bad, I can’t get any order because I will be unreachable,” he said.
The problem became so serious that it influenced where he lived.
“This was the major reason I left Ikorodu. I noticed I was losing clients,” he said.
For him, the equation is simple:
“If I am unreachable, I cannot get an order. And if I cannot get an order, I cannot earn.”
‘A one-hour class can stretch to 90 minutes’
For Debbie Ntigeli, an online tutor in Ajah, Lagos, unstable connectivity can turn a one-hour lesson into a 90-minute struggle.
“With how unstable some of the network providers have been lately, I sometimes experience network delays and disconnections, which interrupt the flow of the lesson,” she said.
“It also affects my ability to share learning materials and use interactive tools with my learners.”
Sometimes she has to move around her environment searching for a stronger signal.
“A class that is supposed to last for one hour can sometimes extend to an hour and 30 minutes because of time lost to network interruptions,” she said.
The cost of staying connected also comes directly from her pocket.
“I spend about N25,000 monthly on data. Data is one of my major teaching-related expenses,” she said.
For Ntigeli, connectivity is therefore not an optional expenditure. It is part of the cost of earning an income.
When the shop lives on a phone
For Lagos fashion entrepreneur Tomiwa Ibukunle, the vulnerability of an online business became clear during the global WhatsApp, Facebook and Instagram outage in October 2021.
On an ordinary day, WhatsApp Business brought her about 20 orders.
But when the platforms went down, she received only five.
For an entrepreneur whose shop largely exists on a smartphone screen, the lesson was painful:
When connectivity disappears, the shop can disappear with it.
Another fashion seller, Dolapo, initially thought her own network was responsible when messages and calls stopped working.
Then she realised: “WhatsApp was down.”
For her, the platform was her enquiry desk, order channel and customer-service platform.
A similar experience confronted Lagos fashion vendor Adaeze Nathan during an Instagram outage in 2026.
When messages stopped sending, she discovered that the problem was not her internet connection but the platform itself.
The experiences expose a new vulnerability for Nigeria’s small businesses. For entrepreneurs whose storefronts, customer relationships and payment channels exist largely online, connectivity is no longer a convenience. It is infrastructure.
The infrastructure behind the disappearing bars
Behind these individual experiences is a larger infrastructure challenge.
The Nigerian Communications Commission, NCC, disclosed that more than 5,000 fibre-optic cut incidents were recorded in the first six months of 2026, largely linked to road construction, excavation and other civil works.
NCC Executive Vice Chairman, Dr Aminu Maida, warned that the damage goes beyond the cables.
“To a machine operator on a construction site, it may appear to be a simple buried cable. To the nation, it can mean failed calls, delayed payments, interrupted services and missed opportunities,” Maida said.
He stressed that Nigeria must build roads while protecting the fibre networks that connect the economy.
The scale of Nigeria’s digital dependence is reflected in data consumption. NCC figures show that Nigerians consumed more than 1.5 million terabytes of data in May 2026, rising to about 1.53 million TB in June.
Industry raises alarm
The telecom industry says the problem is compounded by vandalism, inadequate infrastructure and other operational challenges.
The Association of Licensed Telecom Operators of Nigeria, ALTON, said network sabotage and vandalism, including stolen fibre cables and base-station equipment, continue to degrade connectivity.
Its Chairman, Engr Gbenga Adebayo, said such incidents affect millions of subscribers.
The Association of Telecommunications Companies of Nigeria, ATCON, also identified inadequate last-mile connectivity and limited fibre penetration as challenges, particularly in underserved areas.
MTN Nigeria said it experiences between 35 and 40 fibre cuts daily across the country, arising from road construction, vandalism, sabotage and other factors.
The company also disclosed that an average of one to two telecom sites are vandalised every day, with generators, batteries, solar equipment and other critical infrastructure stolen or damaged.
In 2025 alone, MTN recorded 452 incidents of site vandalism, according to its General Manager, Network Services, Asura Mshelia.
He warned that repeated attacks could make further investment in affected locations difficult to justify.
Power: the other side
Even where fibre infrastructure remains intact, electricity remains a threat to network reliability.
Airtel Africa Chief Executive Officer, Sunil Taldar, said inadequate power supply was one of the biggest challenges facing telecom operators in Nigeria.
“To compensate for non-availability of power, what do mobile operators do? We run most of our sites through diesel,” he said.
“So, what we’re doing is we are delivering a network, but we are also becoming power generators. Now, that’s not our core job.”
Taldar said diesel-powered sites cost almost four times more to operate than those running on grid electricity.
He also warned that when telecom networks go down, the impact extends beyond telecommunications.
“Each time when a telecom network comes down, it’s not only the telecom network which is coming down in a particular area, it’s part of the economy which is coming down,” he said.
For Nso, however, the issue is far simpler than fibre routes, vandalism, power supply or broadband targets. What matters to her are the customers waiting in her shop, the transactions that need to be completed and the money that needs to be transferred.
Whenever the signal disappears, she moves from one corner of her shop to another, raises her phone and waits, hoping to find a stronger connection. Sometimes the transaction goes through, sometimes it fails, and at other times she is left wondering whether making another attempt could create a second problem.
For people like Nso, Dawalere, Ntigeli and thousands of other Nigerians whose livelihoods increasingly depend on digital connectivity, “network problem” is no longer merely a telecommunications complaint. It has become a business problem, an income problem and, increasingly, a livelihood problem.
When the network disappears, therefore, the question is no longer simply whether someone can browse the internet. It is whether they can work, sell, teach and earn a living.
The post How failed calls trigger huge economic losses appeared first on Vanguard News.

items.content:
..Strengthen Justice Delivery
By Kingsley Omonobi
ABUJA — The Nigeria Police Force and the Nigerian Bar Association (NBA) have agreed to strengthen professional collaboration, improve communication and promote greater mutual respect in a bid to enhance justice delivery and public safety.
The Inspector-General of Police, IGP Olatunji Rilwan Disu, disclosed this when he received the President of the NBA, Mrs Oyinkansola Badejo-Okusanya, SAN, and members of the Association’s National Executive Committee on a courtesy visit to the Force Headquarters, Abuja, on Tuesday.
Disu congratulated Badejo-Okusanya on her emergence as NBA President, describing the engagement as an opportunity to build a stronger and more structured relationship between the Nigeria Police Force and the legal profession.
He stressed that respect for every individual, office and profession must remain fundamental to professional interactions.
According to him, while lawyers are principally concerned with protecting citizens’ rights and the Police with protecting lives and property, the responsibilities of both institutions converge in the administration of justice.
The IGP also called for greater professionalism and responsibility in the recording and dissemination of encounters involving police officers.
He stressed that personnel should not be subjected to ridicule or have the demanding circumstances of their duties trivialised for social media entertainment, particularly when officers operate under challenging conditions in the discharge of their constitutional responsibilities to protect lives and property.
As part of efforts to strengthen institutional cooperation, Disu identified improved professional engagement, measures to reduce delays in criminal trials and the establishment of a dedicated NPF/NBA mechanism for seamless and open communication as key areas requiring sustained collaboration.
He said such a mechanism would provide a structured channel for addressing professional concerns, improving coordination and resolving issues before they escalated into unnecessary confrontations.
The IGP reaffirmed that the Police and the legal profession were partners in the pursuit of justice, acknowledging that disagreements could arise in the course of their respective duties.
He stressed, however, that such differences must be managed professionally, respectfully and with civility.
Disu expressed his readiness to work with the new NBA leadership towards building a stronger and more productive partnership.
The Nigeria Police Force, he said, remained committed to strengthening collaboration with the NBA and other justice-sector stakeholders towards protecting fundamental rights, improving access to justice, promoting professionalism and building a more effective, responsive and trusted criminal justice system.
Speaking during the visit, the NBA President emphasised the need for closer synergy between the Police and the legal profession, particularly through specialised training for lawyers and improved engagement between police lawyers and members of the wider Bar.
Badejo-Okusanya said the NBA had a responsibility to remain responsive to the needs of its members across the country and advocated an end to recurring clashes between lawyers and police officers.
She stressed that both professions had complementary responsibilities within the justice system.
The NBA President further highlighted a UNICEF-supported initiative on children’s access to justice, under which the NBA was proposing the presence of a police lawyer at every police station to provide appropriate legal support to children who come into contact with the juvenile justice system.
She said the proposal underscored the importance of ensuring that vulnerable children were adequately supported and protected throughout the justice process.

NNAUSA, an association of Ngwa indigenes resident in the United States, had adopted Otti as its preferred candidate for the 2027 governorship election in Abia State.

items.author: Nwafor
items.content:
By Ugochukwu Alaribe
UMUAHIA — The Coalition of Concerned and Patriotic Ngwa Citizens, CCPNC, has faulted the endorsement of Abia State Governor Alex Otti for a second term by the Ngwa National Association, USA, NNAUSA.
NNAUSA, an association of Ngwa indigenes resident in the United States, had adopted Otti as its preferred candidate for the 2027 governorship election in Abia State.
However, the CCPNC, in a statement by its Convener and Secretary, Mr Chukwuemeka Obinna and Engr. Joe Nkoro, respectively, disagreed with the endorsement, saying it did not reflect the views of all Ngwa people.
The group argued that Otti had not done enough to merit the support of the Ngwa people for a second term and urged residents at home and in the diaspora to critically assess the endorsement.
It also challenged the leadership of NNAUSA to undertake an independent assessment of communities across Ngwa land before taking further positions on the governor’s performance.
The statement read in part: “We state without fear of contradiction that the position taken by the leadership of NNAUSA was borne out of sheer ignorance, elitist detachment, and utter selfishness.”
However, the group was urged to substantiate its claims with specific evidence.
The CCPNC alleged that there were infrastructure and development challenges in several communities across Ngwa land, and called on NNAUSA to visit the communities to assess the situation firsthand.
It said: “We hereby challenge the executive body of NNAUSA to immediately suspend their remote political declarations and send an independent, unbiased delegation to communities across Ngwaland.
“Let them walk the inner roads of our villages, visit our local schools, interact with rural dwellers, and see things for themselves.”
The group also criticised what it described as the governor’s treatment of the Ngwa people since he assumed office.
According to the statement, the Ngwa people played an important role in supporting Otti’s political aspirations and electoral victory, and therefore expected greater attention to development needs in the area.
The CCPNC alleged that some developmental needs in Ngwa communities had not received adequate attention and questioned the basis for NNAUSA’s endorsement of the governor.
It said the association should consider the views and experiences of residents in the affected communities before making political endorsements.
The coalition maintained that its position was intended to draw attention to what it described as the need for accountability and broader consultation ahead of the 2027 election.

items.author: Team Inc42
items.content:
Private equity (PE) giant TPG yesterday offloaded Shadowfax shares worth ₹200 Cr via an open-market transaction.
According to BSE data, the PE major, via its entity NewQuest Asia Fund IV (Singapore), sold 80 Lakh shares of the logistics giant at ₹250.03 each to rake in the amount.
Of the shares that flooded the market, Hong Kong-based hedge fund Oxbow Master Fund lapped up 47.9 Lakh shares at ₹250 apiece for a sum of ₹119.6 Cr. There was no clarity on who picked up the rest of the shares.
The block deal was undertaken at a premium of 0.09% to the stock’s last closing price on Tuesday.
This is not the first time that early backers have diluted their shareholding in the listed logistics company in the past few months. Just last month, TPG also offloaded Shadowfax shares worth nearly ₹300 Cr in a block deal. Prior to this in July, Walmart-owned Flipkart and Eight Roads collectively sold Shadowfax shares worth nearly ₹1,654 Cr.
The bulk deals come as investors look to book profits amid a sharp uptick in Shadowfax’s share prices. The stock has surged nearly 23% in the past three months and is up more than 108.2% on a year-to-date (YTD) basis. This jump has come on the back of healthy performance by the startup on the financial front.
The logistics major reported an 8X surge in its consolidated net profit to ₹65.4 Cr in Q1 FY27 as against ₹8 Cr in the year ago quarter. Meanwhile, operating revenue jumped 65% YoY and 10% QoQ to ₹1,358.1 Cr in the quarter ended June 2026.
Following the results, Shadowfax also revised its FY27 revenue growth forecast to 38-40%, a significant jump from the 28-30% guidance projected just a quarter ago.
Founded in 2015 by Abhishek Bansal and Vaibhav Khandelwal, Shadowfax operates a logistics network serving ecommerce, quick commerce and D2C brands. The company was listed on the stock exchanges earlier this year.
It currently operates across more than 16,372 pincodes and plans to increase its network of dark stores from 47 to 100 by March 2027 as it looks to strengthen its quick commerce business.

items.content:
Britain, France, Canada and nine other countries on Tuesday announced plans to restrict trade with Israeli settlements in the occupied West Bank, citing escalating settler violence and settlement expansion that they said were undermining prospects for a two-state solution.
Denmark, Finland, Iceland, Ireland, Norway, Poland, Portugal, Spain and Sweden joined Britain, France and Canada in declaring their intention to introduce national measures or support European restrictions on trade in goods from Israeli settlements.
"The situation is rapidly deteriorating amid unprecedented levels of settler violence and settlement expansion," the foreign ministers of the 12 countries said in a joint statement. They said Israel's actions in the West Bank were undermining the possibility of a two-state solution.
They called on the Israeli government to immediately halt settlement expansion and the extension of civilian administrative powers and demanded accountability for settler violence and investigations into allegations against Israeli forces, while stressing that settlements were illegal under international law.
The announcement followed Israel's decision last month to open tenders for about 1,200 housing units in the West Bank's E1 area, a move the 12 countries described as "unacceptable" and one that would further isolate East Jerusalem from the rest of the territory.
Britain's Foreign Secretary Ed Miliband told parliament that the UK would impose an import ban on goods from illegal settlements in the occupied territories, accusing "settler terrorists" of carrying out ethnic cleansing against Palestinians and alleging that the Israeli government had often turned a blind eye.
French Foreign Minister Jean-Noel Barrot said the West Bank was "on the brink of explosion", citing unchecked settlement expansion, a surge in violence by extremist settlers and attacks that he said had been condemned by Israeli authorities themselves.
The measures immediately triggered a diplomatic response from Israel. Foreign Minister Gideon Saar ordered the closure of the British consulate in Jerusalem and announced a ban on the entry of 12 British nationals, including former Labour leader Jeremy Corbyn and several British lawmakers.
They included Zarah Sultana, Fahad Ansari, Naz Shah, Diane Abbott, Hannah Spencer, Carla Denyer, Sian Berry, Ellie Chowns, John McDonnell, Richard Burgon and Adrian Ramsay. Saar described Miliband's accusations in parliament as "outrageous lies" and said the Israeli government had been left with no choice but to respond to what he called hostile British actions.
Israel also ordered the removal of British representatives from the International Gaza Support Centre in Kiryat Gat and said British activities to train Palestinian Authority forces in the West Bank under the British Support Team in Ramallah would be terminated.
The Israeli foreign minister accused Britain's Labour government of pursuing a hostile policy towards Israel since coming to power in 2024, warning governments against attempting to pressure Israel into acting against its national and security interests.
The Green Party condemned the entry ban imposed on its lawmakers, saying it would not be "bullied into silence" and urging the British government to go further with restrictions, including an arms embargo and wider sanctions.
The West Bank has been occupied by Israel since 1967, while violence there has increased since the Gaza war began following Hamas's October 7, 2023 attack on Israel. The United Nations estimated that about 737,000 Israeli settlers lived in the West Bank, including East Jerusalem, as of October 2024.

items.content:
Terming the PTI's upcoming protest a "constitutional crisis", the capital's high court on Tuesday formed a larger bench to hear a plea seeking court order to stop Imran Khan's party from staging a protest in the federal capital on September 27.
Islamabad High Court (IHC) Chief Justice Sardar Muhammad Sarfraz Dogar, while hearing the petition filed by a private citizen Waqas Ahmed also issued notices to respondents and sought replies by tomorrow (September 10).
The court also sought assistance from Attorney General for Pakistan Mansoor Awan. The larger bench that will hear the matter is led by Chief Justice Dogar and comprises Justice Muhammad Azam Khan and Justice Muhammad Asif.
The court summoned the chief secretaries and inspectors general of police of all four provinces in their personal capacity. It also directed the Islamabad chief commissioner, deputy commissioner and inspector general of police (IGP) to appear before the court.
The court summoned the advocate generals of all four provinces and the advocate general Islamabad. During the hearing, the petitioner's counsel said his client was a businessman operating in Islamabad and was an affected party because the PTI planned to bring the protest to Islamabad.
He argued that the cases against PTI founder Imran Khan were pending before the courts and that all such cases should be decided according to law. He said if the PTI's argument was accepted, all people across Pakistan whose cases were pending in courts would be allowed to take to the streets.
The counsel further questioned whether, after the alleged attack on the GHQ on May 9, 2023, there was now a plan to attack Adiala Jail, where Imran Khan is currently detained. He described the proposed protest as completely illegal.
Referring to the PTI's November 2024 protest in Islamabad, the counsel claimed that three Rangers personnel had been killed during the demonstration. He questioned how such deaths could have occurred if the protesters were unarmed.
He referred to a newspaper report claiming that the previous PTI protest had caused losses of Rs240 million. He questioned why such allegations were repeatedly made against the PTI and not against other political parties. He alleged that the party was seeking relief from the courts through pressure.
Justice Dogar asked whether the protesters would come along with the Khyber-Pakhtunkhwa (K-P) chief minister and government machinery.
The counsel replied in the affirmative and presented before the court a November 21, 2024 letter issued by the Ministry of Interior, arguing that government machinery had allegedly been used during the 2024 protest despite the ministry's directions.
The petitioner's counsel further argued that the PTI leadership was coming to Islamabad to support a convicted prisoner.
He said two cases involving Imran were pending before the IHC and the court had repeatedly asked the relevant party to advance arguments on the appeals, but the arguments had not been presented.
The counsel questioned whether, if two million people were brought to Islamabad, the government could ask the court to suspend sentences in the pending appeals. The court, terming the matter a "constitutional crisis," sought replies from the respondents and adjourned the hearing till Thursday.

items.author: Adesewa Olofinko
items.content:
Nigeria's National Peace Policy is a framework intended to bring greater coordination to conflict prevention and peacebuilding
Originally published on Global Voices
ACC. H. O. Idoko, Nigeria Security and Civil Defense Corps (NSCDC) representative, speaking at the National Peace Policy review in Abuja, 4-6 August, 2026. Photo by Triple Peace Africa. Used with permission.
The world is spending more on war and defense than ever before. Global military expenditure reached a record USD 2.7 trillion in 2024, according to the Stockholm International Peace Research Institute (SIPRI), as governments increased spending amid wars in Europe and Western Asia and growing security tensions elsewhere.
Africa is part of that trend. Military expenditure on the continent rose by 8.5 percent in 2025 to USD 58.2 billion. Nigeria’s spending rose even more sharply, increasing by 55 percent to USD 2.1 billion, according to SIPRI.
Yet for Nigeria, a bigger defense budget has not resolved a problem that has become increasingly dire. The country is confronting insurgency, banditry, mass kidnapping, communal violence, and rising organized crime, with the nature varying significantly from one region to another. Between July 2025 and June 2026, at least 7,825 people were abducted in 1,713 kidnapping-related incidents nationwide, and at least 1,142 people were killed. In July, President Bola Tinubu approved the recruitment of 28,000 additional soldiers and the creation of new army divisions, the latest in a series of moves to expand the country’s security forces.
This situation is driving lawmakers to review the country’s National Peace Policy, a framework intended to bring greater coordination to conflict prevention and peacebuilding while addressing some of the conditions that allow violence to take root and recur.
Dr. Sanda Julie, Director-General, Plateau State Peacebuilding Agency, speaking at the National Peace Policy review meeting held in Abuja, Nigeria, August 4-6, 2026. Photo by Triple Peace Africa. Used with permission.
Rethinking Nigeria's approach to peace
Nigeria’s first attempt at a National Peace Policy dates to 2012, when the Institute for Peace and Conflict Resolution (IPCR) led the process and produced a draft. That policy was never formally adopted or operationalized. With a population of more than 240 million people and hundreds of ethnic and linguistic groups, Nigeria is one of the world’s most diverse societies. That diversity is in itself not a source of conflict. But political competition, disputes over land and resources, communal tensions, weak institutions and perceptions of exclusion often interact in the country, turning local grievances into violence.
Through August, government agencies, peacebuilding organizations, development partners and technical experts met in Abuja and in three geopolitical zones — Kano, Enugu and Lagos — to review the old policy and shape a new one that would connect federal, state and local actors.
Chris Ngwodo, director-general of Nigeria's Office for Strategic Preparedness and Resilience (OSPRE), speaking with Global Voices in Abuja, Nigeria, says the goal is to fold conflict prevention into the country’s broader security architecture and look beyond the visible violence of armed confrontation toward the conditions that produce it.
“There are many forms of violence that are not overt violence,” he said, citing structural inequality, failures in the justice system, government neglect and a lack of opportunity as quieter but no less corrosive drivers of conflict.
Ngwodo frames the policy around a familiar idea that peace is not merely the absence of conflict but the presence of justice.
“Structural violence is invisible. Nobody can see it, but it’s present,” he said. “Subjective violence is what happens when people start fighting.” The new policy, he explained, is meant to address both by anchoring itself in restorative, retributive, and distributive justice and in equalizing opportunity.
Asked whether a new policy would solve Nigeria's security problems, Ngwodo didn't hesitate: “It will not.” What the document can do, he argued, is shift the country’s position from reactive firefighting toward predictive architecture by asking not just how to respond to violence, but why certain places are predisposed to it and why it keeps coming back.
“People are not fighting because they are inherently violent,” he said. The real drivers, in his account, are usually governance failures, lapses in justice administration, long-standing grievances, neglect, and limited opportunity.
Since the last policy attempt, Nigeria’s peacebuilding landscape has grown considerably. OSPRE itself didn’t exist in 2012, nor did the state peace commissions that now operate across the country. The task now, Ngwodo said, is aligning that infrastructure and scaling it up.
L-R: Director General, Institute of Peace and Conflict Resolution (IPCR), Dr Joseph Ochogwu, Chairman, House Committee on peacebuilding and social cohesion, Sadiq Tafida, Special Adviser to the Nigerian president on Homeland security, Maj Gen Adeyinka Famadewa (Rt), and Director-General, Office for Strategic Preparedness and Resilience, Chris Ngwodo at the National Peace Policy review stakeholders meeting in Abuja, Nigeria. Photo by Triple Peace Africa. Used with permission.
Beyond the military response
Nigeria has long contributed to regional peacekeeping through the Economic Community of West African States (ECOWAS) and via troops and diplomats deployed to Liberia, Sierra Leone, Guinea-Bissau, Sudan and Côte d’Ivoire. At home, however, the government’s response to insecurity has leaned heavily on the military.
At the Abuja meeting, the presidential adviser on homeland security, Maj General Adeyinka Famadewa (Rt), said Nigeria could not “shoot its way out” of its security problem. He added that while military operations can disrupt armed groups and retake territory, they’re poorly suited to resolving the political, economic, and social conditions that let violence return once an operation winds down.
A representative of Germany’s development agency, GIZ African Union Office, Chijioke Iwuamadi, made a similar case for prevention, arguing that investing in prevention and long-term peacebuilding could be more effective and less costly than repeatedly responding to crises after they erupt.
Can Nigeria afford to prevent violence?
Nigeria does not have a single conflict. It has many overlapping and regionally distinct ones. An insurgency in the northeast has run for more than a decade while banditry and mass kidnapping have destabilized rural communities in the northwest and elsewhere. Communal violence and organized crime follow their own logic.
These fault lines interact. Religion intersects with ethnicity. Land disputes become communal conflicts. Political competition deepens existing grievances, while migration, demographic change and social media, with its capacity to spread misinformation and inflammatory narratives, add further strain. That regional variation is why the policy review followed zonal consultations in an attempt to reflect local differences while still producing something that can operate nationally.
According to the Director General of the Institute of Peace and Conflict Resolution (IPCR), Joseph Ochogwu, institutionalized coordination and a clearly mapped roadmap for the implementation of peace efforts across the country’s geopolitical zones would help avoid duplication, resource wastage, institutional rivalry, and communities falling through the cracks.
Can Nigeria afford to prevent violence?
Nigeria is already spending heavily to respond to insecurity. Military spending rose sharply through 2025, with no inherent contradiction between building military capacity and investing in prevention. But the two operate at different points in the cycle of violence. One responds to threats, the other tries to reduce the conditions that generate them, and Nigeria has to decide how to divide its attention and resources between them.
More than a decade after the first policy attempt, the country’s security landscape has changed. It faces more varied forms of insecurity, with a wider range of responses from government institutions, peace commissions, and civil society organizations. Whether that coordination can translate into fewer conflicts and prevent existing ones from returning will depend on what happens after the consultations end.
Written by Adesewa Olofinko

items.content:
Somewhere in the world, a person dies by suicide roughly every 43 seconds. Multiply that across a year, and the figure the World Health Organization gives us is over 720,000 lives. That number is so large it stops meaning anything until you remember that each one was a person with a name and a family. Suicide is now the third leading cause of death among people aged 15 to 29 worldwide. For every death, there are many more attempts, with some estimates putting it at 20 or more for every one life lost. This is not a niche public health issue tucked away in a footnote. It is a crisis playing out in plain sight, and most of us are simply not taking it seriously.
What tends to surprise people, when they first encounter the data, is where the weight of this crisis actually rests. There is a lazy assumption that suicide is somehow a wealthy world problem, a consequence of loneliness and excess in rich, cold countries. The figures say otherwise. Nearly three in every four suicides recorded globally happen in low- and middle-income countries. These are the very places where mental health budgets are lowest, where psychiatrists are scarce, and where the subject is often too shameful to say aloud. Africa carries a real share of this burden, even though its numbers are among the least reliable in the world. That is not because the deaths are not happening. It is because so many are never recorded as what they are.
The truth is that Nigeria features prominently in this crisis. Estimates of the national suicide rate vary a great deal depending on the source and the year. Some put it in the single digits per 100,000 people. Older WHO data using age-standardised methods put it much higher, at 17.3 per 100,000, which placed Nigeria fifteenth in the world and seventh in Africa, well behind Lesotho at the top of the continental list. That range of numbers is itself a warning sign. When a country cannot settle on how many of its people are dying this way, it tells you that the system for counting them, for understanding them, and for grieving them properly is broken.
Suicide remains a criminal offence under Section 327 of Nigeria’s Criminal Code Act, a colonial-era provision which has outlived any usefulness it may once have claimed. The government pledged to decriminalise it in 2024. The Federal Executive Council only recently approved an amendment to the National Mental Health Act, but it must still pass through the National Assembly to fully become law. A National Suicide Prevention Strategic Framework, running from 2023 to 2030, has also been introduced. However, a law still on the books, threatening a grieving, traumatised person with a prison sentence, does real damage. Families hide the true cause of death to protect the departed and themselves. Survivors of suicide attempts hide their scars rather than risk arrest.
One widely cited study, based on a decade of Nigerian newspaper reports, found that half of the documented cases were under 34, suggesting that a generation is being lost disproportionately young. Newspaper reports are an imperfect source, since they miss cases that never make the press. The pattern they, however, point to fits what clinicians describe: job loss, spousal conflict, untreated depression, and increasingly the sheer economic strain of trying to build an ordinary life with a currency that keeps losing its value and a job market with little room for the young.
A recent meta-analysis pulling together more than 50 Nigerian studies and over 130,000 people found that close to 8% of the general population has experienced suicidal thoughts at some point. Smaller, but still troubling, proportions went on to set up a plan or make an attempt. Numbers like that do not describe a peripheral problem affecting a handful of unlucky people. They describe something running quietly through ordinary households, hidden behind polite greetings and the assumption that everyone is managing fine.
Now, none of this happens in isolation from the wider economic and social situation. Nigeria’s youth unemployment, insecurity in several regions, and the daily grind of inflation on food and fuel do not cause suicide in any simple, direct way. Human distress is hardly ever that obvious, but these pressures pose a serious risk. They strip away the small cushions that normally help people survive their worst weeks: a stable job, a functioning support network, and affordable healthcare. Take those cushions away from enough people at once and the numbers go up.
Here is where I want to challenge a comfortable habit many of us fall into. It is the habit of treating suicide entirely as a policy failure, something only governments and hospitals can provide a solution for. Governments must act. And our own government should move faster on decriminalisation, training more mental health workers, and making care affordable outside private clinics in Lagos and Abuja. However, policy alone will not close this gap, because most of the moments that matter happen far from any clinic. They happen at a family dinner table, in a WhatsApp thread that goes quiet, in a colleague who stops laughing at the usual jokes, and in a friend who cancels plans for the third week running. This is where personal responsibility comes in. It is not blame directed at anyone who has struggled or died. It is an honest reckoning with what each of us owes the people around us.
That responsibility looks quite ordinary in practice. It means noticing when someone close to you withdraws and asking directly rather than assuming they would prefer to be left alone. It means taking a friend’s throwaway comment about not wanting to be here seriously, rather than laughing it off. If you are struggling yourself, it means resisting the cultural instinct to carry it silently until it becomes unbearable and instead telling one person—a pastor, an imam, a doctor, a sibling, or anyone—before the crisis point rather than after. It means employers building workplaces where a request for help is not interpreted as a weakness. It means journalists reporting on suicide responsibly, without describing methods or sensationalising the act, because how we talk about this publicly shapes how safely people can discuss it privately. None of these things requires a budget line or an act of the National Assembly. They require attention and the will to act on what we notice.
The truth is that the rising suicide numbers are not an abstraction happening somewhere else. They are unfolding in families down the road, offices, lecture halls, and market stalls across cities, villages, and every town in between. Fixing the system is necessary and overdue. However, we need to individually commit to checking on the people we love a little more closely and to saying something the next time our instinct nudges us that something is wrong.
If you are struggling with thoughts of suicide, help is available. In Nigeria, the Suicide Research and Prevention Initiative (SURPIN) helpline can be reached toll-free on 0800 078 7746, and the national emergency number 112 is available around the clock. You do not have to carry this burden alone.
Ojenagbon, a health communication expert and certified management trainer, lives in Lagos.

items.author: Business Desk
items.content:
The United Kingdom (UK) has declared Israeli settlers terrorists for carrying out ethnic cleansing against Palestinians. Foreign Secretary Ed Miliband today said the settlers’ actions have received backing from parts of the Israeli government, according to The Telegraph.
In the UK government’s strongest condemnation yet, Miliband announced a series of sanctions targeting trade and services linked to Israeli settlements.
The measures include:
A ban on imports from illegal Israeli settlements in the occupied territories.
Sanctions on services such as construction and financing linked to settlements.
A ban on UK advertising for properties in illegal settlements.
Personal sanctions against individuals accused of supporting settler violence.
Restrictions on arms licences and exports that materially contribute to the occupation.
Miliband also said the UK now considers Israel’s occupation of the West Bank unlawful in its entirety.
He told Parliament that Palestinians in parts of the West Bank were facing ethnic cleansing carried out by what he described as “settler terrorists.” He also accused the Israeli government of failing to stop the violence and said some Israeli officials had supported the forced displacement of Palestinians.
The UK expects legislation covering the trade ban and sanctions to be introduced within nine months.
Israel rejected the British position. The occupation’s foreign minister Gideon Saar accused Miliband of spreading “outrageous lies” and said Britain was acting against Israel.
Saar also announced retaliatory measures, including plans to close the UK consulate in Jerusalem and exclude Britain from the US-led Gaza coordination mission.
The UK is among 12 countries announcing sanctions on trade with Israeli settlements, alongside Canada, Denmark, Finland, France, Iceland, Ireland, Norway, Poland, Portugal, Spain and Sweden.

Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif on Tuesday said reducing energy costs is among the government’s top priorities as it works to support industry, businesses and economic growth.
The Prime Minister made the remarks during a meeting with a delegation of prominent industrialists and business leaders, where he discussed government measures aimed at improving the economy and promoting trade and industry.
PM Shehbaz thanked the business community for its proposals during the budget-making process, saying several of their recommendations had been incorporated into the federal budget.
He said the government was continuing to take steps to bring down the cost of energy, which remains a key concern for businesses and industries.
The Prime Minister also highlighted progress on the digitization of the Federal Board of Revenue (FBR), saying a major part of the process had been completed.
He said the FBR collected Rs. 800 billion through enforcement measures during the last financial year.
PM Shehbaz said the government was also focusing on developing a skilled workforce according to the requirements of industry. The objective was to equip young people with skills that match market demand.
The business delegation was briefed on government measures to improve the economy and facilitate businesses, trade and industry.
The government said port charges at the country’s ports had been reduced while their operational capacity had also been improved.
Work is also underway to upgrade the M-10 Motorway and develop the Pipri Freight Corridor to improve connectivity between Karachi’s ports and inland areas.
The Prime Minister also highlighted the planned M-13 Kharian-Rawalpindi Motorway, saying its construction would reduce travel distance between Lahore and Islamabad.
He said the upgradation of Pakistan Railways would further improve the country’s transport infrastructure and enable faster movement of commercial goods.
The government also highlighted the growth in Pakistan’s IT exports, saying its measures had helped the sector achieve a record increase.
PM Shehbaz also revealed that the government was training 1 million people in information technology and artificial intelligence to build a workforce capable of meeting the growing demand for digital skills.

items.author: Qaisar Kamran
items.content:
For visual artist and sculptor Khalil Chishtee, art is not merely a profession or a medium it is a way of life shaped by memory, place and everyday experiences.
His latest solo exhibition, Nisbat Road to Troutman Street, brings together a new body of work inspired by two places that have played an important role in his life: Nisbat Road in Lahore, where he grew up, and Troutman Street in Brooklyn, New York, where he has been based for many years.
The exhibition opens at Sanat Initiative in Karachi on Tuesday.
Speaking to The Express Tribune, Chishtee said the title of the exhibition reflects both his personal journey and the visual similarities he has observed between the two locations.
"I was born and brought up in Lahore," Chishtee said. "Near the city of Lahore, there is a place called Nisbat Road where I spent my youth."
He later studied at the National College of Arts (NCA) and taught sculpture for 11 years. During his time in Lahore, he also worked on a number of commissioned sculpture projects before moving to the United States.
Now based in Brooklyn, Chishtee said his memories of Lahore continue to influence his artistic practice.
"Nisbat Road, Lahore, is a very famous place," he said, recalling how the area was once closely associated with film posters and painted film boards.
For Chishtee, the walls of Lahore during his childhood were an important part of the city's visual culture.
"Posters on the walls, paintings on the walls, graffiti, it was a very normal visual culture in the 70s when I was growing up," he said.
He later found a similar form of visual expression in Brooklyn's Bushwick neighbourhood, particularly around Troutman Street, which is known for its vibrant street-art culture.
This idea of layers became central to his latest work.
"You see a glimpse of something else from below," he explained, describing how layers of paint, posters and other materials can reveal traces of what came before.
The concept also has a personal meaning for the artist. As people grow older, he said, memories from different periods of their lives begin to overlap.
While the works may initially appear to be paintings, Chishtee said they are created using an entirely different process.
"I am not a painter, so I don't know how to paint," he said.
Instead, he uses discarded plastic bags, including shopping bags and kitchen bin bags, to construct his works. The material is layered, torn and manipulated to create colourful surfaces and figures.
"These are not paintings," he said. "These are colourful bags."
Chishtee has been creating plastic structures since 2005 and is particularly known for his life-size human figures made from waste materials. He describes the practice as recycling and upcycling.
The artist said he does not use glue in the process and uses heat to create lines and textures within the plastic.
"I can't call this painting, because it is not painted," he said, explaining that the medium is essentially plastic waste.
The human figure remains at the heart of his work.
"I am a very figurative person," Chishtee said, explaining that he has been drawing figures since childhood.
For him, observing the human form involves paying attention to even the smallest details, from fingers and posture to the physical presence of a person.
"You go to the soul of the person inside," he said.
Chishtee also sees his use of discarded plastic as more than an environmental statement. He said he began working with the material long before sustainability and environmental art became popular trends.
"When I started doing this material in 2005, it was not a trend," he said.
"Trends change. What the heart says does not change."
For Chishtee, environmental responsibility is therefore part of his lifestyle rather than a theme adopted for an exhibition.
Reflecting on the importance of art, he said, "I think there is nothing more important than art."
But he believes art extends far beyond the artwork itself.
"Art is not just art," he said. "Art is the problem of your life."

Pakistan’s business community has expressed confidence in the government’s economic direction and pledged to increase investment and support export growth following a meeting with Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif.
Prominent business leaders, including Arif Habib, Umar Saeed, Jazz CEO Aamir Ibrahim, Shahzad Saleem and Javed Balwani, said the government had responded positively to several proposals raised by the business community during the budget process.
Arif Habib
Speaking after the meeting, Arif Habib said the Prime Minister had invited members of the business community to review the direction of the economy and discuss the measures taken in the federal budget.
He said the business community appreciated the government’s efforts to engage with the private sector and expressed hope that the country would see higher investment and export growth during the current year.
The government had committed to working with the business community as a partner to improve the economy, he added.
Umar Saeed said the government and cabinet had implemented several requests made by the business community during the budget discussions. He said the business community had now given its confidence to the government and was ready to make further investments.
Saeed also praised the coordination between the business community and the federal cabinet, saying such cooperation had not been seen in the past to the same extent.
Jazz CEO Discusses AI Factories in Pakistan
Aamir Ibrahim said the meeting focused heavily on increasing exports, covering both traditional industries and emerging sectors.
He said telecommunications, digital infrastructure and artificial intelligence were among the key areas discussed during the meeting.
Ibrahim said Pakistan should focus on developing AI infrastructure, including data centres and AI factories, to create new opportunities beyond traditional export sectors such as textiles.
He said Pakistan could eventually export digital intelligence and AI-related services alongside its existing exports.
More feedback
Shahzad Saleem described the meeting as productive, saying the Prime Minister listened carefully to the concerns and suggestions presented by business leaders.
He said the Prime Minister took note of the issues discussed and gave directions during the meeting for some of the problems to be resolved.
Saleem also stressed the need for regular meetings between the government and industry to maintain closer coordination and address business concerns.
Javed Balwani appreciated the government’s decision to establish offices of the Federal Board of Revenue (FBR) and Pakistan Revenue Automation Limited (PRAL) in Karachi and Lahore.
He said continued interaction between the Prime Minister and the business community could help resolve issues affecting businesses and support improvements in exports and the overall economy.

items.author: Daily Trust
items.content:
Presidential Candidate of the Nigeria Democratic Congress (NDC), Peter Obi, has called on the Inspector-General of Police and the Director-General of the Department of State Services (DSS) to intervene following the disruption of his planned visit to Yelewata community in Benue State.
Obi arrived in Makurdi on Tuesday morning and was heading for Yelewata in Guma Local Government Area, where he had planned to sympathise with families affected by the June 13, 2025, armed attack and make personal donations to victims.
However, his convoy was stopped by a group of Benue youths along the Makurdi-Gboko Road, less than two kilometres from the airport.
Chanting, “Obi go back, Obi go back”, some of the youths wielding sticks, reportedly threw stones as security personnel deployed to the area watched the confrontation.
Following the incident, Obi and members of his team turned back and returned to the airport. He subsequently left the state without visiting Yelewata.
Speaking before his departure, the former Anambra State governor described the incident as “ridiculous” and “very, very worrisome,” saying he had travelled to Benue to condole with families affected by the killings and offer support to victims.
“We arrived Benue, Makurdi precisely this morning at 9am, on our way to the Yelewata community to condole and show solidarity to the families affected by last year’s killings,” Obi said.
He said he had planned to visit the community as part of his decision to travel across the country, meet Nigerians directly and understand their challenges.
According to him, more than 270 people were killed in the Yelewata attack, prompting him to make the visit as he began his campaign activities.
“Only to arrive Makurdi this morning and trying to drive out, I was blocked by teeming thugs, shouting ‘Obi go back, Obi go back.’ And I was wondering, are we still in Nigeria? Or am I in another country?” he said.
Obi said he decided against forcing his way through the blockade because doing so could have resulted in violence and endangered lives.
“I discontinued because I didn’t want to say we must go on as we have our own teeming crowd, but not wanting to cause confusion and possibly endanger the lives of other people. I decided to remain as civil as possible,” he said.
The NDC candidate subsequently appealed to the nation’s security authorities, particularly the Inspector-General of Police and the DSS Director-General, to intervene and ensure that political activities across the country were conducted peacefully.
“I am using this occasion to appeal to the security agencies, the Inspector-General of Police, IGP, the Director of DSS and other agencies to please intervene and be able to call various state governors to order. This rascality cannot be allowed,” Obi said.
He warned that political violence could escalate if security agencies failed to protect political actors and their supporters.
“We have a country and we too have followers. We have people who can confront these people on our own if the state and the government can no longer provide us security. We cannot go on this way. It is unacceptable,” he said.
Obi urges issue-based 2027 campaign
Obi said the 2027 presidential contest should focus on the problems confronting Nigerians rather than violence, intimidation and political confrontation.
He identified insecurity, kidnapping, hunger, killings and poverty as issues that presidential candidates should address as they seek the support of voters.
“I participated yesterday in the commissioning of the office of the Presidential candidate of APM appealing that we need unity, love, justice, and let this campaign be concentrated on ideas, issues that concern Nigerians today of insecurity, kidnapping, hunger, killing and everything and how we are going to pull our people out of poverty,” he said.
He urged other presidential candidates to travel around the country, interact directly with communities and listen to voters ahead of the 2027 elections.
“Go around Nigeria so you can feel the people, see their faces, ask them questions and they ask you questions about what you want to do for them to be able to ameliorate the suffering Nigerians are going through today,” Obi said.
He also appealed to young people allegedly involved in political violence not to allow themselves to be used by politicians.
“I call on the youths that are being used. The abuse you are allowing them to use you for today will take its revenge on you,” he said.
“We are not coming here fighting anybody because our elections will be run on ideas, on issues. And I urge people to please let’s concentrate on that. Let’s not allow a country to get into anarchy. Anarchy consumes everybody,” he said.
‘Government knew I was here’
Obi said his experience as a former governor made it difficult for him to believe that the incident could have occurred without the knowledge of the state government and security agencies.
“I have been governor myself. I know that this cannot happen without the government and security agencies in this state being fully aware that I am here,” he said.
He recalled that he served as governor of Anambra State for eight years and said he would have intervened had a similar incident occurred under his administration.
Obi also questioned why he should be prevented from moving around Benue during the campaign period.
“This is a campaign period. I did not come here on election day so you cannot say I came disturbing the election,” he said.
He further recalled that he had previously turned back from visiting Benue after the governor reportedly indicated that he did not want to meet him.
“Remember last time I wanted to come, the governor said he did not want to see me. I turned back. But now is the election period where as a presidential candidate I am free to move around because election campaigns have started,” Obi said.
He said his objective was simply to see conditions in the state firsthand and interact with residents.
Reacting to the incident, the Benue State government accused Obi of courting trouble.
Commissioner for Information, Solomon Iorpev, said this while reacting to the disruption of Obi’s convoy during a visit to the state on Tuesday.
Iorpev said Obi ought to have formally notified the state government ahead of his visit, describing the action of the former governor as a breach of protocol.
The commissioner said given his status as a former governor and prominent political figure, the government had a responsibility to make adequate security arrangements for him.
“A high-profile person who has been a former governor of a state is coming into the state; he should have written a letter to the State Government.”
“We are supposed to guarantee his safety and protection, but in an instance where no letter was written, we could not guarantee his safety.
“This is not the first time he is doing this. He is just looking for our trouble. We are peace loving and hospitable people,” he said.
Iorpev said he was not aware of those who blocked the convoy, but added that Obi’s visit coincided with a meeting involving youths from all the 23 Local Government Areas of Benue.
