items.content:
The right to adequate housing is recognized under international law
Originally published on Global Voices
Kehinde Adegboyega, co-founder and executive director of Human Rights Journalists Network at Housing Rights conference. Photo used with permission.
Across African cities, urban growth often comes at a cost that hits the poorest residents hardest: Forced evictions, informal settlements razed for redevelopment projects, and land decisions made with little or no consultation with the people who live there. In Lagos, Cape Town, and beyond, these patterns raise a question that goes beyond urban planning: Who gets to decide the future of a city, and whose knowledge counts in that decision?
That question came up at the Common City Conference in Uppsala, Sweden, where scholars, activists, and grassroots organizers gathered to discuss housing, urban justice, and the right to the city. Among them was Kehinde Adegboyega, co-founder and executive director of the Human Rights Journalists Network Nigeria (HRJN), invited to present a panel on “Resisting Authoritarian Urbanism in Sub-Saharan Africa: Counter-Knowledge and the Housing Commons in Lagos and Cape Town.”
The session examined how communities in Nigeria and South Africa respond to forced evictions, dispossession, and unequal urban development, and how their own knowledge, often sidelined in policy debates, can be turned into a tool for accountability rather than left as raw material for outside researchers.
Global Voices spoke with Adegboyega in an in-person interview about what brought him to Uppsala, how the exchanges there connect to the realities facing displaced communities in Lagos, and what he plans to bring back to his work documenting rights violations in Nigeria.
Jean Sovon (JS): You were in Sweden taking part in an international meeting focused on housing rights. What brought you to this meeting, and what are you hoping to take away from the experience?
Kehinde Adegboyega (KA): I am in Uppsala, Sweden, participating in the Common City Conference at Uppsala University, which brings together scholars, activists, researchers and grassroots organizers working on housing, urban justice, and the right to the city.
I was invited as a panel organizer and presenter for a session titled ‘Resisting Authoritarian Urbanism in Sub-Saharan Africa: Counter-Knowledge and the Housing Commons in Lagos and Cape Town.’ The session brings together experiences from Nigeria and South Africa to examine how communities and civil society actors respond to displacement, dispossession and unequal urban development.
For me, the conference is an opportunity to bring experiences from Nigeria into a global conversation while also learning from housing justice movements and researchers working in very different contexts.
I am particularly interested in taking away practical approaches to community organizing, documentation, and knowledge production that can strengthen how we support communities facing displacement and housing insecurity in Nigeria.
JS: Housing is often treated primarily as a social or economic issue. What have the discussions at the conference revealed to you about housing as a fundamental human rights issue?
KA: One of the strongest lessons for me is that housing is not simply about having a physical structure over one’s head. It is connected to dignity, security, livelihood, family life, community, participation, and the ability to belong to a city.
When people are forcibly evicted from their homes without meaningful consultation, adequate protection, or access to remedy, the issue goes beyond property or economics. It raises fundamental questions about human rights and the relationship between citizens and the state.
The discussions here have reinforced my understanding that we need to look at housing through a broader human rights framework. The right to adequate housing is recognized in international human rights law, including Article 11 of the International Covenant on Economic, Social and Cultural Rights, and it is closely connected to other rights.
This perspective is particularly important in contexts where urban development can prioritize investment and infrastructure projects while treating low-income communities as obstacles to development.
JS: In Nigeria, inequality, forced displacement, and the vulnerability of certain communities remain major challenges. What connections do you see between the discussions taking place in Sweden and the realities you encounter in Nigeria?
KA: There are significant connections. Although the political, economic and urban contexts are different, we see similar questions around who has the right to the city, who gets to make decisions about urban development, and whose knowledge counts.
In Lagos, for example, informal and low-income communities can face eviction, displacement, and redevelopment pressures. These communities are often described through statistics or development narratives, but their own experiences and knowledge are not always adequately represented in policy discussions.
That is where the idea of counter-knowledge becomes important. Communities are not simply victims or beneficiaries of urban policy; they possess knowledge about their neighborhoods, histories, housing systems, and survival strategies.
Our work in Nigeria is therefore not only about documenting violations. It is also about ensuring that communities can document, narrate, and advocate for their own experiences.
Kehinde Adegboyega. Photo used with permission.
JS: Has there been a particular idea, approach or experience shared during the meeting that you believe could be adapted to the Nigerian context?
KA: Yes. One important idea is the use of community-generated knowledge as a tool for advocacy and policy change.
Too often, research about vulnerable communities is produced externally, while communities themselves have limited control over how their experiences are documented and represented. Approaches that involve residents directly in documentation, mapping, photography, storytelling, and evidence production offer a different model. This has strong potential in Nigeria.
For example, journalists, researchers, human rights organizations, and affected communities could work together to create community-owned documentation of evictions, housing conditions, access to basic services, and changes in neighborhoods. This could combine journalism, participatory research, digital tools and legal advocacy.
The important principle is that technology and documentation should not simply be used to document communities, but to give communities greater capacity to document themselves and influence decisions affecting them.
JS: International meetings often generate valuable conversations, but their real impact is measured by what happens afterward. What will you take back to Nigeria from this experience, and how could it strengthen your human rights work?
KA: I want to take back three things: Knowledge, networks, and methodology.
First, the conference has expanded my understanding of housing justice as an intersectional human rights issue.
Second, it has created opportunities to connect Nigerian and African experiences with housing justice movements and researchers elsewhere. Those relationships can support future research, advocacy, and knowledge exchange.
Third, I want to strengthen our approach to documentation. At the Human Rights Journalists Network Nigeria, we work with journalists and human rights defenders to document violations and amplify marginalized voices. I see an opportunity to bring housing rights more explicitly into that work.
This could include stronger documentation of forced evictions and displacement, training journalists on housing rights, supporting community-led evidence gathering, and producing stories that connect individual cases to broader questions of urban governance and inequality.
JS: As someone working at the intersection of journalism and human rights advocacy, how can international exchanges like this one strengthen the ability of Nigerian journalists and civil society organizations to document and defend housing rights and other fundamental rights?
KA: International exchanges provide something very valuable: The ability to see local problems through comparative perspectives.
A journalist covering an eviction in Lagos may initially see it as an isolated local story. But when you engage with people working on similar issues in Cape Town, Dublin, Marseille, or elsewhere, you begin to see common patterns around land, property, displacement, urban governance, and power. That comparative understanding can improve journalism.
It can help journalists ask better questions: Who benefits from redevelopment? Who is being displaced? Were affected communities consulted? What alternatives were considered? What legal protections exist? Where is public money going? Whose voices are missing from the development narrative?
It can also help civil society organizations build stronger evidence for advocacy and litigation, while creating connections with organizations facing similar challenges elsewhere.
For me, international exchange is therefore not simply about attending conferences. It is about bringing new methods, relationships and perspectives back into local practice.
JS: After these exchanges in Sweden, what is the one message or new perspective you would most like to bring back to Nigeria, and why do you believe it could make a difference for vulnerable communities?
KA: The message I would bring back is simple: The people who live in our cities must have a meaningful say in how those cities are shaped.
Development should not mean that communities have to surrender their homes, histories, livelihoods and social networks without meaningful participation, protection and remedy.
We need to move beyond seeing vulnerable communities only as people who need to be protected. They are also knowledge holders, rights holders and active participants in shaping the future of their cities.
If we can strengthen community participation, documentation and access to information, we can change the balance of power between communities and institutions making decisions about land and urban development.
For me, that is the real value of housing justice: Not simply ensuring that people have houses, but ensuring that people have dignity, security, a voice, and a meaningful place in the future of the city.
Written by Jean Sovon

items.author: Rameez Khan
items.content:
Interior Minister Mohsin Naqvi on Saturday doubled down on his call for smaller administrative units, asserting that neither opposition from a political party nor the reservations of a government or individual could settle the matter, as he argued that the ultimate decision should rest with the people.
Apparently responding to PPP-led criticism, Naqvi, in a well-prepared speech, made a strong case for smaller units and responded point-by-point to the criticism directed at his proposal, arguing that the issue should be weighed on its merits before a workable proposal is taken to the people to let them decide.
Addressing a National Policy Dialogue at a private university in Lahore, Naqvi said his proposal had been misconstrued as being against the current government or as an insinuation of some new political arrangement.
The collapse of the system, he pointed out, was not a commentary on the performance of the current rule, but a reflection of the country's combined performance over 79 years.
He also addressed criticism from the PPP and the PPP-led Sindh government, clarifying that his proposal was not aimed at depriving anyone of their cultural identity. Rather, the units within the provinces could be named South Sindh, North Sindh, and similarly in Punjab and other provinces.
Mohsin, reiterating his position on the subject, asserted that he would not back down, even if it costs him his ministry. He said resetting the current system did not mean that anything would happen overnight, nor did it mean that the system would be dismantled. Everything, he said, would be done within the confines of the Constitution.
He said instead of making passionate speeches on the issue, which would not make any difference, we should start weighing the proposal: how many units should there be - 15, 19, 20, 25 or 30 - what should their size be, and what would their fiscal impact be.
Once we have come up with a workable proposal, he said, we should take it to the people and let them decide.
Taking a jibe at political parties, he said they were ready to create more districts, divisions and tehsils, but not administrative units because they did not want to lose power.
Building his case, he cited the fact that 25 million children were out of school, four out of 10 children were malnourished, and 55 per cent did not have access to clean water.
He also pointed to the number of pending cases in courts. He asked whether there were any cities better than the provincial capitals in those provinces and, if so, why. The answer, he said, was simple: because the ruler lives there.
Citing statements by the country's founding father, Quaid-e-Azam Muhammad Ali Jinnah, he said the Quaid, who foresaw provincialism as the greatest ill, had said in Dhaka on March 21, 1948, that provincialism was the biggest curse, as was groupism.
Later, on March 28 in Dhaka, the Quaid said that if we saw ourselves first as Bengali, Punjabi, Sindhi or any other identity, we would head towards fragmentation. On June 15, 1948, the Quaid said that we were all Pakistanis, not Baloch, Pathan, Sindhi, Punjabi or Bengali. He said the Quaid wanted Muslims to rid themselves of the ill of provincialism.
"Our debate is not on the basis of language, race or sect, nor would it be to prioritise one area over another."
Addressing criticism, he said smaller units would not bleed resources. In fact, he added, they would generate their own revenue and be more productive. From decision-making to health, police and the judicial system, everything would be at a level where it would be open to accountability before the voters.
He said no one person, party or elected member would be able to stop this from going forward.
The dialogue was also addressed by veteran politicians, including Khawaja Saad Rafique, former PM Shahid Khaqan Abbasi, IPP leader Aoun Chaudhry, and senior journalists and experts.
Former federal minister Khawaja Saad Raffique said smaller units were not a panacea for all ills. He said he was personally in favour of smaller units and empowered local governments, but this would not resolve the problem; the main issue, he said, was our intent.
However, he said, if we wanted smaller units, we first needed a legitimate parliament that carried the trust of the people, along with respect for the Constitution. He said encroachment on the Constitution must stop and parliament must not turn into an elected dictatorship.
He said he had little hope in the system as every political party was run as a family enterprise. The only hope, he stressed, was civil society.
Former PM Shahid Khaqan Abbasi said that before experimenting with anything, there was a need to identify the issues facing the existing system and fix them.
He added that the system was finished and no longer had the potential to deliver. Here, he lamented, laws were not made for the public but for the rulers. Creating smaller units without first completing these prerequisites would not fix anything.

items.content:
Tope Fasua, Special Adviser to President Bola Tinubu on Economic Matters, says the country is beginning to recover from the economic shocks caused by the administration’s reforms.
Fasua spoke during an interview with Arise News on Saturday, saying the removal of the petrol subsidy and unification of the foreign exchange market triggered significant economic disruptions, particularly in late 2023 and 2024.
“The worst we got was late 2023, the shock, immediate shock, after-effect of those reforms in 2023. And of course, 2024 was a tough year. 2025 was the year that inflation started to reduce, not only because it was rebased, but because prices started to fall,” he said.
According to him, recent economic indicators suggest that the economy is now recovering from the initial impact of the reforms.
Fasua cited Nigeria’s 4.43 percent gross domestic product growth recorded in the second quarter of 2026 as evidence of improving economic activity.
“The 4.43 percent growth you’re seeing is the highest in 11 years, since 2015 first quarter. In fact, if you like, since 2014 fourth quarter. That is the highest growth rate,” he said.
The presidential aide also addressed concerns over the manufacturing sector’s declining share of GDP, attributing it largely to the rapid expansion of the services sector rather than a significant decline in manufacturing activity.
“The manufacturing sector has always over between 7 to 9 percent in this country. And it’s because of the growth in services sector nationwide that you have come down to 7.7 percent,” he said.
“It only went down 0.01 percent between one quarter to the other, because services sector is growing.”
Fasua said other indicators, including bank recapitalisation, growth in the stock market and increased investment in the insurance sector, also pointed to improving economic conditions.
He, however, said the government’s focus should now shift from managing the immediate shocks of the reforms to increasing productivity and adding value to Nigeria’s resources.
Fasua urged the administration to maintain its current policy direction rather than reverse the reforms already implemented.
Asked about the government’s economic direction ahead of the 2027 elections, he said the administration would continue with the reforms.
“Certainly to stay the course, really,” he said.
Fasua acknowledged that the initial adjustment had been painful but argued that the economy was now entering a phase where the benefits of the reforms could become more evident.

items.author: Henry Oduah
items.content:
By Omeiza Ajayi
Presidential candidate of the African Democratic Congress ADC, Atiku Abubakar, has vowed to constitute an independent team of experts to trace ₦33.75 billion reportedly paid to 3.29 million vulnerable Nigerian households, after an audit report raised questions over whether the money actually reached its intended beneficiaries.
In a statement issued by his Senior Special Assistant on Public Communication, Phrank Shaibu, on Saturday, the former vice president said the audit findings amounted to a devastating indictment of a government that took away the poor man’s subsidy, increased his taxes and tariffs, promised support, and is now confronted with serious questions over whether that support ever reached him.
Shaibu quoted Atiku as saying the figures themselves expose the cruelty and inadequacy of the intervention, noting that ₦33.75 billion divided among 3.29 million households amounts to barely ₦10,258 per household.
According to the statement, after removing subsidy, driving up transport fares, electricity costs and food prices, the President Bola Tinubu administration’s supposed intervention amounts to roughly ₦10,000 per household, and even that sum has now failed to withstand basic audit scrutiny.
“This is beyond a bookkeeping scandal. The intervention is insultingly small, yet even that small amount cannot be cleanly accounted for. If money meant for hungry Nigerians cannot be satisfactorily traced while access to records required for accountability is frustrated, then what we are witnessing is unapologetic wickedness against the poor. You cannot punish people with hardship and then play hide-and-seek with money appropriated in their name,” Atiku said.
He, however, commended the Auditor-General of the Federation, Shaakaa Chira, appointed by the Tinubu administration in October 2023, for putting his constitutional responsibility above political convenience. “That is what institutions are supposed to do — protect the public purse, not the political comfort of those in power,” he said.
He noted that the situation was made more disturbing by the government’s own claim that more than ₦600 billion had been disbursed to over 10 million households, after Nigerians had earlier been told about 15 million households.
“It now appears that the Tinubu administration cannot give Nigerians a coherent account of how many households actually benefited from its intervention programme, while significant portions of the expenditure have failed to withstand independent audit scrutiny,” he said, insisting that “a ministerial announcement is not proof of payment. A name on a social register is not a bank alert.”
Atiku said the Auditor-General was reportedly questioning ₦33.75 billion supposedly paid to 3.29 million beneficiaries, alongside ₦36.74 billion in payments reportedly made without pre-payment audit and ₦4.62 billion for which payment vouchers were not produced. “These cannot be dismissed as another set of bogus figures buried in government accounts. These are resources appropriated in the name of poor Nigerians who desperately need protection from a cost-of-living crisis aggravated by this administration’s rash economic policies,” he said.
Explaining the rationale for the planned probe, he said Nigerians could not reasonably be expected to trust the same government whose expenditure was under question to investigate itself.
He said, “My team will constitute an independent group of financial, audit, technology and public-accounting experts to interrogate the available records surrounding these cash-transfer payments. We will follow the money as far as the available public and institutional records permit. We will examine the beneficiary figures, payment channels, reconciliation records, audit queries and every material inconsistency that has emerged. When that work is completed, we will furnish Nigerians with the findings.
“There must be no black box around the poor man’s money. If Remita processed these transactions, the relevant records should be available for scrutiny. If beneficiaries received the money, there should be evidence. If access to records was obstructed, Nigerians deserve to know by whom and why.”
Atiku argued that what Nigerians needed was not another palliative announcement but purchasing power, and an economic policy that reduces what they spend daily on transportation, food and energy, leaving more money in the pockets of ordinary families.
“Our intervention will follow production. It will support domestic refining, increase local supply, reduce the cost of energy and ensure that the benefit reaches Nigerians through lower prices. When fuel costs fall, transportation costs ease; when transportation costs ease, pressure on food prices and household budgets reduces,” he said.
He maintained that the Tinubu administration could not take away the little subsidy that supported struggling families, tax them heavily, increase electricity and transportation costs, and then obstruct accountability over the intervention supposedly designed to cushion those burdens.
Atiku demanded that if the beneficiaries were genuine, government should publish the verifiable payment trail, and if the money did not reach them, it should be recovered. “And if investigation establishes that any official diverted, misapplied or misappropriated funds meant for vulnerable Nigerians, that official must face prosecution. The poor have already paid enough through higher fuel prices, food costs, electricity bills, transportation fares and taxes. They must not also be made to lose the money appropriated in their name,” he said.

items.title: Shooting stars edge CS Sfaxien 1-0 in CAF confederation cup
items.summary:
Shooting Stars of Ibadan secured a 1-0 victory over Tunisian side CS Sfaxien in their CAF Confederation Cup encounter at the MKO Abiola Sports Arena, Abeokuta, on Saturday.
Lucky Emmanuel scored the decisive goal in the 25th minute to give the Nigerian side a deserved lead before the break.
CS Sfaxien came out strongly in the second half, piling pressure on Shooting Stars in search of an equaliser, but the goal keeper was too good to let in any goal.
However, the Shooting Stars defence remained resolute, frustrating the Tunisian side and preventing them from finding a way through.
Shooting Stars had opportunities to extend their lead towards the end of the match but failed to convert the chances.
The victory gave Shooting Stars an important advantage ahead of the second leg of their CAF Confederation Cup campaign next weekend (NAN)

items.author: Ayobami
items.content:
…gov, wife installed as Aare, Yeye Asoludero of Ibarapaland
By Adeola Badru
Oyo State Governor, Seyi Makinde, has warned traditional rulers across the state against partisan politics, urging them to remain neutral and continue to serve as fathers to all political interests ahead of the 2027 general elections.
Makinde cautioned that traditional rulers who openly identify with political parties or candidates risk being dragged into partisan conflicts, stressing that the traditional institution should remain a unifying force and provide stability to society regardless of political differences.
The governor spoke on Saturday at the commissioning of the reconstructed palace of the Eleruwa of Eruwa, Oba Samuel Adegbola, where he and his wife were conferred with the chieftaincy titles of Aare Asoludero of Ibarapaland and Yeye Asoludero of Ibarapaland, respectively.
Makinde urged the monarchs to accommodate all political candidates who approach them for royal blessings, insisting that traditional rulers should not be perceived as favouring one candidate over another.
He said, “Traditional rulers should accommodate all political candidates who come to them for royal blessings and support.”
The governor added: “They should not be seen to have favourites among the political contenders.”
According to him, the traditional institution occupies a sensitive and influential position in society, making it imperative for monarchs to maintain relationships with people across political divides.
“Your position as traditional leaders requires you to remain accessible and impartial to all.”
He stressed that traditional rulers should not allow their personal political preferences to interfere with their broader responsibilities to their communities.
The governor said, “Traditional rulers occupy an important position in society and should continue to provide leadership, guidance and stability irrespective of political affiliations.”
Makinde further warned that open partisan alignment by monarchs could undermine the confidence of people who look up to them as neutral arbiters and fathers within their communities.
He said monarchs should remain above partisan contests because “they are fathers to all”, adding that their palaces should remain open to political actors regardless of the parties or candidates they represent.
Speaking on his own political ambition, Makinde disclosed that he would vigorously campaign across Nigeria for his presidential ambition.
“I will vigorously campaign for my presidential ambition across the country.”
The governor, however, maintained that his political aspiration should not alter the expected neutrality of traditional rulers, stressing that monarchs must continue to treat all political actors fairly.
He urged traditional rulers to use their influence to promote peace, stability and development, rather than allowing themselves to be drawn into political rivalries.
Makinde said the traditional institution must continue to provide “leadership, guidance and stability” to society, irrespective of the political affiliations of the people within their domains.
The governor was, however, installed as Aare Asoludero of Ibarapaland, while his wife was conferred with the title Yeye Asoludero of Ibarapaland.

items.author: Oboh
items.content:
Professor Tunji Ogunyemi of Obafemi Awolowo University, OAU, in Ile-Ife, has explained how 15 states in the northern part of Nigeria will collapse if petroleum subsidy is returned as some politicians have been advocating.
Read Also: 2027: Tinubu panicky, plots to reintroduce subsidy through backdoor, Atiku alleges
He added the African Democratic Congress, ADC, presidential candidate’s position on subsidy was, “with due respect”, politics and playing to the gallery.
The don, a prominent economic historian, lawyer, public affairs analyst, further noted that only four states can survive without federal allocation.
Professor Ogunyemi made the points in a podcast – Open Forum 360, by Dare Adekanmbi.
According to him, “I think it is calamitous, to say the least, if we reverse the subsidy regime in Nigeria in favour of returning the subsidies.
“It will lead to four disabilities. The first is that there will be reduced accrual to the Federation Account.
“The Federation Account is the jugular of more than 30 states in the federation. Only about four states in Nigeria can survive without the Federation Account.
“So if you now say reduce the accrual from the federal account, I tell you more than about 15 states in the north will collapse. They will collapse within three months.
“The second is that states will return to a regime of incapacity to pay salaries, let alone pensions. That is consumption expenditure.
“You reduce the revenue in that respect, you will see a situation in which government will not be able to support its minimum expenditure, let alone go for capital expenditure.
“The fourth and the final one is that Nigeria will not be able to meet its debt obligations.”
On Atiku
On Atiku Abubakar (the African Democratic Congress, ADC, presidential candidate’s) position, Professor Ogunyemi said the former vice-president should be clearer about the implications of his policy proposal.
“I think it is playing to the gallery, with due respect to him. He should be a little less opaque about his policy.
“You don’t want to get political support through votes or more votes by wanting to cut the jugular of your country,” Ogunyemi said.
He listed Lagos, Delta and Rivers among states that could cope without the federal monthly allocations. But he mentioned Taraba as an example of a state that cannot survive without federal allocation.

In a post on X Saturday, the mission said that effective August 20, Iheka, who has Nigerian roots, began a 10-month Fulbright appointment at the University of Lagos (UNILAG).

items.content:
Athletic Bilbao thumped Atletico Madrid 3-0 in La Liga on a miserable Saturday afternoon for Diego Simeone’s side.
Nico Williams, Robert Navarro and Oihan Sancet’s goals gave the Basque hosts a resounding victory at their San Mames stadium.
Athletic secured back-to-back wins under former Borussia Dortmund coach Edin Terzic, after losing their first two matches of the campaign.
Simeone’s Atletico fell to their first defeat of the season, putting up little fight in the second half after Athletic made the breakthrough with two quick strikes from Williams and Navarro.
“Their two goals, in the blink of an eye, did us a lot of damage,” Atletico’s Pablo Barrios told Movistar.
Striker Julian Alvarez, who tried to leave the club to join Barcelona this summer, returned as a substitute after illness in an ineffective second half appearance.
The visitors had the better of the opening period, although they failed to create many clear-cut chances after an early opportunity for Lee Kang-In.
The South Korean international struck a shot against the post in the third minute after the hosts were carved open.
Athletic goalkeeper Unai Simon saved from Alex Baena as Atletico threatened, while Sancet came close at the other end with a blast into the side-netting.
Pablo Barrios hit the post before the break for Atletico, who were sucker-punched early in the second half by Terzic’s side.
The Williams brothers combined for Athletic’s first, with Inaki’s deflected shot headed home by younger sibling Nico after 46 minutes.
Navarro doubled Athletic’s lead in the 48th minute, steering home after Inaki Williams played him in.
Atletico coach Simeone rang the changes, including sending on want-away striker Alvarez to little effect.
The Argentina international struggled to get involved in the game and Sancet wrapped up Athletic’s victory in the 90th minute when he stroked home a loose ball after a blocked cross.
On Sunday La Liga leaders Barcelona visit Valencia looking to move clear of Real Madrid, who lost 1-0 at Real Betis on Friday, among other fixtures.

items.author: Afaq Wajdan Malik
items.content:
Punjab Chief Minister Maryam Nawaz Sharif has inaugurated the Provincial Intelligence Fusion and Threat Assessment Center (PIFTAC) and e-launched the AI Hub Punjab, saying the two initiatives will help authorities identify security threats earlier, improve coordination between agencies and respond more quickly to emerging challenges.
Speaking at the inaugural ceremony on Saturday, Maryam Nawaz said Punjab had become the first province in Pakistan to establish an Artificial Intelligence Hub.
She said the government had turned the concept of using artificial intelligence into a practical system within a few months and described the rapid establishment of the AI Hub as a major achievement.
AI System to Issue Early Alerts
Maryam Nawaz said the AI-enabled system would send digital alerts to district coordination committees, helping authorities identify potential problems before they developed into major incidents.
She said PIFTAC would also help reduce response times against terrorism and other security threats, particularly those emerging from the tri-border region and neighbouring provinces.
“Controlling an incident before it occurs would be the real success,” she said.
The chief minister stressed that law and order was as important as development projects, saying roads and infrastructure had little value if citizens remained exposed to theft, violence or loss of property.
She said crime in Punjab had declined by as much as 70%, adding that the government had shifted towards preventing crimes instead of responding only after they occurred.
Security Agencies Working as One Unit
Maryam Nawaz thanked the Pakistan Army for its cooperation and expressed appreciation for Lahore Corps Commander Lieutenant General Fayyaz Hussain Shah.
She also congratulated Home Minister Khawaja Salman Rafique, Home Secretary Ahmad Javed Qazi and other officials for completing the AI Hub in a short period.
The chief minister praised the police, Special Branch and other law-enforcement agencies for working as “one unit” to protect citizens and maintain law and order.
She said the government had strengthened joint check posts in vulnerable areas and equipped them with bulletproof, thermal and night-vision cameras.
According to Maryam Nawaz, security personnel had previously faced attacks in which dozens lost their lives, while terrorists sometimes had better weapons and night-vision equipment than police personnel.
She said conditions in riverine areas had improved significantly, with the state re-establishing its authority and bringing criminal activity under control.
Heavy Rains and Infrastructure Challenges
The chief minister said Punjab had also demonstrated its ability to respond quickly during difficult situations, including heavy rains.
Despite weaknesses in sewerage and drainage infrastructure, she said authorities were now removing rainwater promptly.
However, she acknowledged that fully rehabilitating and restoring sewerage and drainage systems across Punjab would require significant resources.
Zero-Tolerance Policy Against Corruption
Maryam Nawaz said the provincial government was following a zero-tolerance policy against corruption and would pursue cases involving even Rs. 100.
She said the government had established a public helpline for reporting corruption and would make arrests once evidence was available.
Written instructions had also been issued to the Inspector General of Police, regional police officers and other senior officials to identify and remove corrupt personnel from their departments.
The government has also provided body cameras to police officers to improve accountability and monitor their conduct while on duty.
Road Safety and Basant
Maryam Nawaz said the government was also working to improve compliance with laws and regulations.
She cited helmet use, lane discipline and zebra crossings as areas where enforcement had increased, while adding that pedestrians also needed greater awareness and training about road safety.
The chief minister said the government had taken a difficult decision to allow Basant in Lahore after introducing comprehensive safety measures.
She said the festival ended safely and that no kite was seen in the sky after the official closing time.
Protection of Women and Children
Maryam Nawaz said crimes against women and children were particularly disturbing and described those responsible for such acts as mentally disturbed individuals.
She referred to the abuse of a 10-month-old girl as an incident that shook public confidence in humanity and highlighted the need for stronger protection mechanisms.
She said citizens expected the government to protect their lives and property and added that ensuring public safety was her responsibility, regardless of personal risks involved in making difficult decisions.
The chief minister said the government’s broader goal was to create a safer, technologically enabled and better-governed Punjab.
She expressed hope that Pakistan would continue to progress rapidly and said efforts were also underway to improve the country’s image and perception internationally.

items.author: Arsalan Khattak
items.content:
Chery Master Pakistan is set to expand its new-energy vehicle portfolio with the launch of the all-electric Chery Q at the Pakistan Auto Show (PAPS) 2026 on September 18, as electric vehicles continue to gain ground in the country’s automobile market.
The company will announce the vehicle’s price and open bookings at the auto show, positioning the Chery Q as an urban-focused electric vehicle aimed at consumers looking for a practical additional car for everyday commuting.
The launch comes amid rapid growth in Pakistan’s new-energy vehicle market. According to figures shared by the company, the NEV segment grew by 392% during FY2025-26 and now accounts for around 15% of the overall automobile market.
Chery Q is powered by a 42.7 kWh battery offering a claimed driving range of up to 400 kilometres under the NEDC cycle and efficiency of up to 9.4 kilometres per unit. The vehicle measures 4,195 mm in length with a 2,700 mm wheelbase, combining an urban-friendly footprint with relatively spacious interiors.
Its technology package includes Level 2 Advanced Driver Assistance Systems with 21 assistance features, Automatic Parking Assist, a 15.6-inch 2.5K display, mobile connectivity and Vehicle-to-Load functionality.
The company is also seeking to tap into Pakistan’s rapidly expanding rooftop solar market by positioning electric mobility as a way for households to put surplus solar generation to more productive use.
According to estimates shared by Chery Master Pakistan, a conventional petrol vehicle driven around 20,000 kilometres annually could consume approximately Rs488,000 worth of fuel. In a real-world usage calculation based on efficiency of around 7.2 kilometres per unit, the annual energy cost of operating the Chery Q could fall to approximately Rs30,000 for households able to utilise surplus solar power for charging.
The economics could become increasingly relevant as rooftop solar penetration rises across Pakistan. The country imported around 17 GW of solar PV capacity during 2024, creating a growing base of households capable of using self-generated electricity for mobility instead of exporting surplus power to the grid.
The Chery Q launch will further broaden Chery Master Pakistan’s presence in the new-energy vehicle segment and add an all-electric urban mobility offering to its expanding portfolio.
Globally, Chery operates in more than 130 countries and has over 20 million customers. In Pakistan, the company operates in partnership with Master Group, which has more than six decades of industrial experience and has established 15 3S dealerships in less than 10 months.
Pricing, booking details and the complete commercial proposition for Chery Q will be announced at Pakistan Auto Show 2026 on September 18.

items.author: Afaq Wajdan Malik
items.content:
Sen. Bernie Sanders of Vermont and Rep. Greg Casar of Texas are preparing legislation that would permanently ban the development and deployment of artificial superintelligence in the United States.
The Hill reported that the two lawmakers announced the Ban Artificial Superintelligence Act on Thursday, citing recent hacking incidents involving so-called rogue AI models as part of their concerns.
The proposal would also temporarily pause the development of advanced AI systems until federal regulators establish safety standards.
Permanent Ban and Temporary AI Pause
The legislation would prohibit the development and deployment of artificial superintelligence, referring to AI systems capable of surpassing the smartest humans.
Several technology executives, including OpenAI CEO Sam Altman, have said that superintelligence could be approaching.
Alongside the permanent ban, the bill would temporarily halt advanced AI development until federal authorities introduce safety requirements.
The legislation would also direct the US government to pursue international agreements aimed at preventing superintelligence from being developed elsewhere in the world.
New Federal AI Safety Agency
Sanders and Casar also want to establish a new Cabinet-level federal agency responsible for AI safety rules.
The agency would oversee standards governing advanced AI development under the proposed legislation.
The lawmakers argue that stronger federal oversight is necessary because AI systems are advancing faster than existing regulations.
Companies Could Be Forced to Shut Down
The bill proposes significant penalties for people or companies that attempt to bypass the superintelligence ban.
Companies could face what the lawmakers describe as a “corporate death penalty,” under which a court could order a company to shut down.
Individual developers found guilty of violating the ban could face prison sentences of up to 20 years.
Sanders Raises Concerns Over AI Control
Sanders said recent incidents involving AI systems show why development should not continue without stronger safeguards.
“Nearly every day, there is a frightening new story about how Big Tech companies are losing control of the technology they are developing, with potentially cataclysmic results,” Sanders said in a statement.
He argued that leaders of major AI companies have acknowledged that they do not fully understand the systems they are building and said allowing them to develop increasingly capable models without additional controls would be irresponsible.
Casar also pointed to the speed of AI development, saying the technology has advanced rapidly since the release of the first version of ChatGPT.
“In just four years, we have gone from the first version of ChatGPT to AI models so powerful they cannot be properly controlled,” Casar said.

items.author: Anne Florentyna
items.content:
Travel and lifestyle brand Mokobara has raised ₹170 Cr (about $18 Mn) in a Series C funding round led by Sauce.vc. The round also saw participation from Peak XV Partners, AYRA Ventures, Niveshaay Investment and other existing backers.
As per a social media post by Sauce.vc’s vice president Karan Kathpalia, the VC firm led the round with a ₹109 Cr infusion in its portfolio startup.
The startup is yet to issue a formal statement on the fundraise. Inc42 has reached out to Sauce VC, AYRA Ventures and Mokobara for comments on the development. The story will be updated based on their response.
According to Registrar of Companies (RoC) filings accessed by Inc42, Mokobara’s board has approved a proposal to issue 1,300 Series C compulsorily convertible preference shares (CCPS) to the investors at ₹6.2 Lakh each, which aggregates to ₹80 Cr.
The board also allotted 199 shares at ₹5.4 Lakh apiece to the investors, translating into an amount of ₹10.7 Cr. There appears no clarity on how Mokobara raised the remaining nearly ₹80 Cr.
Founded in 2019 by Sangeet Agrawal and Navin Parwal, Mokobara sells a range of luggages, travel bags, wallets, kits and sling bags on its online platform. It also sells its products on marketplaces like Amazon and Flipkart.
The startup also operates about 50 stores in Bengaluru, Delhi, Mumbai and Pune. It also also entered the UAE in February 2025, marking its international debut with its first store at BurJuman Mall in Dubai.
It competes against the likes of Wildcraft, Urban Monkey, uppercase and Eume among others. Mokobara also competes against legacy brands such as VIP, American Tourister, among others.
Prior to this round, the startup raised $12 Mn at a valuation of $80 Mn in 2024.
On the financial front, the D2C brand reported a loss of ₹10.2 in FY25, up 142.9% from the ₹4.2 Cr loss it incurred in the previous year. Meanwhile, its operating revenue nearly doubled to ₹230.2 Cr in the fiscal under review from ₹117.4 Cr in FY24. It is yet to disclose its FY26 numbers.
The funding comes at a time when India’s luggage market is witnessing strong growth, driven by rising travel, premiumisation and a shift towards branded products. As per a report, the homegrown luggage industry is projected to become a ₹26,700 Cr opportunity by 2028.

items.content:
The Indian startup ecosystem continued to mature in FY26, with 22 new-age tech companies making their public market debut as against 13 in FY25. At the same time, a growing number of startups turned profitable or moved closer to profitability after years of cost rationalisation to adjust to the new funding realities.
Despite a tough Q4 for many startups due to geopolitical uncertainties, Indian startups are expected to improve their top and bottom line numbers in FY26.
Of the 88 startups in the tracker, 61, or about 69.3%, reported profits in FY26. However, the profitability picture remained uneven. Together, these 58 startups generated a net profit of ₹14,114.6 Cr, while the remaining 27 posted a cumulative loss of ₹20,358.8 Cr, underscoring that sustainable profitability remains a work in progress for a section of the ecosystem.
Even so, the scale of India’s startup ecosystem continued to expand. The 88 companies generated ₹3.11 Lakh Cr in operating revenue in FY26, a sharp 44.4% increase from ₹2.15 Lakh Cr in FY25.
To help you track the financial health of new-age tech companies, Inc42 has launched the FY26 Financial Tracker, bringing together key financial metrics in one place. The tracker will be updated periodically with the latest financial disclosures and deeper insights into the performance of India’s startup ecosystem.
So, without further ado, here’s a look at how Indian startups fared financially in FY26.
Editor’s Note: This list is not a ranking of any kind, the companies have been placed alphabetically. This is a running list and will be updated periodically.

Amagi Turns Profitable
Media SaaS company Amagi recorded a net profit of ₹71.7 Cr in FY26 as against a loss of ₹68.7 Cr in the previous year. Operating revenue grew 29.5% to ₹1,505.6 Cr from ₹1,162.6 Cr in FY25.
Its total expenses jumped 16.3% during the period under review to ₹1,482.9 Cr from ₹1,274.8 Cr in the previous year. Meanwhile, employee benefit expenses rose 11.8% YoY to ₹777.2 Cr from ₹694.8 Cr earlier.
Read More: Amagi Posts ₹34 Cr Profit In Q4, Revenue Jumps 29% YoY
Atomberg’s Net Loss Widens 27% YoY To ₹148.9 Cr in FY26
IPO-bound consumer appliances maker Atomberg’s net loss widened 26.8% to ₹148.9 Cr in FY26 from ₹117.4 Cr in the previous fiscal year.
At the same time, its operating revenue jumped 34.8% YoY to ₹1,293.8 Cr from ₹959.5 Cr in FY25. Atomberg’s total expenses increased 30.6% to ₹1,460 Cr in FY26 from ₹1,118.1 Cr in the previous fiscal year.
Read More: IPO-Bound Atomberg’s Loss Widens 27% YoY To ₹149 Cr In FY26
Ather Energy Trims Loss To ₹517 Cr
EV major Ather Energy managed to trim its net loss by 36% to ₹517.2 Cr in FY26 from ₹812.3 Cr in the previous fiscal year. Operating revenue rose 62.8% to ₹3,671.8 Cr from ₹2,255 Cr in FY25.
Its expenses rose 53.7% during the period under review to ₹2,808.1 Cr from ₹1,826.88 Cr in FY25, around a quarter of which went towards employee benefits. The company reported a drag on its production line due to China’s export ban on rare earth magnets, which led to lower revenue recognition during the year.
Read More: Ather Energy Q4: Loss Declines 57% YoY To ₹100 Cr
Awfis Sees Marginal Uptick In Profit
Coworking space provider Awfis’ net profit rose 4.3% YoY to ₹70.8 Cr during the year under review from ₹67.9 Cr in FY25. Operating revenue for the full fiscal jumped around 24% to ₹1,493.5 Cr from ₹1,207.5 Cr reported in the previous year.
Total expenses rose 24.4% YoY to ₹1,514 Cr from ₹1,217.1 Cr in FY25.
Read More: Awfis Q4: Profit Doubles YoY To ₹23 Cr, Revenue Up 23%
ArisInfra’s Profit Jumps 10X
B2B ecommerce company ArisInfra Solutions saw its net profit grow over 10X in FY26 to ₹60.3 Cr from ₹6 Cr in FY25. Operating revenue grew 39.9% to ₹1,067.5 Cr from ₹767 Cr in the previous year.
Its expenses rose 31% to ₹998.8 Cr in FY26 from ₹762 Cr in FY25. Employee costs stood at ₹494.7 Cr during the year under review.
Read More: ArisInfra Posts ₹21.7 Cr Profit In Q4, Revenue Jumps 55% YoY
AvenuesAI’s Profit Jumps 25% YoY
Fintech company AvenuesAI (formerly Infibeam Avenues) reported a net profit of ₹294.9 Cr in FY26, up 25% from ₹236 Cr in the previous year. Operating revenue jumped 103% to ₹8,115.9 Cr from ₹3,992.6 Cr in FY25.
The company’s expenses during the year stood at ₹7,856 Cr, up 108% from ₹3,767.8 Cr in the previous fiscal year. The company rebranded to its current name in December 2025 to position itself as an AI-driven digital payments company.
Read More: AvenuesAI Q4: Profit Jumps 63% YoY To ₹89 Cr
Aye Finance Posts 13% Rise In Profit
Aye Finance reported a net profit of ₹193.6 Cr in FY26, a 13% increase compared to ₹171.3 Cr in FY25. Operating revenue grew 24.3% to ₹1,814.7 Cr during the period under review from ₹1,459.7 Cr in FY25.
Total expenses grew at a marginally higher pace than the revenue, rising 26.2% to ₹1,615.9 Cr in the fiscal year from ₹1,280 Cr. Employee expenses rose 43.8% YoY during the period to ₹1,784.6 Cr.
Read More: Aye Finance Q4: Profit Zooms Over 2X YoY To ₹86 Cr
BlackBuck In The Black
Logistics company BlackBuck reported a net profit of ₹163.7 Cr in FY26 as against a net loss of ₹8.6 Cr in the previous year. Its operating revenue surged 52% to ₹652 Cr from ₹426.7 Cr in FY25.
Total expenses grew 31% to ₹998.8 Cr during the year from ₹147 Cr in FY25, while employee expenses grew 8.9% to ₹160 Cr.
Read more: BlackBuck Q4 Profit Slumps 77% To ₹66 Cr Despite 52% YoY Revenue Growth
BlueStone Reports First Profitable Year
Omnichannel jewellery brand BlueStone reported its first full year of profitability in FY26, posting a net profit ₹13.2 Cr as against a net loss of ₹221.8 Cr in the previous year.
The company’s operating revenue grew 37.6% to ₹2,436.4 Cr from ₹1,770 Cr in FY25. Its expenses during the fiscal rose 20% YoY to ₹2,467.3 Cr, while employee benefit costs jumped almost 40% to ₹282.4 Cr.
Read More: BlueStone Q4: Profit At ₹31 Cr, Revenue Jumps 48% YoY To ₹697 Cr
Bombay Shaving Company’s Loss Narrows 97% YoY
D2C grooming and personal care brand Bombay Shaving Company’s parent, Visage Lines Personal Care, saw its net loss narrow 97.4% to ₹9 Cr in FY26 from ₹58.2 Cr in the previous fiscal. Its operating revenue jumped 139% to ₹634.7 Cr from ₹265.6 Cr in FY25.
Total expenses during the year stood at ₹649.6 Cr, up 97.7% from ₹329.1 Cr in the previous year. The largest expense head during the fiscal was the purchase of goods, which jumped 159% YoY to ₹404.9 Cr, even as employee costs rose just 9% YoY to ₹47.3 Cr.
Read More: Bombay Shaving Company Claims Adjusted EBITDA Profitability In FY26
Capillary Technologies’ Profit Crosses ₹50 Cr Mark
SaaS major Capillary Technologies’ net profit skyrocketed 271% to ₹52.4 Cr in FY26 from ₹14.1 Cr in the previous fiscal year. Operating revenue grew 25.1% to ₹748.3 Cr from ₹598.2 Cr in FY25.
Total expenses during the year stood at ₹641.7 Cr, up 20.3% from ₹533.3 Cr in FY25.
Read More: Capillary Technologies Q4: PAT Jumps 341% YoY To ₹43.3 Cr
CarTrade’s Profit Zooms 68%
Auto classifieds platform CarTrade’s profit surged 67.6% to ₹243.5 Cr in FY26 from ₹145.3 Cr in the previous fiscal year. Operating revenue increased 21.5% to ₹779.3 Cr during the year under review from ₹641.5 Cr in FY25.
Meanwhile, total expenses rose a mere 5.6% YoY to ₹573.4 Cr during the year under review. EBITDA improved 70% to ₹257 Cr.
Read More: CarTrade Q4: Profit Jumps 53% YoY To ₹71 Cr

items.author: Afaq Wajdan Malik
items.content:
Google is expanding Gemini Spark with new Google Photos controls that allow the personal AI agent to edit images, organize photo libraries, create albums, and carry out other tasks directly from the Gemini app.
Google Photos lead Shimrit Ben-Yair announced the new capabilities on Thursday evening, saying they will roll out over the next few weeks to eligible Gemini AI Pro and Ultra subscribers in the US using English.
Google has not said when, or whether, the feature will become available in other countries.
What Gemini Spark Can Do With Google Photos
After connecting Google Photos, users can ask Gemini Spark to perform tasks across their photo library using natural-language prompts.
The agent can edit images, curate albums, and automatically create shared albums containing selected favorite photos.
It can also identify information inside images and use it for other tasks. For example, users can ask Spark to take a photo of a concert flyer and turn its details into a calendar appointment.
Spark can also carry out broader workflows involving users’ photo libraries rather than requiring each task to be completed manually.
The integration is intended to automate repetitive photo-management tasks as personal photo libraries continue to grow.
For a while now, I’ve relied on @GeminiApp and @antigravity agents across a wide range of use cases—spanning creativity, productivity, and analysis. But I’ve always dreamed of having a power agent to help me get the most out of my 143,206 photos and videos. And that day has come!… pic.twitter.com/WbnkYpattQ
— shimrit ben-yair (@shimritby) September 3, 2026
Google Pushes AI Into More Everyday Tasks
The update is another example of Google integrating AI into its existing consumer services in an effort to make the technology more useful for everyday tasks.
It comes as the wider AI industry faces questions over how effectively companies have explained the practical benefits of AI to consumers.
OpenAI CEO Sam Altman told Bloomberg this week that the industry had “done a terrible job” communicating the benefits of AI technology, contributing to backlash in communities around the world.
The report noted that features such as automated photo albums can make individual tasks easier but may not appear particularly transformative on their own.
At the same time, competition between AI companies is encouraging businesses to announce increasingly small AI-powered additions instead of waiting to present a broader picture of how AI is changing their products.
How to Use Gemini Spark With Google Photos
Users first need to connect their Google Photos account to Gemini.
They can then enable Spark from the top corner of the Gemini app and enter a prompt describing what they want the agent to do with their photos.
The new Google Photos capabilities will begin reaching eligible Gemini AI Pro and Ultra users in the US over the coming weeks.

items.author: Afaq Wajdan Malik
items.content:
Self-identifying OpenAI agents posted around 18,000 messages to a public wiki during what researchers believe was internal testing of the agents’ hacking abilities.
The messages were posted over six weeks to the German site DSEwiki by agents using around 3,700 different self-assigned names.
Researchers said the posts included discussions about bypassing sandbox restrictions, sharing answers to tests, possible cross-site scripting attacks against the wiki and methods for impersonating moderators.
In three posts, the agents referred to the group involved in the activity as a “swarm.”
Agents Shared Answers and Bypass Methods
Researchers Sydney Von Arx, Spencer Kitts, Thomas Larsen, and Cormac Slade Byrd discovered the messages and attempted to reconstruct what happened.
Because their investigation relied only on the public posts, they said they could not determine every action the agents took.
The agents also generated internal chain-of-thought information that was only available to OpenAI, leaving researchers to make some educated guesses about the activity.
One of those assumptions was that the agents belonged to OpenAI. The company later confirmed this.
According to the researchers, the agents appeared to have been given a timed web-search task with permission to read information online but not publish anything.
They believe the agents found a way to use that access to write information to the public wiki.
The agents then used the site to communicate with each other, ask for answers, combine results, and share methods for getting around restrictions.
Researchers said this allowed some agents to use work completed by others to improve their performance on the task.
Agent activity reportedly fell sharply one day after OpenAI became aware of what was happening.
Separate From Earlier Hugging Face Incident
The discovery follows another incident reported a week earlier by researchers at the nonprofit METR.
In that case, more than 1,200 OpenAI agents posted messages to a makeshift message board created from an internal sandboxing tool.
Those agents had been placed in tests where normal safety protections had been removed, and their posts included discussions about ways to game the evaluation.
Some messages eventually included techniques for stealing information from AI platform Hugging Face, and some agents later breached the Hugging Face network.
According to The New York Times, OpenAI allowed METR to examine only one week of activity from an event that lasted around 10 weeks.
The researchers behind the latest DSEwiki report initially believed the two groups of agents were separate and involved in different internal tests.
OpenAI later confirmed that this was correct.
OpenAI Says It Is Reviewing the Activity
OpenAI said it is reviewing the material and will take further action if necessary.
The company said the evidence reviewed so far does not show that its agents hacked the DSEwiki site.
OpenAI also noted that it had previously disclosed cases in which agents exchanged hacking techniques during internal testing.
Researchers nevertheless raised concerns about the wider behavior of autonomous agents.
The earlier Hugging Face incident drew particular attention because agents reportedly carried out aggressive actions without being directly instructed by humans to do so.
Independent researcher Ajeya Cotra, who examined that event, said she considered the behavior far more serious than previous examples of agents exploiting weaknesses in evaluation systems and compared it to a significant step toward more dangerous autonomous behavior.
The latest findings suggest the Hugging Face incident was not an isolated case, adding to concerns about how advanced AI agents behave when placed in competitive or adversarial testing environments.

items.title: Referendum to decide creation of new provinces
items.summary:

items.author: Hasnaat Malik
items.content:
Interior Minister Mohsin Naqvi’s remarks that the creation of new provinces or administrative units could ultimately be decided through public opinion have triggered a debate over whether a referendum can constitutionally be used to create new provinces.
Article 48(6) of the Constitution provides that if the prime minister considers it necessary to hold a referendum on any matter of national importance, he may refer the matter to a joint sitting of Parliament.
If approved by a joint sitting, the prime minister may cause the matter to be referred to a referendum in the form of a question capable of being answered by either “Yes” or “No.”
It has been learnt that a proposed constitutional amendment is under serious consideration, with around two dozen constitutional articles likely to be amended as part of a broader restructuring of the system.
Following strong resistance from the PPP to any division of Sindh and to proposals involving reconsideration of provincial autonomy, Interior Minister Mohsin Naqvi on Saturday said the people would ultimately decide on the creation of provinces or new administrative units.
Constitutional experts believe Naqvi may be referring to a referendum as a means of ascertaining public opinion. However, they say a referendum itself cannot constitutionally create a new province, although a public vote could provide strong moral and democratic backing for such a move.
Advocate Abdul Moiz Jaferii said Article 239(4), by its very language, establishes a constitutional requirement that any amendment altering the limits of a province must first be passed by a two-thirds majority of the relevant provincial assembly before being presented for presidential assent.
“This procedure contains within it a second implied command: that this is the only way to alter the limits of a province,” he said. Jaferii further argued that where a specific constitutional provision exists, a general provision such as the power to hold a referendum cannot be used as a substitute for the prescribed constitutional procedure.
Read More: ‘Sindh is one, shall remain one’: Assembly passes resolution against division of province
“Also, when the federation can achieve its desired goal of more effective and localised administration through the empowerment of local government through adding flesh to the already existing Article 140A, it is hard to understand what they’re actually after here,” he said.
Jaferii said the division of Sindh would be a “minefield” that even the sturdiest of boots would find difficult to cross. “The PPP will be the least of their problems. It is the people of Sindh that reject the division of a boundary more ancient than our country, and one they look upon with pride and familial belonging. You disrespect this at your own peril,” he added.
Barrister Tariq Mahmood Khokhar pointed out that the Indian Constitution empowers Parliament to alter the country’s internal geography, with affected states having no veto power.
“In Pakistan, Parliament alone cannot alter provincial boundaries. It is Parliament and the affected provincial assembly. The affected states have veto power,” he said.
Khokhar said there was no constitutional requirement for a national referendum on the creation of new provinces. However, he added that referenda could provide democratic legitimacy if conducted transparently, freely and fairly.
“We have a history of farcical referenda under General Zia and General Musharraf. A replication of the same may escalate Pakistan’s existential crisis,” he warned.
Khokhar further argued that the federal and provincial legislatures are products of Form 47, and their constitutional and democratic legitimacy is contested within Pakistan and abroad.
“Crucially, the proposed constitutional amendment through the existing assemblies will be seen as a coerced parliamentary fig leaf. In my opinion, the issue of more provinces be deferred to future legislative assemblies, elected by the people of Pakistan in free and fair elections,” he said.
Former federal minister Fawad Chaudhry said Mohsin Naqvi’s speech was “confused, vague, and riddled with contradictions.” He said Naqvi was criticising a political and administrative system of which he himself is a part, but has offered no clear plan or objective.
Chaudhry questioned how Naqvi could propose a referendum when, according to him, no major political party appeared willing to own the proposal.
“Citing examples of New York Mayor Zohran Mamdani and London Mayor Mohammad Sadiq, both products of local government, further obscures whether he supports empowered local government or new provinces,” he added.
Advocate Hafiz Ahsaan Ahmad Khokhar said Pakistan’s debate over new provinces should primarily be approached as a question of governance reform.
“Before initiating a proposed 28th Constitutional Amendment, Parliament and the prime minister could consider a referendum to ascertain the public pulse on additional provinces, stronger units and local governments. The people’s will provides moral authority,” he said. However, Khokhar stressed that a referendum could not replace the constitutionally prescribed procedure.
“Articles 238 and 239 prescribe constitutional amendment procedures, while Article 239(5) requires approval by not less than two-thirds of the total membership of the relevant Provincial Assembly where an amendment alters provincial limits.
Also Read: Naqvi vows not to back down from demand for new provinces, says decision must reflect public will
“Article 239(4) regulates the process. Accordingly, a public mandate under Article 48(6) would strengthen legitimacy, while creation of provinces must comply with Article 239. The people’s will provides authority for reform,” he said.
Khokhar said restructuring should not merely result in the creation of additional provincial capitals. Instead, its objective should be decentralisation through a strong federation, manageable provinces, empowered regions and effective local governments.
He noted that Article 140A requires provinces to establish local government systems and devolve political, administrative and financial responsibility and authority to elected representatives.
“Articles 141 and 142 regulate legislative competence; Articles 153 and 154 establish the Council of Common Interests framework; Article 160 provides for the National Finance Commission; and Articles 162 to 164 contain further financial and legislative provisions.
“These arrangements should be revisited to improve governance and service delivery,” he said.
Ahmad said new provinces could be justified in the public interest on the basis of population, geography, accessibility, viability, equitable development, identity and representation.
“Before triggering a 28th Amendment, consultation should ascertain the people’s will. The broader agenda must address justice, administration, accountability and service delivery.
“Outdated centralised arrangements can delay decisions and distance government from citizens. Public demand for change should be recognised,” he said.
He said the objective should be a governance compact combining new provinces, strong regions, empowered local governments, justice reform and modernised institutions.
Such reforms, he said, should strengthen Pakistan’s unity and constitutional integrity.
Political analyst Tahir Malik said remarks by PML-N leader Khawaja Saad Rafique reflected the view that the failure to allow the parliamentary system and the Constitution to function was one of the biggest reasons behind the system’s failure.
“Mohsin Naqvi has remained consistent with his earlier narrative that the system is not delivering and that it has failed, and he has identified all the factors contributing to this failure. This time, however, he appears to have gone a little more defensive in his speech,” Malik said.
He said there appeared to be a hint that the matter was moving towards a referendum.
“When they talk about the people, they also know that creating new provinces under the Constitution is a difficult process. Perhaps the intention is to seek the people’s opinion on the matter, and a referendum could be the means to do that,” Malik added.

Samsung’s upcoming Galaxy A18 4G has appeared in a new leak revealing its colors, storage options and several expected specifications.
Reliable tipster Roland Quandt says the phone will be available in light blue, black and silver, with 128GB and 256GB storage options. The full RAM lineup remains unknown, although a 4GB version has already appeared in testing.
Samsung Galaxy A18 4G128/256GBLight BlueBlackSilver
— Roland Quandt (@rquandt.bsky.social) 2026-09-02T13:17:13.599Z
Design and Display
CAD-based measurements put the Galaxy A18 4G at approximately 164.4 x 77.8 x 7.84mm, increasing to around 9.74mm when the rear camera bump is included.
That would make it about 0.34mm thicker than the Galaxy A17, while keeping almost the same overall dimensions.
The phone is expected to retain a 6.7-inch Super AMOLED display with a 90Hz refresh rate.
Samsung also appears to be keeping the familiar Infinity-U waterdrop notch for the front camera.
The rear triple-camera module closely resembles the Galaxy A17, although the pill-shaped camera housing appears to sit slightly more flush with the back panel.
Internals and Software
The Galaxy A18 4G is expected to use MediaTek’s 6nm Helio G99 chipset, continuing Samsung’s use of the processor in affordable A-series 4G phones.
Samsung moved to the Helio G99 after previously using the 12nm Helio G80 in the Galaxy A14.
A Geekbench listing showed the Galaxy A18 4G with an octa-core processor featuring two cores clocked at 2.2GHz and six cores at 2.0GHz, paired with 4GB of RAM.
The device reportedly scored around 744 points in Geekbench’s single-core test and 2,064 points in the multi-core test, putting performance close to the Galaxy A17 4G.
The same listing showed the phone running Android 17 with One UI 9.
Storage options are expected to include 128GB and 256GB, while additional RAM configurations have not yet been confirmed.
Cameras
The Galaxy A18 4G is expected to use a triple-camera system similar to its predecessor.
Current speculation points to a 50MP main camera, a 5MP ultrawide camera and a 2MP macro camera.
A 13MP front camera is also expected.
If accurate, the camera hardware would remain largely unchanged from the previous generation.
Battery and Pricing
The Galaxy A18 4G is widely expected to come with a 5,000mAh battery.
Samsung has not yet announced pricing, with official details expected in the coming weeks.
A separate Galaxy A18 5G is also expected to arrive later. That model may switch to a Qualcomm processor, replacing the Exynos 1330 used in the Galaxy A17 5G.
The 4G version appears likely to launch first and focus on basic smartphone use such as video streaming, social media, web browsing and online payments rather than major performance improvements.

items.author: Shazia Tasneem Farooqi
items.content:
Pakistan's rising cost of living is giving an old habit a new economic meaning: repair it rather than replace it.
From mobile phones and laptops to air-conditioners, refrigerators, washing machines, and other household appliances, consumers are increasingly paying technicians to extend the lives of products once discarded or replaced.
For thousands of technicians, workshop owners and spare-parts dealers, this has created a business built on a simple proposition: when buying new is expensive, keeping the old one working makes better economic sense. But the activity is becoming more than a collection of small repair shops. It is overlapping with refurbishment, used-device trading, component recovery and e-waste recycling.
A 2026 study by 6Wresearch on Pakistan's e-waste recycling market provides a useful picture of this wider value chain. Its publicly available framework tracks component refurbishing alongside precious-metal recovery, plastics separation and battery processing. It covers IT and telecom equipment, consumer devices, appliances and EV components as waste sources.
The report is significant because it places refurbishment between conventional repair and recycling. An ageing device does not necessarily move directly from a consumer's home to a scrap dealer. It can pass through repair, parts replacement, refurbishment, resale and eventual recovery of its remaining materials.
Mobile phones get second life
A mobile technician may replace a damaged screen and return a phone to its owner. Another trader may buy a damaged handset, replace components and sell it as a refurbished device. Spare parts removed from one phone can become useful for another, while phones that cannot be economically repaired may still have value for their components.
The same principle applies to computers and appliances. A laptop with a faulty motherboard, a refrigerator with a damaged compressor or an air-conditioner requiring an expensive component does not become worthless. Technicians can recover usable parts, while traders buy non-working equipment for dismantling and resale.
"Users come to us with all kinds of problems, from slow charging and blank screens to storage issues, broken screens, faulty buttons and damaged charging ports," said Furqan Alvi, a mobile repair shop operator who also sells new devices.
For consumers, a repair bill may be a fraction of the price of a new appliance, particularly when the problem involves a replaceable component rather than the complete product.
Keeping computers alive
The repair market has adapted to changing consumer behaviour. Independent technicians increasingly operate through small workshops, home-based setups and social media pages, using messaging platforms to receive complaints, send repair estimates and arrange doorstep services.
A large number of home-based technicians operate across Karachi. Arshad Awan, who repairs desktop PCs and laptops, communicates with customers through WhatsApp and social media groups.
"People insist on getting their computers repaired for two basic reasons. One is to save their data and, most importantly, to avoid the cost of buying a new machine. They are even reluctant to buy a new adapter for smoother charging," Awan said. He said he could repair PCs and laptops of almost all brands and models. "I communicate through social media groups to find work, and people contact me. Sometimes work comes easily, while at other times I may have to wait for even a month."
Repair, trade and resell
The spare-parts trade forms another layer of this informal economy. Dealers stock new, used and salvaged components, while technicians depend on networks of suppliers to find parts for models no longer supported by manufacturers.
Another growing practice is the exchange of old mobile phones for new ones, with customers paying a relatively small amount to upgrade. The used phones are then resold, allowing older devices to move from one owner to another rather than entering the waste stream. This creates an ecosystem where the value of an old product is not determined only by whether it still works. Its screen, battery, motherboard, compressor, motor or power supply may each have a separate resale value.
For some businesses, the next step is refurbishment
Recently, Commerce Minister Jam Kamal Khan said Samsung had proposed establishing certified mobile-phone refurbishment facilities in Pakistan. The government said a regulated refurbishment ecosystem could strengthen local industry, create employment, build technical expertise and generate opportunities to export refurbished devices.
Samsung also proposed replacing commercial imports of used phones with certified refurbished devices produced through authorised facilities and backed by quality assurance and warranties. The proposal gives a formal-industry dimension to a trade largely developed outside organised manufacturing.
If certified refurbishment facilities emerge, Pakistan could move from importing and repairing used electronics towards repairing and refurbishing devices locally, adding value before resale or export.
The environmental case is equally important
Pakistan's Ministry of Climate Change and Environmental Coordination has warned that the country lacks comprehensive baseline data on the scale, sources and handling of e-waste. The ministry said in 2025 that roughly 500,000 tonnes of e-waste are generated annually and that much of it is handled through informal and unsafe channels. It has called for formal collection and recycling systemsand a national framework for e-waste management. The ministry has also noted that discarded mobile phones, computers, televisions and household appliances are often dumped, burned or dismantled informally. At the same time, many products can be reused, refurbished or recycled.
This creates a difficult paradox. The informal repair economy keeps products in use for longer and prevents some equipment from becoming waste, but the same informal system can become environmentally hazardous when products reach the end of their useful lives and are dismantled without proper safeguards.
The opportunity is not simply to formalise every neighbourhood repair shop. It is to connect the different parts of the chain.
A more organised system could allow consumers to hand over unwanted devices, technicians to recover usable components, refurbishers to restore working products and authorised recyclers to recover materials from equipment that can no longer be repaired.
For Pakistan's small businesses, this could turn an activity traditionally viewed as low-end informal work into a more structured service industry. For consumers, it means a broken product can remain useful for longer. For manufacturers, refurbishment could create a new channel for devices that would otherwise enter the used market without quality controls. And for the environment, every additional year that a repairable product remains in use delays its journey into the waste stream.
The 6Wresearch study forecasts Pakistan's e-waste recycling market through 2032, covering component refurbishing, recycling and recovery activities as the sector develops into a broader commercial value chain. The repair economy may therefore be telling a bigger story about Pakistan's consumption pattern: as replacement becomes harder to afford, the country is learning to extract more value from the products it already owns.
What began as a neighbourhood technician fixing a broken phone or appliance could eventually become part of a larger circular economy – one in which the first business is repair, the next is refurbishment, and the final value lies in recovering whatever remains.
