items.content:
Federal Minister for Finance and Revenue Senator Muhammad Aurangzeb on Friday said the government was committed to maintaining macroeconomic stability and steering the economy from stabilisation towards sustainable growth.
He also stressed the need to stay on course in structural reforms and strengthen the private sector's role through privatisation and public-private partnerships (PPPs).
Addressing an event titled "Mobilising Private Capital: National Strategic Dialogue on PPPs and Privatisation", organised by the Asian Development Bank (ADB), the minister said Pakistan had made significant progress in addressing the structural twin deficit, which had declined from 12.5% of GDP to 2.6% over the last two and a half to three years.
He said the progress on the fiscal side was driven by increased revenues following the transformation of the Federal Board of Revenue (FBR) in terms of people, processes and technology, with revenues growing by 40% over the last two years. At the same time, he said, the government was working to reduce expenditures, including those related to running the civil government and debt servicing, while acknowledging that there was still a long way to go.
Aurangzeb said the FBR's tax-to-GDP ratio had improved from 8.8% to 10.3% and needed to reach 11-12% in the short term. On the external side, he said the country's position had been supported by strong remittance flows and growth in IT services export, which reached $4.6 billion last year, including $1.6 billion contributed by freelancers.
However, he said goods' exports had remained broadly flat at around $30 billion and it was an area that required greater focus. The minister said reforms in the energy sector, state-owned enterprises (SOEs) and privatisation were interlinked, adding that structural reforms in the energy sector were essential for progress on SOEs and privatisation.
He mentioned that 27 transactions had been given to the Privatisation Commission, while some SOEs that were "beyond repair" were closed down, including the Utility Stores Corporation, Passco and PWD. He said debt servicing, reduction in public debt and pension reforms were also part of the government's public finance reform agenda.
Aurangzeb pointed out that Pakistan had received three sovereign rating upgrades since April 2025, enabling it to return to international capital markets after a hiatus of about four years. The order book for the latest $3 billion transaction was twice the amount issued, with a diverse investor base comprising Asian, Middle Eastern, European and US investors. "This is a great vote of confidence in terms of our direction as far as the economy is concerned," he remarked.
Looking ahead, the minister said the government aimed to achieve economic growth of more than 4% during the current fiscal year and increase foreign exchange reserves from $18.4 billion as of June 30 to $21 billion by the end of the fiscal year. The government was also closely monitoring the ongoing regional conflict and its potential impact on growth and inflation projections.
The minister said the government was working to reduce its over-reliance on the banking system for borrowing needs by developing debt capital markets and diversifying the investor base, including insurance companies and other non-bank financial institutions.
He revealed that the Ministry of Finance was working on a rupee-denominated, dollar-settled bond and was also exploring the possibility of tokenizing some existing Eurobond debt, following what Hong Kong had done. Aurangzeb said greater participation of local investors and conglomerates in privatisation transactions would send a strong signal to foreign investors, adding that conglomerates were increasingly willing to work together through consortiums.
Speaking at the event, Adviser to the Prime Minister on Privatisation Muhammad Ali said that public-private partnerships (PPPs) and privatisation were critical instruments for the future economic growth of Pakistan.

items.author: ZAFAR BHUTTA
items.content:
The import of sugar and then its export to dispose of unsold stocks, which is happening now, have raised serious questions about data maintenance relating to the commodity's availability, stocks and domestic consumption. This has also sparked questions about the role of the Sugar Advisory Board and the food ministry, which deal with sugar inventories in the country.
The government had imported sugar over fears of low supply in the domestic market but later it came to know that the imported sugar could not be consumed.
Out of the total import of 500,000 tonnes, the Trading Corporation of Pakistan (TCP) imported 300,000 tonnes while the consumption reached only around 200,000 tonnes. Now, the government has allowed sugar export to avoid losses, which may be caused by the imported sweetener's stocks in the country.
Cabinet members were informed in a recent meeting that the government had imported sugar in 2025, but it could not be consumed and "now it is going to export the commodity to dispose of those stocks".
Sources in the Ministry of Commerce told The Express Tribune that Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif took the cabinet members into confidence during the meeting over the sugar export decision. The PM alluded to the fallacious information being spread by certain elements through the media about sugar export.
The premier observed that the initiative was being taken in a very transparent manner to avoid losses that would accrue if the imported sugar was not sold before the approaching expiry of its shelf life.
He advised the deputy prime minister/minister of foreign affairs to apprise the cabinet of the factual situation. The deputy PM shared with the forum that owing to various factors, including heat waves and crop diseases, sugarcane production had suffered a decline of 15% during the 2024-25 crushing season.
Because of the low production and other supply-side constraints, he said, sugar prices rose significantly in the domestic market. To stabilise prices for the benefit of consumers, the cabinet, on the recommendation of the Economic Coordination Committee (ECC), allowed import of up to 500,000 metric tons of white crystalline sugar in June 2025. However, only 300,000 tons were imported.
He further informed the cabinet that around 192,000 tons of the imported sugar was sold domestically while around 108,000 tons were lying with the TCP, which required urgent disposal in view of its fast approaching shelf life.
The deputy PM pointed out that since sugar prices had recently risen considerably in the international market, the export of the imported sweetener would be beneficial to the country, which would help in recovering both its landed and carrying costs.
The PM emphasised that it must be clear to all that the government had allowed sugar import solely with the objective of ensuring its adequate availability in the domestic market and enabling people to purchase the essential commodity at affordable prices. He noted that timely imports during the previous year helped in arresting the upward trend in domestic prices, adding that it was extremely regrettable that certain elements were distorting facts for their ulterior motives.
It was also highlighted that farmers had been struggling to get inputs at lower rates and were forced to pay higher prices for fertiliser and fuels. Now, they are facing the worst situation due to the rising cost of high-speed diesel.
They have also been facing delayed payments by sugar mills, which are largely owned by the elite class. Even brokers have made money through import and then export of sugar.

items.content:
Hawala networks are once again becoming a source of concerning headlines, as operators of the notorious informal money transfer system are reportedly using digital assets and the latest fintech to move money under the noses of regulators and law enforcement.
A new joint report by the FATF and the OECD says hawala networks are now moving billions of dollars around the world every year. More than 80 per cent of reporting jurisdictions now identify hawala and similar service providers as principal channels for professional money laundering, and the networks continue to innovate to offer a product that is comparable, and arguably even better, than anything the formal banking system has to offer. Among the ways is that hawala operators often offer competitive exchange rates with 'zero fee' instant transfers, unlike banks and other legal money transfer services, which charge fees and taxes, and could take several minutes, hours, or days, depending on the value of a transaction and the countries involved.
Hawala operators can do this because they generally minimise the actual movement of money, allowing operators to avoid converting currencies and letting them pocket the entire exchange rate margin, and since the payments are processed in local currencies, free instant transfer services such as Raast in Pakistan or Zelle in the US allow the operators to offer international payments that are cheaper and faster than any legal provider. Also, contrary to regulators' claims, hawala providers usually don't con their clients - they just don't do much in the way of 'know your customer' checks, which makes them a popular tool for terrorists and large-scale financial criminals, along with working-class folks. This has created what some critics are calling "money laundering as a service".
Local and international regulators need to catch up soon, lest the criminal networks become too big to fail. Meanwhile, licensed and legal providers need to look into ways to offer products that can compete on cost and speed.

items.content:
New York City's decision to impose a one-year moratorium on student-facing generative AI from pre-school through eighth grade is an unusually blunt response to a complicated problem. The policy affects nearly 600,000 students and prohibits the use of generative AI tools, while allowing limited, supervised programmes for high-school students.
The reasoning is understandable. Schools are not merely places where children acquire information. They are where they learn to think, write, argue, collaborate and persist through problems. If an AI chatbot can produce an essay or solve a mathematical problem within seconds, the danger is that students learn to outsource precisely those cognitive struggles that education is supposed to cultivate. The OECD's latest research warns that generative AI can improve the quality of students' immediate work without necessarily producing corresponding learning gains. Unsupervised use can encourage disengagement and weaken sustained attention and perseverance. There are also legitimate concerns over plagiarism and privacy. A child who cannot distinguish a confident AI fabrication from fact is poorly equipped for an information-saturated world. Schools also have a responsibility to know what technologies are collecting about children.
Yet a blanket ban carries its own risks. AI is not disappearing. Students will encounter it at universities, workplaces, and in everyday life. Keeping it outside the classroom may leave them less prepared to understand its biases and limitations. UNESCO, in fact, recommends developing AI competencies in schools, including ethics and critical judgement along with the ability to understand and create AI systems. Banning AI without first improving teaching quality and developing digital literacy could simply preserve an outdated model of education. At the same time, allowing children unrestricted access to chatbots would be equally irresponsible. It is a difficult balancing act.

items.author: Farrukh Khan Pitafi
items.content:
On August 15, 2024, I produced an hour-long video commentary for my YouTube channel (@fptalks) and tried to publish it. For some magical reason, it would not upload from Pakistan. I used several service providers, VPNs and other means. When all attempts failed, despite trying for nearly 20 hours, I gave it to a friend travelling abroad to try to publish from there. They dutifully did this within hours and did not encounter any issues. The video titled "Adani, Hindenburg, SEBI and the missing big picture" (https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=Ig3m7rcc7JE) is still online. Here is a condensed version for your convenience:
"I initially did not want to touch the Adani, Hindenburg, and SEBI issue to avoid alienating anyone, given the immense power of the Adani Group and the Modi government. However, watching the Indian media mishandle this story, often missing the forest for the trees due to a lack of competence, made me realise that a much bigger picture is being ignored.
Last January, Hindenburg Research released a meticulously documented report accusing the Adani Group of cooking its books and manipulating stocks. Hindenburg has a history of targeting weak or manipulative companies, taking short positions, and profiting when those stocks fall. They have a strong track record of bringing down corporate giants, and now they have released fresh allegations.
The real origin of this conversation lies in global market projections and fears of a wider recession. Looking around the world, the US and European markets do not currently have the fundamental exposure that would trigger a severe global economic collapse. In Asia, Japan's economic stagnation is already factored in, and China's structural issues are managed by a highly efficient bureaucracy that quickly rebalances systemic problems.
Then comes India. Pretending the Indian economy has no structural problems or contagion risks is foolish. A decade ago, the non-performing asset (NPA) crisis was massive. Former RBI Chief Dr Raghuram Rajan tried to tackle it, but after a change in government, he was let go, leading to a decade of opacity. We do not actually know the true extent of the problem today.
Many suspect the economic numbers are cooked. The touted growth figures severely contradict the lack of employment and the crippling cost-of-living crisis facing the working and middle classes. When strongmen are at the helm, often relying on ideology and a muscular image rather than sound economics, data manipulation is common.
Meanwhile, conglomerates like Ambani and Adani have grown exponentially into larger-than-life entities dominating both the conversation and the business landscape. We should not fool ourselves into thinking all corporate operations are perfectly sound; just look at past internal conflicts like the one within the Tata Group and the tragic death of Cyrus Mistry.
The latest Hindenburg allegations expose a critical failure of regulatory independence. SEBI's own leadership is now facing scrutiny. When the state actively paralyses its regulatory bodies to shield a favoured corporate monopoly, all transparency vanishes. Global markets and international lenders rely on this transparency. If they sense the system is rigged, foreign direct investment will flee. Western stakeholders will simply cut their losses and pull their capital to avoid contagion. Creating an artificial bubble around a single conglomerate is unsustainable, and when it inevitably deflates, it threatens to drag the broader economy into a severe recession.
The nexus between big business and corrupt politicians is an untenable model. If you think the rich can survive a civilisational collapse in ivory towers, consider two examples. First, look at Bangladesh. Sheikh Hasina was deeply entrenched, having appointed the Chief Justice and the Army Chief, and having dismantled the opposition. Yet, when the people took to the streets, she had to flee to save her life. Second, consider the film Don't Look Up, where corrupt billionaires and politicians ignore an imminent threat, only to meet a disastrous end after trying to escape the consequences of their greed.
Selfishness and greed will get these elites nowhere. They need to start cooperating with authorities and stop dismantling regulatory frameworks. If they do not, it is their funeral. Our generation may have tolerated these excesses, but the younger generation will not let itself suffer the same way."
Two years on, here is where we stand. The Adani-Hindenburg confrontation eventually resulted in the SEBI chief's departure and Hindenburg abruptly shutting up shop. The Adani group was later implicated in a bribery scandal, which led to a US Department of Justice probe. With the change in the US administration, the parties settled, and the charges were dropped. Meanwhile, FDI in India has nearly flatlined. Net FDI inflows cratered from about $28 billion in 2022-23 to just $960 million in 2024-25, before a tepid rebound to $6.95 billion the following year.
Meanwhile, the Indian government does not seem to have learned any lessons. In the heyday of Operation Sindoor, PM Modi went to NITI Aayog, the body that replaced the planning commission, and returned claiming India had surpassed Japan to become the world's fourth-largest economy. I challenged the claim back then, but who listens? In hindsight, it has proven to be a blatant lie. India has slipped one position and is now sixth, behind the UK.
It seems whenever the Modi government faces turbulence, it manipulates numbers to look good. A recent controversy was generated when the Ministry of Statistics and Programme Implementation claimed an inflated 7.8 per cent GDP growth rate, a figure critics argue was engineered by shifting the base year and artificially depressing baseline data. Despite such statistical gymnastics, the underlying reality of widespread joblessness and a grinding cost-of-living crisis remains impossible to mask with headlines. Two years on, young people are making their presence felt on the streets, as I predicted.
But the problem is not just a financial contagion which could ambush the global economy like a bolt from the blue. The bigger concern is the Indian government's insistence that its claims be treated as the final word. Whether we like it or not, India has immense influence in the world. The Canadian PM who accused Indian intelligence operatives of killing Canadian citizens is out and forgotten. The US President who mocked Modi's water-drinking was declared unfit and dropped from his party ticket. The British PM, last seen resisting Modi's hug in a viral clip, is gone and called incompetent. Indian censorship contagion is withering free speech worldwide. How can it be allowed to stand?

items.title: Kashmir PM, CPEC and the crisis of credibility
items.summary:

items.author: Imtiaz Gul
items.content:
Four recent developments explain the credibility - or the absence of it - of Pakistan's self-centred, visionless rulers and the inability of the archaic, rent-seeking bureaucracy. Both remain anchored in a mindset that has resulted in squandered opportunities. These developments also highlight the contradictions and gaps between words and actions, ideals and practice. There is little doubt that the country is facing an acute crisis of credibility and integrity. Every delay in critically important plans, every constitutional or moral violation and every defiance of Supreme Court orders makes this crisis more serious.
Firstly, the selection of Azad Kashmir's Prime Minister on a technocrat seat is nothing but a brazen affront to the people at large. Voters had rejected Iftikhar Gillani in the general election, but Nawaz Sharif - on the face of it - dumped his long-time associate Shah Ghulam Qadir, only to undermine his own slogan: "Honour the vote." Why would the voter - betrayed in February 2024 - trust him or the system anymore?
Secondly, on August 30, the Central Development Working Party (CDWP) recommended reducing the estimated cost of the "Construction of Water Supply Scheme to Gwadar Town from Mirani Dam under Balochistan Socio-Economic Development Projects Phase-III" by around 20 per cent, to Rs23.82 billion, against the Rs29 billion proposed by the Balochistan government. Planning Minister Ahsan Iqbal directed the provincial government to initiate a study on wastewater treatment in Gwadar, observing that the city should not be allowed to become another Karachi, with sewage polluting the sea.
The forum, however, asked ECNEC to approve the project subject to satisfactory resolution of outstanding technical observations, particularly regarding demand figures, hydrology, confirmation of the water source, procurement strategy, land acquisition status, a self-sustainable operation and maintenance (O&M) strategy and a realistic implementation plan.
Staggering, isn't it? Eleven years after the signing of multiple CPEC projects, with Gwadar at the centre of it all?
Equally intriguing was another meeting on August 28, chaired by Ahsan Iqbal, which formally rejected a Frontier Works Organization (FWO) proposal for developing the 460km Rohri-Multan section of ML-1 and decided to explore alternatives for this section. The estimates did not adequately include locomotives, coaches and operating costs.
Isn't it telling that a minister who has been crying hoarse about CPEC being a game-changer, including the Gwadar and ML-1 projects, is now seeking alternative sources of funding? He nevertheless deserves commendation for two things: a) refusing to clear the FWO proposal for the Rohri-Multan section because of multiple deficiencies; and b) ordering an independent audit of the costing prepared by the organisation itself.
The August 28 meeting offered yet another sad comment: planners have not finalised the ML-1 proposal, let alone secured alternative sources of funding. Nor do they appear serious; reportedly, only junior officials represented the federal ministries involved. This suggests that the bureaucracy does not expect the project to take off anytime soon.
It is a sad story indeed. Until shortly before Covid-19 struck in late 2019, the Chinese leadership was more than keen to finance the entire ML-1.
"Brother, $7–8 billion are peanuts for us, but tell your people to come prepared with feasible plans on ML-1. We have also worked very hard to get here and expect others to follow the same path," a very senior Chinese official told me when I asked about the possibility of funding for ML-1.
What the meeting confirms is that Beijing's promised financing for the project is no longer forthcoming. For years, the promised investment was presented as the backbone of ML-1. Now the government is struggling to fill the gap.
But with its incompetence, the Pakistani bureaucracy - presumably including those with vested interests in the West and those disinclined towards Chinese investment and influence in the country - stalled the Chinese goodwill, and the project seems to have finally hit a dead end as far as Beijing is concerned.
It is perhaps a blessing in disguise that the Chinese stepped back from their earlier commitments on ML-1 financing. Why? Our politicians and bureaucracy have already messed up Chinese power-sector investments through spiralling circular debt, delayed loan repayments and hurdles in profit repatriation.
The larger issue relates to the rule of law. Locals and foreigners alike are shocked by the way superior court orders are flouted by the authorities. The latest reversal, on September 2, of a 2022 Islamabad High Court (IHC) judgment on naval farms and the sailing club offered yet another glimpse into the exceptionalism exercised by the higher courts when it comes to protecting deeply entrenched power elites. Of late, Supreme Court and IHC orders concerning former Prime Minister Imran Khan have been spurned more than once.
Such defiance of the rule of law hardly inspires confidence among the people at large or foreign investors. They see that if companies from even a "time-tested friendly country" such as China face enormous administrative and legal challenges, what could possibly happen to investors accustomed to having absolute confidence in the judiciary and the rule of law?

items.author: Amna Hashmi.
items.content:
A Chinese shipyard recently logged more new vessel orders in six months than all of most nations' merchant fleets. In the first half of this year alone, Hengli Heavy has received 207 orders, an all-time record for one yard, anywhere, ever. It was not announced at the press conference. There was no treaty signed. It emerged, practically as an afterthought, in a report of the quarterly earnings. That is how the biggest shifts in the global order tend to arrive now: not with a declaration but with a balance sheet.
Officially, this is just business catching up to disruption. The Strait of Hormuz has become a live warzone by any honest reading, transits swinging wildly, from 91 in one week down to 73 the next, as Iran targets vessels using the strait and Washington blockades Iranian ports. In August alone, in less than two weeks, two mariners were lost there, on ships with nothing to do with the war. Record levels of container ships are stuck at ports in China, Asia and Europe, driving up freight costs. All actors claim it is a commercial reaction. Abu Dhabi's national oil company just purchased 11 tankers and gas carriers for $1.3 billion, opting to build its own shipping capacity instead of relying on an open market it no longer feels will hold. That is not a hedge against weather. That is a hedge against war.
We have been here before and we called it something else at the time. Britain and Germany had been developing their navies at an alarming rate in the years preceding 1914, and both governments saw the expansion, without any irony, as a commercial necessity, a trade protection, an insurance for prosperity, and nothing else. German officials spoke of safeguarding shipping lanes. British officials said the two-power naval standard was just for stability. Historians' did not refer to it as an arms race in its time. They called it prudence or growth or the ordinary hum of industrial nations doing what industrial nations do. It was only after the ships were constructed and the war had already begun that the term "arms race" was coined to describe what anyone had seen happen in actuality.
It's important to mention that the merchant sailors paid for that denial before soldiers did. In 1917 Germany's unrestricted submarine campaign was against civilian cargo vessels and tankers, not against warships, because it was cheaper to starve Britain's supply lines than engage its navy. In those years Lloyd's of London took great care to recalculate their insurance figures and they referred to it as a problem of the numbers, not a crisis to be named. The same sort of loss occurred in the Strait of Hormuz: the mariners were easier to target than the fleets and states that were actually at war.
That is the pattern worth sitting with now. Countries rarely declare a rearmament. They announce that they are adapting to markets, to risk, to a supply chain that has grown "temporarily" unpredictable. I must clarify that the tankers being built today are not warships and the analogy should not be extended too far. But the psychology is the same when a buildup is justified only through the language of commerce, and when the actors all state, individually, that they are merely reacting to the situation that others have created. There's no aggressor in their story. All are merely defending their trade routes.
Between a shipyard's long list of orders and a state oil company's $1 billion spent to purchase tankers, a more subtle mobilisation process is already in motion and it's being financed, constructed and launched as public discussion remains stuck on sanctions lists and diplomatic statements. History does not usually let us watch an arms race happen while it is still deniable. This time it gets to be seen in practice as logistics, under the guise of supply-chain resilience, as has always been the case. We have a word for that kind of insistence. It's just that we only use it after the ships have set sail.

items.author: Palak Sharma
items.content:
Urban Company pioneered the home services model in the Indian startup ecosystem and completely changed the game.
It applied the food delivery aggregation idea to a far more fragmented problem: services at home. A plumber, electrician, cleaner or beautician no longer had to be someone the customer knew in the neighbourhood. The platform could find one, schedule the appointment and bring the service to the home. And it made it highly affordable for consumers who are unused to spending heavily on such repairs and services.
But there is an interesting question hiding behind that convenience: when a customer pays for a service through Urban Company, how much actually reaches the person doing the job, and how much does the platform keep? How is the low cost of service enough to sustain this model?
This tension has governed the long journey of Urban Company from 2014 onwards. And even after the company has gone public, this model continues to be a source of consternation for the stakeholders, as well as something of a mystery for those outside the value chain.
The question gets more interesting as Urban Company has expanded beyond its original marketplace. The company now combines its core consumer-services business with its consumer-product business Native, its on-demand home-help offering InstaHelp, and its international operations.
Revenue from operations grew 44% YoY to ₹528 Cr in Q1 FY27, but Urban Company swung from a ₹7 Cr profit in Q1 FY26 to a ₹92 Cr loss.
For UC, the net transaction value (NTV) is as important as the revenue it bagged. This shows the true scale of the company. Its NTV crossed ₹1,465 Cr in Q1 FY27, giving a sense of the transaction value flowing through the platform. But scale does not translate into a straight line towards profitability.
And that’s where it gets interesting. The NTV and revenue gap points to the first question at the heart of the business: how much does Urban Company keep from transactions at a unit level?
To understand how the business really makes money, we need to look beyond the headline transaction value and break down what Urban Company actually earns.
Urban Company’s Revenue Trail: What It Keeps, What It Pays
As we hinted above, Urban Company’s scale is best understood through the metric it calls net transaction value (NTV).
The company facilitated ₹1,465 Cr worth of transactions in the quarter, but reported operating revenue of ₹528 Cr. The gap between the two is important because Urban Company does not recognise the entire value of every transaction made on its platform as revenue.
Take a typical home-service booking. A customer pays for a cleaning, beauty or repair service through Urban Company, but the service is fulfilled by a professional on the platform. Urban Company generally acts as an intermediary between the two, providing the technology, customer acquisition, training and other infrastructure needed to facilitate the transaction.
Therefore, the money paid by the customer does not flow entirely to Urban Company, similar to how Uber and Rapido work.
However, here, UC earns from both sides of this marketplace once a transaction takes place.
The company monetises the transaction through the fees it charges both consumers and professionals. Customers may pay a convenience fee when they book a service, while service professionals pay commissions and other platform-related fees for operating on Urban Company.
As a result, the full value of the booking becomes NTV, but only the amount Urban Company is entitled to retain is recognised as revenue from the marketplace transaction.
While Urban Company does not disclose the rupee value of consumer convenience fees and professional commissions separately, its commissions and fees accounted for 28.3% of average gross earnings of service professionals in 9M FY26, although this should not be read as the company’s overall take rate.
UC also earns membership fees from consumers who subscribe to its membership programme, adding a recurring revenue stream beyond individual service bookings.
From services, UC earned ₹290.2 Cr in revenue in the June quarter of FY27, and the remaining ₹66.2 Cr came from the sale of products.
The company also sells tools and consumables to its service professionals, which are used while delivering services to customers. These include products that professionals need to perform jobs on the platform, allowing Urban Company to monetise the supply side beyond commissions and platform fees. The company refers to this as its B2B2C product business.
Beyond this, Urban Company’s Native business, which sells its own home-improvement products such as water purifiers and electronic door locks, contributed ₹95 Cr in revenue in Q1 FY27, while its international services business added ₹65 Cr, excluding KSA (UC’s joint venture in Saudi Arabia).
The company’s newer InstaHelp business, which connects consumers with professionals for on-demand home-help services, contributed another ₹11 Cr in revenue — but came with a much steeper cost, raising the question of why Urban Company is willing to absorb losses to scale it.
The InstaHelp Turn
Urban Company turned profitable in Q1 FY26, when it reported a PAT of ₹7 Cr. A year later, revenue climbed 44% YoY from ₹367 Cr to ₹528 Cr, yet the company slipped to a ₹92 Cr loss.
It reported a consolidated adjusted EBITDA loss of ₹65 Cr in Q1 FY27, despite the core business generating ₹67 Cr in adjusted EBITDA. Its core India consumer services business was even stronger, so what was the reason for this loss?
That’s the company’s decision to enter the instant home services market through InstaHelp. The company entered this fast-emerging segment, where startups such as Snabbit and Pronto entered a few months earlier.
The race is increasingly about building dense neighbourhood-level networks of customers and service professionals, with players spending heavily to acquire both sides of the marketplace. However, expansion of InstaHelp has been met with a lot of headwinds, particularly because this segment requires perfect markets to operate in.
Unlike the company’s traditional services, which tend to be higher-value and less frequent, InstaHelp is designed around high-frequency, lower-ticket bookings. The frequency part is where UC is betting its money, so naturally urban and metro areas are the primary target market.
In Q1 FY27, InstaHelp clocked 3.82 Mn orders, up 43% QoQ, taking its NTV to ₹53 Cr. Revenue stood at ₹11 Cr. But the business reported an adjusted EBITDA loss of ₹132 Cr, making it the company’s largest investment and the biggest drag on its profitability.
However, loss is not the entire story. Urban Company’s adjusted loss per order improved to ₹346 in Q1 FY27 from ₹447 in Q4 FY26, a 23% sequential improvement.
Management attributed this improvement to the increasing density of InstaHelp’s micro-markets.
Micro-market density is key to scaling up this business, which relies heavily on utilisation of the service professional base. As more households in a particular neighbourhood use InstaHelp, a professional can potentially complete more jobs within a smaller geographic radius.
This improved utilisation means Urban Company is able to extract more profits per order than before. Otherwise, it would have to spend a considerable amount on acquiring new users and setting up operations without high utilisation, resulting in higher losses.
This is more pertinent because the AOV for each InstaHep order was only ₹138.
During the Q1 FY27 earnings call, the management estimated that professionals need to earn around ₹130–160 per hour sustainably, while consumer pricing would eventually need to reach roughly ₹200 per hour, implying an AOV of around ₹300 for InstaHelp to break even.
So there are no bets on InstaHelp in terms of profitability in the near future. Instead, the management expects this business to remain loss-making for years and has said it does not intend to make money from InstaHelp over the next five years. UC sees InstaHelp as a frequency-growing and cross-selling opportunity.
The Cost Of Running Urban Company
Urban Company’s business may look asset-light on the surface, but running the marketplace comes with several layers of costs. Some expenses are directly tied to a booking, and others are needed to keep customers and service professionals on the platform.
The first layer is the cost of fulfilling the service. In Q1 FY27, Urban Company spent ₹51 Cr on B2B2C products and ₹49 Cr on Native products.
It spent another ₹18 Cr on services, which primarily represents payouts to service partners for categories where Urban Company recognises the net transaction value as revenue. This includes pest control and revamp services in India.
The ₹17 Cr “direct expenses” include payment gateway, communication and background-verification costs. After these expenses, the company generated a gross profit of ₹393 Cr.
But the marketplace has to do more than facilitate a service. Urban Company spent ₹45 Cr on customer and professional support, refunds and associated AI costs, while other semi-variable expenses including partner incentives, cloud hosting, warehousing, logistics, damages and Native warranty costs stood at ₹109 Cr.
That brought contribution profit to around ₹239 Cr.
The next layer is the cost of building and operating the company itself. Employee costs were ₹146 Cr in the quarter, customer marketing was ₹80 Cr and G&A and other indirect expenses added another ₹78 Cr. Together, these costs took the company from ₹238 Cr of contribution profit to a ₹65 Cr Adjusted EBITDA loss.
If we look at this segment-wise, not all of those costs behave in the same way.
The core India consumer services business generated ₹73 Cr in Adjusted EBITDA in Q1 FY27, while International contributed ₹3 Cr. Native was still in investment mode, with an adjusted EBITDA loss of ₹9 Cr, while InstaHelp accounted for the largest drag with a ₹132 Cr loss.
This highlights that Urban Company is continuing to spend on newer businesses and the infrastructure needed to scale them.
The Bets Beyond The Core
Urban Company’s expansion strategy is interesting because it is trying to grow beyond its core marketplace without becoming everything to everyone.
Native is the clearest example. The business currently operates in water purifiers and smart locks, but management is explicit about what it does not want Native to become.
“We’re not trying to build a consumer durables company,” CEO Abhiraj Singh Bhal said on the Q1 FY27 earnings call. Instead, Urban Company wants to serve categories that overlap with its existing users and core services, using technology and its service network to build premium products, he added.
The numbers suggest the strategy is gaining traction. Native’s NTV grew 51% YoY to ₹119 Cr in Q1 FY27, while net revenue rose 60% to ₹95 Cr. While Native’s adjusted EBITDA loss remained broadly unchanged at around ₹9 Cr, the sharp increase in NTV helped narrow its adjusted EBITDA margin to -7.3% from -11.4% a year earlier.
But the more interesting part of the Native story is what happens after the product is sold. Around 75% of the early water-purifier customers who reached their first replacement cycle renewed their filters through Urban Company, creating a recurring, higher-margin revenue stream.
Yet there is a contradiction in the model. Urban Company wants Native to remain tightly connected to its core platform, but that also limits how far the business can expand.
Management said it may enter only one more category over the next five years, rather than aggressively broadening the portfolio. In other words, Native is being positioned less as a standalone consumer-durables business and more as another layer of the Urban Company relationship.
The international business tells a different story.
The subsidiaries in the UAE, Singapore and Saudi Arabia cumulatively generated ₹237 Cr in NTV in Q1 FY27, up 76% YoY. The UAE and Singapore markets are already becoming profitable. The company expects the Saudi JV to become profitable in the coming quarters. Bhal described international as a potential second core profit engine for Urban Company.
Who Really Owns The UC Experience?
For all the technology, pricing and financial engineering behind Urban Company, the most important part of the transaction still happens at the customer’s doorstep.
That makes the service professional central to the company’s proposition but also creates tension at the heart of its model. To deliver a consistent customer experience, the company has built significant controls around how those professionals work, from training and certification to ratings, matching, availability, cancellations and performance mechanisms.
And this is not just a theoretical concern.
Over the years, Urban Company’s partners have protested against several of these mechanisms. Workers have raised grievances around commissions, ID blocking, ratings, auto-assignment and cancellation policies.
Recently, women gig workers in Noida protested over working hours, weekly days off and basic workplace facilities, while Bengaluru partners have also objected to the pressure associated with newer instant-service formats.
That control is becoming even more significant as the company pushes into higher-frequency services such as InstaHelp.
A professional serving a customer once every few months is one thing; a model built around repeated, short-duration bookings requires professionals to be available, geographically dense and responsive to demand.
Urban Company’s argument is that this structure can work for both sides. Better density should mean higher utilisation, which can improve partner earnings, reduce churn and allow the company to invest more in training, technology and quality. In turn, better service should strengthen customer trust and generate more bookings.
The model is built on a delicate flywheel — more professionals should create better availability and utilisation, which should improve customer experience, drive more bookings and, eventually, make the marketplace more profitable.
The company is no longer simply trying to earn a fee on every home service; it is trying to build a high-frequency platform around the household.
The opportunity is significant, but so is the execution challenge.
Urban Company has already shown that its core marketplace can generate healthy profits. The next phase will test whether those profits can sustainably fund newer growth engines, while the professionals powering the platform also see enough benefit from the additional volume and control.
Ultimately, Urban Company is trying to build a system that works better for customers, professionals and the company. Now, whether it can keep all three sides of that equation aligned may determine how far this business model can scale.
The post Inside Urban Company’s Marketplace Model: What It Earns From Every Booking appeared first on Inc42 Media.

items.author: Gaurav Bagur
items.content:
Bessemer Venture Partners-backed digital payments startup Innoviti managed to cut its net loss by over 57% YoY to ₹26.7 Cr in FY26 from ₹62.1 Cr loss incurred in the previous fiscal. The startup managed to cull its loss despite its top line taking a hit during the fiscal, falling by 16.7% to ₹118.9 Cr in the year under review as against ₹142.6 Cr in FY25.
During the fiscal, Innovit’s revenue from services fell by 17.8% YoY to ₹101.5 Cr. Of this, ₹97.3 Cr came from offline revenue, which shrank 20% from ₹121.4 Cr in the previous year. Its online revenue doubled to around ₹4.2 Cr.
Additionally, the startup registered an operating revenue of ₹17.4 Cr from lease rentals in FY26. This figure also came down by about 9% from ₹19.1 Cr in the year-ago period.
Apart from its operating revenue, it also reported ₹3.3 Cr in other income, bringing its total income for FY26 to ₹122.2 Cr.
In its filing with the MCA, accessed by Inc42, the startup said that it expects to turn EBITDA positive in FY27, aided by operational improvements, cost-efficiency measures, and new customer additions.
Founded in 2002 by Rajeev Agrawal and Amrita Malik, Innoviti offers three core products: sales acceleration software Innoviti Genie, revenue assurance software Innoviti Unipay and payment collection app Innoviti Link.
The startup claims to process over ₹80,000 Cr of gross transaction volume (GTV) annually from across 2,000 Indian cities and over 20,000 merchants.
Earlier this year, Innoviti received the certificate of authorisation by the RBI to operate as a payment aggregator (PA), permitting it to operate as a PA for both online and offline payments. It had earlier received RBI authorisation for online payment aggregation in March 2024.
It has raised over $115 Mn in funding to date from investors like Bessemer Venture Partners, Catamaran Ventures, Alumni Ventures, FMO, and others. Most recently, it raised a $11.4 Mn Series M funding round in February.
Innoviti has also been looking to make its public market debut for a few years now. In August 2024, it had said it would go for an IPO within a year. It then repeated the sentiment in January 2025 but is yet to make any headway in the public markets direction.
Where Did Innoviti Spend In FY26?
Innoviti managed to slash losses by paring its expenses by nearly 28% in the year under review.
The startup spent ₹148.9 Cr in total during FY26, as against ₹206.6 Cr in the previous fiscal year. Here’s how the fintech startup’s expenditure broke down:
Subvention and Service Fees: Accounting for the largest expense, the startup trimmed its spending under this head by 24% YoY to ₹62.5 Cr.
Employee Benefit Expenses: Innoviti spent 11.7% less on personnel related expenses in FY26 as its employee benefit expenses fell to ₹38 Cr from ₹43.1 Cr.
Depreciation, Amortisation and Impairment Expense: Expenses related to depreciation, amortisation and impairment plunged over 66.5% to ₹10.9 Cr from ₹32.6 Cr in FY25.
Finance Costs: Innoviti’s expenditure on interest and borrowings saw the sharpest reduction, dropping 64.1% YoY to ₹1.5 Cr from ₹4.3 Cr previously.

items.content:
Lere Olayinka, Senior Special Assistant on Public Communications and Social Media to the Federal Capital Territory (FCT) Minister, Nyesom Wike, on Friday clashed with ARISE Television anchor, Rufai Oseni, during a live television programme.
Olayinka, who appeared on The Morning Show, refused to respond to questions from Oseni, saying he did not want to engage in a discussion with someone who described other people as “emudani.”
The exchange followed a question from Oseni on the inclusion of former Minister of Humanitarian Affairs, Betta Edu, in the presidential campaign council despite corruption allegations against her.
Rather than answer the question, Olayinka objected to what he said was Oseni’s earlier description of some people as “emudani” and said he would not take questions from the journalist.

Atiku: Tinubu’s policies making youths sell their organs
“Well, I’m very sorry to say this, Oseni Rufai, I don’t want to answer any question from you. I want to concentrate.
“I want this conversation to be among reasonable human beings, people who will not come and tell, who will not come and describe other people as ‘emudani’,” Olayinka said.
Co-anchor of the programme, Ayo Mairo-Ese, intervened, reminding Olayinka that he was addressing all three anchors, including Reuben Abati, when he agreed to appear on the programme.
She subsequently brought the interview with the minister’s aide to an end, saying he could be invited again when he was “ready to speak to the three of us”.

items.title: ‘Sindhu Desh Naa Manzoor’ chants bring Sindh Assembly to a standstill
items.summary:
The Sindh Assembly was thrown into turmoil on Friday as opposition lawmakers turned the House into a battleground over the province’s identity, repeatedly chanting “Sindhu Desh Naa Manzoor” (Sindh Desh unacceptable) and drowning out proceedings before the Speaker, Syed Owais Qadir Shah, was forced to adjourn the sitting after only a brief session.
The uproar erupted at the very outset of the proceedings, with MQM lawmakers raising the slogans as the speaker called for order. His appeals went unheeded as the opposition continued its protest, rendering debate virtually inaudible and effectively paralysing the House.
The disruption came amid mounting political tensions over demands for the Sindh Assembly to formally condemn the Sindhudesh separatist movement, a day after the House passed a resolution against the division of Sindh.
سندھ اسمبلی اجلاس میں اپوزیشن کا شور شرابہ!#SindhAssembly #Opposition #Government #ExpressNews #BreakingNews #LatestNews pic.twitter.com/enMI5
items.author: Muhammad Saleem Jhandeer
items.content:
The Sindh Assembly was thrown into turmoil on Friday as opposition lawmakers turned the House into a battleground over the province’s identity, repeatedly chanting “Sindhu Desh Naa Manzoor” (Sindh Desh unacceptable) and drowning out proceedings before the Speaker, Syed Owais Qadir Shah, was forced to adjourn the sitting after only a brief session.
The uproar erupted at the very outset of the proceedings, with MQM lawmakers raising the slogans as the speaker called for order. His appeals went unheeded as the opposition continued its protest, rendering debate virtually inaudible and effectively paralysing the House.
The disruption came amid mounting political tensions over demands for the Sindh Assembly to formally condemn the Sindhudesh separatist movement, a day after the House passed a resolution against the division of Sindh.
سندھ اسمبلی اجلاس میں اپوزیشن کا شور شرابہ!#SindhAssembly #Opposition #Government #ExpressNews #BreakingNews #LatestNews pic.twitter.com/enMI54xDsy
— Express News (@ExpressNewsPK) September 4, 2026
Amid the commotion, Law and Parliamentary Affairs Minister Ziaul Hassan Lanjar laid an audit report before the House, while Human Settlements Adviser Najmi Alam responded to lawmakers’ written and supplementary questions regarding katchi abadis.
Alam said only settlements established before 2011 would be eligible for leases, noting that any settlement established afterwards would not be leased and would instead be considered an encroachment.
Read: ‘Sindh is one, shall remain one’: Assembly passes resolution against division of province
He added that a no-objection certificate from the Board of Revenue was mandatory for leasing and that no new settlement could be established without the required NOC.
According to the adviser, 50 per cent of the revenue collected from katchi abadis was spent on those same settlements. He attributed Karachi’s growing population partly to continued migration into the city.
On the Lines Area project, Alam said it fell under the local government department and that a project director had already been appointed. A board meeting would be held within 10 to 12 days to decide plots for resettlement, he said.
Alam further stated that plots in katchi abadis would not be allotted to anyone who already owned property elsewhere.
The government had also sought land from the revenue department to establish a “Sasti Basti” (inexpensive settlement) where low-income families could build homes through instalments, he said, clarifying that the government would provide plots rather than construct houses for them.
Alam said removing settlements built over storm-water drains was the responsibility of district administrations.
Alam added that work was underway, on the chairman’s instructions, to regularise ownership for people in Tharparkar and Umerkot who lacked documentation. To prevent buying and selling in katchi abadis, survey forms were also being distributed, he said.
During the proceedings, MQM lawmaker Amir Siddiqui drew the House’s attention to a water shortage in Karachi, particularly in Adam Colony and Soldier Bazaar, saying residents were facing severe difficulties.
In the absence of the local government minister, Parliamentary Secretary Qasim Siraj Soomro said water was being supplied across Karachi on a 12-hour rotation. He attributed the zero billing in the affected areas to residents’ failure to pay water bills.
Another MQM lawmaker, Faisal Rafiq, raised the issue of problems that had remained unresolved for 44 years.
The continuing uproar, however, disrupted legislative business to such an extent that Siddiqui declined to speak on an adjournment motion.
The speaker eventually adjourned the sitting until 2:30pm on Monday.
MQM tables its own anti-Sindhudesh resolution
The MQM-P and the Sindh government traded sharp accusations after opposition lawmakers alleged that the Pakistan People's Party (PPP) administration had blocked their bid to move a resolution against the Sindhudesh movement, only for the MQM to later submit the resolution independently.
Speaking to reporters after the assembly session, Opposition Leader Ali Khursheedi accused the government of displaying “arrogance and prejudice”, saying the opposition’s proposals had been kept out of a resolution on the issue of new provinces.
Khursheedi said the MQM lawmakers had opposed what he described as “frivolous conduct” and had also demanded that separatist movements be explicitly condemned. “We wanted to move a resolution against Sindhudesh today, but the government displayed arrogance,” he said, alleging that the speaker appeared to be under pressure.
Read More: PA digs in as 'new provinces' debate enters third day
He claimed that Chief Minister Murad Ali Shah had reprimanded the speaker, who appeared pressured during the proceedings.
MQM deputy parliamentary leader Taha Ahmed Khan accused the PPP of showing “prejudice and an authoritarian attitude”, saying his party would protect what he called its “defensive line”. “We are against all separatist movements,” he said, insisting that a resolution against the Sindhudesh movement should be brought before the House because such a movement was active in Sindh.
Khan said it was regrettable that the government had not allowed the resolution to be presented, stressing that “this is our homeland, Pakistan”. He further alleged that people subscribing to the Sindhudesh ideology were sitting on the government benches and accused the PPP of refusing to entertain any discussion against the movement.
He said Sindhis were patriotic and argued that those refusing to support an anti-Sindhudesh resolution could not claim to be supporters of Sindh.
Later, however, Taha Ahmed Khan, accompanied by other MQM-P lawmakers, submitted a resolution against Sindhudesh and all separatist movements in Pakistan, effectively putting the issue back on the assembly’s agenda.

items.author: Anadolu Agency
items.content:
The Freedom Flotilla Coalition announced a new international maritime mission to the Gaza Strip, with vessels making stops at European ports before a planned attempt to reach the enclave in October.
“We are sailing again because Israel hasn’t stopped its genocide and because Palestine is still not free,” the coalition said in an appeal for international support.
The mission seeks to challenge Israel’s blockade of Gaza and mobilize public pressure across Europe, the coalition said in a statement published on Wednesday.
The voyage is already underway, with the coalition’s Handala II vessel having visited ports in Norway, Sweden and Denmark during June and July.
Another vessel, the Kate, departed from the British city of Bristol in August and subsequently made stops in Ireland, Germany and France, according to the statement.
The vessels are expected to visit ports in Spain, Portugal and Italy before continuing toward Gaza, where the coalition plans to arrive in October.
The mission brings together human rights advocates, trade union activists, elected representatives, journalists, medical professionals and other supporters of Palestinian rights, the coalition said.
The coalition said it would work with local communities to pressure governments to block weapons and energy shipments to Israel, end diplomatic and military cooperation with it and impose sanctions.
“The Freedom Flotilla sails again because our governments continue to fail to uphold their obligations,” said Zohar Chamberlain Regev, a member of the coalition’s steering committee.
“At every port, we will carry the demand that Palestinians be free to live with dignity,” she added.
“In October, we intend to carry that demand and the solidarity of people around the world to Gaza’s shores.”
The coalition urged governments to demand safe and unobstructed passage for the flotilla and to make clear that any attack, seizure or detention of its participants would have consequences.
It also called for immediate and unrestricted access to Gaza and an end to Israeli restrictions on the entry of food, water, medicine and other essential supplies.
Read More: Israel's Ben-Gvir plans to relocate 1.86m Palestinians from Gaza over 7 years: report
Governments should defend freedom of navigation and use diplomatic, economic and legal measures to end the blockade, it added.
“We know that sailing toward Gaza carries serious risks,” said Edward Digilio, an engineer from the US state of Maryland participating in the initiative.
“But silence and inaction carry a much greater cost for Palestinians and the world,” he said, describing the mission as “an expression of shared humanity and a refusal to accept the destruction of an entire people as normal.”
The coalition said Israeli forces had attacked and detained hundreds of flotilla participants during an earlier mission in the spring of 2026. It said volunteers reported severe beatings, broken bones, gunshot wounds, repeated tasering and sexual assault while in Israeli custody.
It also recalled Israel’s May 2010 raid on the Gaza-bound Mavi Marmara, during which 10 activists were killed.

items.author: Reuters
items.content:
OpenAI ​on Thursday unveiled a new artificial intelligence model it calls its best yet but cautioned that it also sometimes attempts to evade ‌human monitoring, even as the company faces growing scrutiny after its agents breached other companies' systems.
OpenAI has been grappling with the fallout after its agents broke free from a secure test in July and hacked into open-source platform Hugging Face’s systems, while attempting to cover its own tracks. The incident has sown safety concerns — similar ones occurred at rival Anthropic — as developers race to deploy increasingly ​advanced models.
The concerns center on agentic AI, which is designed to perform tasks with little to no human intervention. The promise of agents running ​around the clock is central to investors' confidence in the appeal of AI as a transformative technology.
New model promises speed and versatility
OpenAI calls its latest model GPT-6 Astra, which follows July’s release of GPT 5.6 Sol, and said in a blog post that it is faster and ​capable of performing more tasks than any prior iteration. Among Astra’s skills: tax preparation, game development, architectural rendering, legal memo formatting and apartment hunting.
“Astra marks a new frontier ​in the speed, accuracy and safety of computer use,” OpenAI said. Earlier on Thursday, OpenAI President Greg Brockman said in a briefing that Astra marked "a real shift in what kind of work people can delegate to AI and how it can empower them.”
For instance, the company said, Astra cut the time required for cat-sitter research from 30 minutes, when performed by a ​human, down to 5 minutes, 27 seconds. And for a job search, just 2 minutes, 51 seconds, compared with 5 hours without Astra.
However, OpenAI also said that ​Astra is more likely to intentionally conceal or disguise its step-by-step methods for problem-solving, known as reasoning, making it harder for humans to later evaluate its techniques. On more complicated ‌problems, Astra ⁠cannot yet consistently obscure its methods, OpenAI said, though it is improving at covering its own tracks.
In a briefing Thursday morning, OpenAI's chief scientist indicated monitoring was getting more difficult, along with alignment, the principle that AI should reflect human values.
Read More: OpenAI agents hijacked German website in previously undisclosed AI breakout this spring
"As the models become more capable, understanding exactly what they can do gets harder," said Jakub Pachocki. "This doesn't guarantee that as intelligence continues to increase, our methods will be sufficient because progress in intelligence does not guarantee progress in alignment."
Monitoring challenges grow with capability
Agent monitoring is a key component ​of OpenAI's reassurance to regulators, lawmakers ⁠and the public to help it avoid another security incident. Further, the company this week told two U.S. House Democrats in a letter that it is developing "automated shutdown capabilities" for its models.
Astra can also help companies find weaknesses in their systems faster, ​OpenAI said, but that also makes "those weaknesses easier to exploit.” For those reasons, the company said it may have ​to perform extra security ⁠checks that “can sometimes slow, pause, or stop legitimate work, including defensive cybersecurity.”
Last month, OpenAI said it was pausing some model development in part to ensure the models can be monitored. OpenAI's chief scientist said it was “very valid” to worry that models could develop to disable or completely evade monitors, while adding that OpenAI was trying to fix those issues.
OpenAI ⁠is scrambling ​to gain ground on Anthropic among business customers as its rival captures market share ahead of ​a widely anticipated initial public offering later this year.
Astra is targeted at a wide range of enterprise customers who OpenAI said it hopes will be drawn to its speed and versatility. It is ​available to a limited set of customers today and over the coming days will be more widely released.

items.author: Our Correspondent
items.content:
The judicial commission probing the Mir Raza Ali murder case on Friday summoned Gulistan-e-Jauhar Station House Officer (SHO) Kamran Qureshi and head clerk Zeeshan to appear before it on September 7.
The commission formed by the Sindh High Court chief justice issued the summons while recording the statements of Ahmed Bhurday, Bhurday's brother Abdullah, driver Ehsanullah and Deputy Superintendent of Police (DSP) Arshad Afridi during Thursday’s proceedings.
According to the written order issued by the commission on Friday, Ehsanullah told the judge that the company had taken back the vehicle provided to him, while the landlord of the house where he had been residing had also evicted him. He said he was now staying at the Ferozabad police station.
Read: Judicial commission questions Mir Raza Ali's business partner over irregularities
The commission directed the investigating officer, DSP Siraj Lashari, to contact the company management and the landlord and address their concerns. It further directed him to assure them that no coercive action would be taken against them in connection with the case.
The commission observed that Ehsanullah was not a suspect in the case and had fully cooperated with Ali’s family during their search for him. He had provided details of his rides and submitted a location map and other ride-related information to the commission.
It was remarked that instead of being rewarded for assisting the family, Ehsanullah appeared to be treated like a suspect and was seemingly facing punishment for helping them.
Read More: Mir Raza case: Judicial commission directs IO to seek re-employment, housing for cab driver
During the proceedings, Bhurday also assured the commission that he would submit a copy of a notice issued by the Sindh Revenue Board, along with receipts for payments received through an online delivery application.
Due to a shortage of time, the commission directed Haisam, Raziq and SHO Adil Afzal to appear at the next hearing. It also summoned SHO Qureshi and court clerk Zeeshan. The commission would resume proceedings on September 7 at 11am.
Case developments
A judicial commission was formed at the request of the Sindh government to probe the death of Ali, who was allegedly kidnapped from PECHS before his body was found in bushes near a wedding hall in Karachi's Gulistan-e-Johar on July 29. The case had initially been surrounded by uncertainty over whether he had been murdered or had died by suicide. The first post-mortem findings contained discrepancies and omissions, leading to a second post-mortem that confirmed his murder. Consequently, considering the probe "botched", the family filed a petition in the SHC seeking the formation of JIT.
During earlier hearings regarding the formation of JIT, the investigating officer probing the death of Ali told the SHC that investigators were treating the case as murder and had ruled out suicide based on the post-mortem findings. DSP Siraj Lashari said the investigation had restarted “from zero” on August 13 and was being conducted using digital evidence, including CCTV footage. Investigators had recovered a bullet casing but had yet to find the weapon, while final post-mortem and forensic reports were still awaited.
Separately, the judicial commission convened its second hearing on Monday, September 1, wherein it grilled Medico-Legal Officer (MLO) Dr Usama Sheikh over discrepancies in the first post-mortem report filed by him. The commission also recorded the statements of the victim's family and Edhi volunteers who shifted his body during the hearing. After the conclusion of the second hearing, Nasir said the first account of the MLO proved that he was correct about the "botched probe" and, since the commission is not tasked with the probe and can only oversee it, he reiterated that a JIT was crucial for a transparent investigation into the case.
In the latest hearing convened by the commission on Thursday, the commission noted that Ali's business partner Ahmed Bhurdey gave out unnecessary details that suggested his involvement in the murder rather than absolving him of the crime. It suggested that Bhurdey was worried about Ali's financial backlog more than he cared about what happened to his childhood friend. The commission also grilled the SDPO Arshad Afridi for suggesting that Ali committed suicide after showing the CCTV footage to the family.

items.author: Press Release
items.content:
Copyright protected content copied from PhoneWorld website.
Yango Ride has released its 2024–2025 Safety Report, highlighting continued progress in using technology, verification systems and human-led support to strengthen safety across its markets. In Pakistan, the report reveals a 31% decline in post-trip contacts, reflecting the impact of privacy-focused communication tools designed to help passengers and partner drivers communicate without exposing their personal phone numbers.
The report outlines Yango Ride’s approach to safety across every stage of the journey, from pre-ride verification to protected communication, route monitoring, and post-ride accountability. Globally, reported grave traffic violations declined by 31%, from 9.83 incidents per million trips in 2024 to 6.76 in 2025.
Across MENA and South Asia, reported reckless driving incidents fell by 47%, from 19.25 to 10.1 per million trips, with further declines recorded across Africa and Latin America.
In Pakistan, privacy-protecting communication technology has played an important role in improving the experience after a trip. Through features such as in-app calling and number masking, communication can take place without either passengers or partner drivers needing to share their permanent personal contact details. According to the latest data included in the report, post-trip contacts decreased by 31% in Pakistan, compared with 81% in Peru and 78% in Colombia.
The report also highlights Yango Ride’s verification measures, including driver’s licence, identity and vehicle checks. During 2024–2025, Yango expanded selfie-based anti-fraud measures to Pakistan and other markets to help detect attempts to bypass identity controls.
Globally, Yango Ride blocked 17,275 passenger accounts during 2024–2025 after identifying signs of possible fraud. Its safety framework also uses ratings, reports, GPS signals and driving-style analysis to identify repeated unsafe behaviour and take appropriate action.
Urgent support operates 24/7 across Yango Ride markets, with first contact targeted within five minutes in 90% of urgent cases. Technology helps identify urgent requests, while trained specialists review and respond to each situation.
“Yango Ride is a technology service built to make every connection between a passenger and a partner driver safer and more accountable. The results from 2024–2025 show that consistently applied technology — supported by human expertise and local knowledge — can deliver measurable improvements. Reported grave traffic violations dropped by 31% globally. Post-trip contacts decreased sharply in markets where we rolled out protected communication. These are not isolated results: they reflect a framework that operates before, during, and after every ride, across every market where we work. We will keep investing in prevention, detection, and support — because safety is a continuous responsibility, not a fixed set of features”, — comments Roman Karlash, Chief Executive of Yango Ride.
In Pakistan, Yango Ride has connected its safety tools with public infrastructure through the Punjab Safe Cities Authority. When users contact emergency number 15 through Yango’s in-app safety feature, relevant trip and location details can be automatically shared with the police to support a faster response.
Across Yango Ride’s global operations, an incident or near miss is reported on average once every 64,000 kilometres travelled. Going forward, Yango is increasingly focused on earlier risk detection and prevention.
The 2024–2025 Safety Report reflects Yango Ride’s commitment to integrating safety throughout the mobility experience, using technology, local partnerships and continuous improvement to support safer journeys.

items.author: Onsa Mustafa
items.content:
Copyright protected content copied from PhoneWorld website.
A new leak has provided an early look at Samsung’s upcoming Exynos 2700 chipset, which is expected to power some Galaxy S27 series models. The leaked information reveals details about the processor’s CPU, GPU, cache, and AI capabilities.
The leak comes from a die shot shared by SemiAnalysis. The image appears to show the internal layout of the Exynos 2700 and includes labels that reveal several key specifications.
According to the leak, the Exynos 2700 could feature a 10-core CPU based on new Arm CPU designs. The setup is reportedly made up of two C2 Ultra cores and eight C2 Pro cores. One C2 Ultra core could reach 4.24GHz, while the second may run at 3.36GHz.
Exynos 2700 Leak Reveals Major Details of Galaxy S27 Processor
The eight C2 Pro cores are reportedly split into two groups. Four cores could operate at 3.74GHz, while the remaining four may run at 2.88GHz. This is an unusual configuration because the two Ultra cores appear to have different maximum clock speeds.
For comparison, Samsung’s Exynos 2600 reportedly uses one C1 Ultra core at 3.8GHz, three C1 Pro cores at 3.25GHz and six C1 Pro cores at 2.75GHz. The Exynos 2700 therefore appears to bring a different approach to CPU design.
The leaked chip could also include 24MB of system-level cache along with around 16MB of L3 cache. These larger cache sizes could help the processor handle demanding applications and multitasking more efficiently.
However, the reported 4.24GHz peak clock speed is lower than the speeds expected from Qualcomm’s upcoming flagship chips. This suggests that Samsung may be focusing on overall efficiency and architecture improvements rather than simply pushing CPU frequencies higher.
The graphics side could also receive an upgrade. The Exynos 2700 is expected to feature an Xclipse 970 GPU, reportedly with eight workgroup processors (WGPs). This appears to be similar to the GPU configuration previously associated with the Exynos 2600.
Another major highlight is the size of the NPU, or Neural Processing Unit. The leaked die shot shows a relatively large NPU, suggesting that Samsung could be putting more focus on on-device AI performance. This could help the Galaxy S27 series handle AI features more quickly without relying as heavily on cloud processing.
See Also: Samsung Exynos 2700 Shows Impressive Performance Against Snapdragon Chips
Samsung is also reportedly planning to place the Exynos 2700 alongside its DRAM. This design could allow a shared Heat Path Block to cover both components. The approach may improve heat management and help keep temperatures under control during heavy workloads.
The Exynos 2700 is expected to appear in selected Galaxy S27 and Galaxy S27 Plus models. Recent reports have also suggested that Samsung could use the chip in some Galaxy S27 Ultra variants, although this remains unconfirmed.
For now, the leaked specifications should be treated with caution. Samsung has not officially announced the Exynos 2700, and its final specifications could still change before the Galaxy S27 series launches.

items.author: Press Release
items.content:
Copyright protected content copied from PhoneWorld website.
The Securities and Exchange Commission of Pakistan (SECP) registered 4,761 new companies during August 2026, reflecting sustained momentum in business formalization, growing entrepreneurial confidence, and the success of SECP’s facilitation and digital transformation initiatives — driven by the seamless functionality of the eZfile portal and near-total (99.9%) online registrations through integrated federal and provincial systems. The milestone has pushed the total number of registered companies in Pakistan to 311,765.
Commenting on the milestone, Dr. Kabir Ahmed Sidhu, Chairman SECP, stated that the continuous surge in corporate registrations reflects the growing trust of entrepreneurs and investors in Pakistan’s transparent and business-friendly regulatory framework, powered by our digital transformation initiatives.
Private companies continued to account for the largest share of new incorporations, with 2,762 companies (58.01%), followed by 1,846 Single Member Companies (38.78%). In addition, SECP registered 113 Limited Liability Partnerships (2.37%), 28 Not-for-Profit companies (0.59%), and 12 other companies (0.25%) including public companies, foreign and TOs during the month. The sustained preference for private and single-member company structures reflects the growing confidence of startups, SMEs, and entrepreneurs in Pakistan’s corporate regime.
Geographically, Punjab remained the hub of business activity, accounting for 2,547 (53%) of new registrations. This was followed by Islamabad Capital Territory with 843 (18%), Sindh with 702 (15%), Khyber Pakhtunkhwa 407 (9%), Gilgit-Baltistan 151 (3%), and Balochistan 111 (2%). The widespread geographical distribution of incorporations demonstrates that entrepreneurial activity continues to expand across all regions of the country.
The Information Technology sector continues to serve as the primary engine of corporate growth, leading the monthly registrations with 872 new incorporations. The broader diversification of Pakistan’s corporate landscape is further evidenced by robust performance across other key industries, including Trading (732), Services (601), Construction (295), Tourism (232), Food and Beverages (216), E-Commerce (152), Real Estate Development (143), Education (129), and Mining and Quarrying (103), with a further 1,286 incorporations across other sectors , reflecting a well-rounded expansion across multiple segments of the economy.
Foreign investors continued to demonstrate confidence in Pakistan’s corporate sector. During August 2026, 134 investors from several countries participated in newly incorporated companies, led by China with 106 investors.
