items.author: Team Inc42
items.content:
Pernia’s Pop-Up Shop parent Purple Style Labs has set a price band of ₹546 to ₹575 per equity share for its upcoming ₹680 Cr initial public offering.
At the upper end of the price band, the multibrand luxury omnichannel fashion platform will command a post-issue market capitalisation of nearly ₹4,604 Cr (about $483 Mn). Its post-issue valuation at the lower end of the band would be approximately ₹4,406 Cr (about $463 Mn).
The IPO will open for subscription on August 31 (Monday) and close on September 2 (Wednesday). Anchor investor bidding is scheduled for Friday (August 28).
Bids can be placed for a minimum of 26 shares and in multiples of 26 thereafter. Consequently, retail investors will have to invest at least ₹14,196 at the lower end of the price band and ₹14,950 at the upper end.
The IPO comprises entirely a fresh issue of shares worth ₹680 Cr, with no offer for sale component.
A large chunk of the proceeds, ₹371.1 Cr, will be used to fund lease liabilities associated with the company’s network of experience centres. Another ₹138.9 Cr will be deployed towards sales and marketing expenses, while the remaining proceeds will be used for general corporate purposes.
During the IPO press conference, founder and CEO Abhishek Agarwal said lease liabilities and marketing would be Purple Style Labs’ key cost levers over the next three years.
He added that the company would focus on deepening its presence in existing markets, including Mumbai, Delhi, and the US, rather than rapidly expanding into new geographies or adding stores.
As part of this strategy, Purple Style Labs plans to replace smaller outlets with larger experience centres offering a wider range of products.
The larger stores are expected to increase customer spending. Agarwal said the average order value at physical stores is about 2.5X that of the online channel, making experience centres an important avenue for selling higher-value products.
Purple Style Labs is also looking to lower its customer acquisition costs. Agarwal said Pernia’s Pop-Up Shop attracted 1.9 Cr unique visitors in FY26 but served fewer than 1 Lakh customers. Given the platform’s existing reach, the company believes it can reduce spending on brand awareness.
According to Agarwal, its marketing expenditure declined from around ₹50 Cr in FY24 to nearly ₹30 Cr in FY26.
Founded in 2015 by Agarwal, Purple Style Labs operates an omnichannel fashion platform spanning around 15 experience centres, websites, mobile applications, telephone sales, retail channels, and exhibitions. Its portfolio includes Pernia’s Pop-Up Shop and designer labels such as Wendell Rodricks and Hemant Trivedi.
The company acquired Pernia’s Pop-Up Shop in 2018. The platform had around 1,109 designer brands in FY26, while its average order value stood at ₹75,504.9 during the fiscal year.
Purple Style Labs opened four large-format experience centres in FY26 – two in Mumbai and one each in Delhi and New York. FY27 will be the first full year of operations for these stores, which the company expects to drive growth and support its path to profitability.
Purple Style Labs also removed around 800 brands from its website, most of which offered products between ₹5,000-15,000 price range. Agarwal said the move was aimed at eliminating the “long tail” of lower-value products and helped increase the company’s average order value.
“We have removed 800 brands from the website. Most of them were in the long tail between 5 to 15,000 price points,” he said.
Ahead of the IPO, the company posted a consolidated net loss of ₹285.4 Cr for the fiscal year ended March 31, 2026, up 51.5% YoY from ₹188.4 Cr in the previous year. Operating revenue rose about 14% to ₹557.8 Cr from ₹489.9 Cr in the previous fiscal year.
However, Agarwal said the reported loss should not be viewed in isolation, pointing to ESOP (Employee Stock Option Plan) expenses and interest costs that weighed on the bottom line. He said the company is now moving from positive EBITDA towards profitability, with FY27 expected to be an important year as the four large-format experience centres opened in FY26 complete their first full year of operations.
Notably, the company’s ESOP expenses stood at ₹118 Cr in FY26 from ₹123 Cr in FY25, while EBITDA fell 27.7% to ₹30.37 Cr from ₹42 Cr during the same period.
Meanwhile, gross merchandise value (GMV) rose 23% YoY to ₹721.6 Cr, while the customer base declined 6% to 66,713. The company’s management attributed the divergence to its focus on higher-value customers and products, with AOV rising from around ₹45,000 to ₹75,000
Purple Style Labs has raised about $95.4 Mn in funding to date, and counts celebrities like Shah Rukh Khan, Salman Khan and his family, Sachin Tendulkar, Madhuri Dixit and Mahesh Babu among its backers.
Ahead of the IPO, it raised around ₹162.5 Cr (about $17 Mn) across multiple tranches this year since receiving SEBI’s nod for its public listing from a clutch of institutional investors like Kairos Ventures, HNIs and family offices.
Prior to that, the company raised $40 Mn in its Series E funding round in 2025 led by SageOne Flagship Growth OE Fund, Alchemy Long Term Ventures Fund, Bajaj Holdings & Investment, and Minerva Ventures Fund. The round also saw participation from celebrities like Salman Khan and Sachin Tendulkar.

items.author: Web Desk
items.content:
The British lawmakers on Wednesday “lauded Pakistan’s leadership and mediation efforts in the Middle East” in a meeting with Deputy Prime Minister and Foreign Minister Ishaq Dar, saying that “Pakistan’s historic role had been internationally recognised and had filled all overseas Pakistanis with pride”.
FM Dar arrived in London on Sunday to undertake a five-day official visit to the UK from August 24-28. During the visit, FM Dar is due to meet UK Foreign Secretary Ed Miliband and the Foreign, Commonwealth and Development Office minister of state for Pakistan, Stephen Doughty, as well as other senior UK government officials.
According to the statement issued by MoFA today, the parliamentarians included Lord Zameer Choudrey, Lord Qurban Hussain, Baroness Shaista Sheehan, Lord Shaffaq Mohammed and Members of Parliament Mohammad Yasin, Yasmin Qureshi, Afzal Khan, Zubir Ahmed and Adnan Hussain.
FM Dar “appreciated the important role played by the British parliamentarians in strengthening Pakistan-UK ties and their staunch advocacy for a just settlement of the Jammu and Kashmir dispute”, according to the ministry.
Deputy Prime Minister/Foreign Minister Senator Mohammad Ishaq Dar @MIshaqDar50 met a group of cross-party Pakistan-origin British parliamentarians at Pakistan House, London. The parliamentarians included Lord Zameer Choudrey, Lord Qurban Hussain, Baroness Shaista Sheehan, and… pic.twitter.com/OcBc91YR45
— Ministry of Foreign Affairs - Pakistan (@ForeignOfficePk) August 26, 2026
FM Dar shared Pakistan’s ongoing diplomatic initiatives for de-escalation and peace in the Middle East. He underscored that “adherence to the Islamabad Memorandum of Understanding by all parties was critical to achieving durable peace and stability in the region”.
Read: FM Dar urges IMO chief to help secure release of Pakistani crew held by Somali pirates
The deputy prime minister also highlighted “the importance of the Makkah Joint Defence Agreement in strengthening regional peace and stability”. He stressed that “the agreement was purely defensive in nature”, according to the Foreign Office.
The meeting also covered recent developments in Azad Jammu and Kashmir (AJK), with the British parliamentarians congratulating FM Dar on the PML-N’s victory in the recent legislative assembly elections.
FM Dar said that “the people of AJK had reposed their confidence in the PML-N because of its past record of delivering economic growth and development”.
He said the new government would “prioritise investment in infrastructure and job creation for the youth of AJK”.
“The Federal Government and the Government of AJK would work with other political parties and stakeholders to build consensus on important governance and constitutional issues,” FM Dar said.
Read: DPM Dar to undertake five-day official visit to UK from August 24-28th
The parliamentarians also shared their views on other matters of common interest and “reaffirmed their commitment to further cementing ties between Pakistan and the UK”, the ministry said.
During his visit to the UK, FM Dar will also meet Commonwealth Secretary-General Shirley Ayorkor Botchwey. The foreign ministry said the deputy prime minister would also "engage with British parliamentarians and representatives of the British-Pakistani community".
The visit assumes significance against the backdrop of Pakistan's increasingly visible diplomatic role in regional and international affairs, with Islamabad seeking to translate its recent diplomatic engagements into stronger relations with major powers.
Diplomatic sources said FM Dar's visit would provide an opportunity to further consolidate Pakistan's ties with the UK and discuss a range of bilateral, regional and international issues.

items.author: Team Inc42
items.content:
Amazon, Flipkart Tighten Seller Rules
With the festive season just around the corner, India’s ecommerce giants appear to be shifting some of the operational risk onto sellers. While Amazon has raised closing charges, Flipkart is introducing new seller penalty rules. So, what’s cooking in the marketplace arena?
Sellers To Cough Up More: Amazon has introduced a graded cancellation fee for Easy Ship and Self Ship services, increasing the charge from 2% to 10% based on order value. The policy targets seller-initiated and unconfirmed cancellations. Furthermore, Amazon will raise closing fees by ₹1 to ₹3 across fulfillment channels to increase merchant discipline as festive volume ramps up.
Yellow Card For Sellers: Walmart-owned Flipkart has also instituted a three-tier system to penalise operational lapses by merchants without locking their accounts. Sellers missing dispatch deadlines face a ₹30 fine and ₹90 for delayed cancellations. With this, Flipkart aims to improve dispatch compliance while keeping vendor storefronts operational.
Merchant In Crossfire: The stricter penalties mean that sellers are likely to face sharper consequences for cancellations and delays. For merchants already operating on thin margins, the impact may be significant during the festive season, when higher volumes can amplify small per-unit increases.
The Q-Comm Question: The policy changes arrive as quick commerce platforms move beyond groceries into fashion, electronics, beauty and general merchandise. This has increased the strain on marketplaces to deliver faster and more reliably, and the new seller mandates look to ease this pressure.
The Festive Season Test: Festive demand will test whether these policies improve fulfilment or deepen seller anxiety. Accurate inventory, faster dispatch and better manpower planning could protect sellers from penalties, but marketplace-side errors, logistics failures and sudden demand spikes may complicate accountability.
As Amazon and Flipkart seek dependable execution, will seller penalties improve delivery reliability this festive season or will they increase friction for small merchants? Let’s find out…
From The Editor’s Desk
Can Supertails Fetch Profits?
Supertails has expanded from an online retailer into a broader pet care platform, spanning accessories, pharmacy, teleconsultations, food, veterinary clinics and quick commerce. It today serves nearly 1 Mn pet parents.
This expansion helped the startup more than double its operating revenue to ₹200 Cr in FY26, while losses remained broadly unchanged despite investments in clinics, dark stores and other infrastructure. It is now targeting ₹350–400 Cr in revenue in FY27.
Rather than aggressively adding cities, Supertails is now focused on improving the productivity of the infrastructure it has already built. It also plans to increase customer lifetime value, improve retention via data and leverage private labels as the margin lever.
Airbound Nets $37 Mn
The drone tech startup has raised about ₹355 Cr in its Series A round led by US-based investment firm Greenoaks to accelerate engineering, commercial-scale manufacturing, and GTM initiatives. With this, it has raised nearly $50 Mn to date.
Founded in 2023, Airbound designs and makes autonomous drones for transporting goods. It also plans to develop a drone delivery network connecting three cities in Andhra Pradesh, gradually scaling it to 10,000 flights a day.
The fundraise comes as enterprises and startups push the pedal on deploying drones for logistics and last-mile deliveries. At the heart of all this is the homegrown advanced air mobility market, which is projected to become a $4.2 Bn opportunity by 2035.
Zoomcar’s Subdued Q1
The Nasdaq-listed rental car platform saw its net loss balloon 28% YoY to $5.4 Mn in the quarter ended June 2026, while net revenue remained largely flat YoY at $2.4 Mn.
The flat revenue came as gross booking value declined 10% YoY to $5.8 Mn in the quarter under review as the company pivoted its business model towards high-value trips rather than volume. As a result, value per booking rose nearly 7% YoY to $66.
Nevertheless, Zoomcar continues to operate under financial strain due to sustained losses and limited liquidity. As of now, Zoomcar is seeking fresh capital via a private placement bridge financing round, with allotments ranging from $1 Mn to $10 Mn.
Pernia Pop Up Shop Files RHP
Months after SEBI nod, Purple Style Labs has now filed its red herring prospectus with SEBI for an IPO, which will comprise solely of a fresh issue of shares worth ₹680 Cr. The public issue will now open for subscription on August 31 and close on September 2.
Founded in 2015, Purple Style Labs is an omnichannel luxury fashion house that operates multiple designer brands. It has raised a private equity funding of about $78 Mn to date and houses categories spanning wedding, occasion wear and menswear.
On the financial front, Purple Style Labs’ net loss jumped 51% YoY to ₹285.4 Cr in FY26, while revenue from operations also rose almost 14% YoY to ₹557.8 Cr in the fiscal under review.
MATTER Bags $25 Mn
The electric motorcycle startup has raised ₹240 Cr in a funding round from existing backers to expand its manufacturing and supply chain capacity, increase investments in brand building and distribution, and broaden its product portfolio.
Going forward, the startup plans to launch four electric motorcycles based on its AERA platform over the next 12–24 months. With this, MATTER has raised around ₹1,000 Cr to date.
Founded in 2019, MATTER develops powertrains, battery systems, control electronics, and software. It also undertakes vehicle assembly. Its electric motorcycle offers a certified range of 172 kilometres on a single charge.
Inc42 Markets
Inc42 Startup Spotlight
How Palm Era Is Reviving India’s Palm Economy
India’s palm economy is shrinking as fewer climbers now harvest trees. This has left palms unused and traditional livelihoods at risk. Palm Era is trying to reverse this decline by turning palm jaggery and other heritage ingredients into a modern clean-label food brand.
Reviving Heritage: Founded in 2022, Palm Era is building a D2C business around palm-based foods. Its flagship product is palm jaggery, positioned as a natural alternative to refined sugar. The startup also sells palm-based powders, probiotic jaggery, digestive bites and other clean-label products.
From Trees To Products: Palm Era’s model is designed to create value beyond raw sap collection. It works with palm climbers to source ingredients and then works with women’s self-help groups to process palm sprouts. This helps create employment beyond the harvesting season.
It also uses processing and packaging to extend shelf life, while presenting palm-based foods as convenient, healthier and chemical-free alternatives for urban consumers.
Finding Scale: Palm Era featured on the Tamil startup reality show Startup Singam, where it secured an investor commitment and gained visibility. The brand claims an annual revenue of about ₹4.33 Cr currently, and is now looking to expand distribution and build a larger market for palm products.
So, can Palm Era turn a fading tradition into India’s next clean-label food opportunity?

By Sola Ogundipe
The Lagos State Health Management Agency (LASHMA) has tasked journalists with driving public awareness and uptake of the state’s mandatory health insurance scheme, warning that the policy cannot succeed if residents remain uninformed or distrust the system.
The agency’s Permanent Secretary, Dr. Emmanuella Zamba, who gave the charge at a two-day capacity-building programme for journalists on the Lagos State Health Scheme and Ilera Eko, said the media must become a stronger force for explaining health insurance, challenging misinformation, exposing gaps and holding institutions accountable.
“Policies alone do not guarantee success; their effectiveness depends on understanding, cooperation and participation, the media therefore has a critical responsibility to explain policies accurately, dispel myths, amplify impact and hold institutions accountable.”
Her message came as the state pushes ahead with mandatory health insurance for all residents under an Executive Order signed by Governor Babajide Sanwo-Olu on July 16, 2024.
“In a megacity like Lagos, health insurance is essential to protecting residents from catastrophic healthcare expenses, providing peace of mind, strengthening the health system and promoting sustainable healthcare financing,” she said.
She urged journalists to use their platforms to explain what ILERA EKO offers, how residents can enrol and access services, while also questioning shortcomings that could undermine confidence in the scheme.
Zamba said LASHMA was investing in media capacity because public awareness and trust would determine whether mandatory health insurance translated into actual coverage.
The agency trained additional 36 journalists following the 56 trained in February 2026 under the first phase of the initiative.
The journalists, their family members and dependants, received one year of free health insurance coverage from LASHMA.
The state has also increased its Equity Fund for vulnerable residents from N1 billion to N3 billion, financed through one percent of the Consolidated Revenue Fund.

items.content:
By Damilola Samuel
Health ministers from 47 African countries have begun discussions in Addis Ababa, Ethiopia, on measures to strengthen healthcare systems and improve the continent’s response to emerging health challenges.
The three-day meeting, which opened on Tuesday, is the 76th session of the World Health Organisation Regional Committee for Africa and brings together health ministers, government officials, development partners and health experts.
The meeting is expected to produce decisions that will influence health policies and investments across the region in the coming year.
One of the major issues before the ministers is how African countries can secure more sustainable funding for healthcare at a time when many countries are dealing with limited resources and growing health needs.
The ministers will also consider the Africa Health Workforce Agenda 2026–2035, which is aimed at helping countries train, employ and retain more health workers.
Opening the session, Ethiopian President Taye Atske Selassie called for African countries to rely more on their own capacity and strengthen cooperation rather than continue depending heavily on external support.
“Africa’s next health chapter must be defined by ownership over dependency, integration over fragmentation and practical action over words,” he said.
Ethiopia’s Minister of Health, Dr Mekdes Daba, said the continent must prepare its health systems for challenges ranging from climate change and emerging technologies to demographic changes, health inequalities and complex emergencies.
The issue of health security is also high on the agenda as African countries continue to face outbreaks and other public health emergencies.
The ministers are expected to consider a framework for strengthening national emergency medical teams so that countries can respond more quickly when outbreaks, disasters and other emergencies occur.
The discussions come as the Democratic Republic of Congo battles its largest Ebola outbreak, highlighting the need for countries to maintain the capacity to detect and respond to infectious disease threats.
The ministers will also examine proposals aimed at protecting Africa’s progress in the fight against polio by maintaining surveillance systems, laboratories, trained personnel and emergency response structures developed during the eradication campaign.
WHO Regional Director for Africa, Dr Mohamed Janabi, said the decisions taken at the meeting would have an impact beyond the three-day gathering.
“The decisions we take this week will shape policies, guide investments and influence future generations,” Janabi said.
Another proposal before the committee is the creation of a Regional Health Data Hub, which is expected to help countries identify health threats earlier, improve the allocation of resources and use reliable data in making health decisions.
The meeting will also consider a long-term framework, A New Era of Health for Africa: United Action for Vision 2035, which focuses on stronger primary healthcare, resilient health systems, sustainable financing, digital transformation and greater ownership of health programmes by African countries.
The WHO said the outcomes of the meeting would guide its support to member states and strengthen cooperation among African countries as they work towards building more resilient and self-reliant health systems.

… As CareCode Hackathon awards ₦10m to young African innovators
By Sola Ogundipe
Africa has been admonished to move beyond dependence on imported healthcare technologies and build solutions around its own health challenges.
Making the call in Lagos during the MedVerge 2.0 health technology gathering hosted by three health initiatives: HelpMum, Dobic Health, and SmartMRS, Dr. Abiodun Adereni, the convener, said the continent had the talent, technology and enormous healthcare challenges required to develop solutions that could improve access, efficiency and quality of care.
Addressing participants, Adereni, said the MedVerge initiative brings together the three healthcare ventures which he founded: HelpMum Africa, which uses technology and AI to tackle maternal and child health challenges; Dobic Health, which is expanding access to technology enabled clinical services; and SmartMRS, an AI powered electronic medical records platform designed to digitise healthcare operations and improve patient care.
“MedVerge is a platform for convergence. We have the talent, we have the problems that need solving, what we need is stronger collaboration and the confidence to develop solutions around our own realities,” Adereni said. He argued that African countries should not wait for solutions developed elsewhere before addressing their healthcare challenges.
“MedVerge was created to bring healthcare and technology professionals together, expose young African professionals to emerging technologies and demonstrate how locally developed solutions could address local health problems,” he said
Noting that the convergence of the three platforms was deliberate, he identified sustainability as one of the biggest challenges facing health innovation in Africa.
“We don’t collaborate enough; stronger collaboration is needed among governments, technology companies, healthcare providers, development organisations and innovators.” he said.
He urged the health sector to learn from the tech and financial services sectors for integration of platforms and ecosystems, even as he called for successful innovations to be transferred to the government and integrated into public health programmes.
“If an innovation has demonstrated value, the government should be able to adopt it, scale it and sustain it as a public health asset,” he said.
Such an approach, he argued, would allow innovations developed by African organisations to reach
larger populations instead of remaining small pilot projects.
Speaking during a fireside session titled “The Days Ahead Are Tough,” moderated by Deborah Oguike, Adereni reflected on his decade of building businesses at the intersection of healthcare, technology and infrastructure.
He said expanding health insurance coverage would provide the financial foundation needed to drive innovation and improve access to quality healthcare. He also disclosed his ambition to acquire a licensed Health Maintenance Organisation and use it to expand Dobic Health’s modern healthcare facilities across Africa.
“Health insurance is the factor that will help scale healthcare innovations. I don’t see AI replacing doctors, but I see it making the work of clinicians faster and more efficient in diagnosis,” he said.
Adereni said Nigeria should aim to become a producer and exporter of health technology rather than remain largely a consumer of solutions developed outside the continent.
“Nigeria should not simply be a market for health technology developed elsewhere. We should be a place where health technology is developed, tested, improved and scaled,” he said.
He argued that Nigeria needed policies that encourage technology adoption, sustainable financing, better infrastructure and stronger partnerships between government and innovators.
The broader message from MedVerge was that Africa’s healthcare future cannot be built entirely by Importing solutions. It has to be built from within.
CareCode Hackathon awards ₦10m to young innovators
In a related development. HelpMum Africa has awarded ₦10 million to three young teams whose innovations emerged from its CareCode Hackathon, an initiative aimed at promoting technology driven solutions to healthcare challenges in Nigeria and across Africa.
The hackathon brought together young innovators to develop and pitch products and ideas focused on the future of healthcare. Five teams – HerPride, Lavender Care, ChopBeta, Bumply and MamaConnect, made it to the final stage of the competition.
At the end of the competition, Lavender Care emerged as the top beneficiary, receiving ₦5 million, ChopBeta won ₦3 million and Bumply received ₦2 million. The awards formed part of broader efforts by HelpMum Africa and its partners to encourage young people to apply technology and innovation to some of the continent’s most pressing healthcare challenges.
The initiative was highlighted alongside a second panel session, “AI’s Next Chapter in Healthcare,” which brought together leading health technology founders to examine the growing role of artificial intelligence in healthcare and its potential to reshape how health services are delivered.
HelpMum Africa, Dobic Health and SmartMRS reaffirmed their commitment to supporting healthcare innovation, entrepreneurship and technology driven solutions across Nigeria and the continent.
The post Africa must harness technology to fix healthcare crisis — Adereni appeared first on Vanguard News.

items.author: Nwafor
items.content:
By Sola Ogundipe
The Director-General of the National Agency for the Control of AIDS (NACA), Dr. Temitope Ilori, has cautioned Nigerians against HIV cure claims, stressing that modern treatment can only suppress the virus to undetectable levels and enable people living with HIV to live long, healthy lives.
Ilori, who spoke during a media training on HIV Pre-exposure Prophylaxis (PrEP) and other prevention strategies, said people who test positive to HIV should commence antiretroviral (ARV) treatment promptly and remain on medication.
At the event held in collaboration with the Federal Ministry of Health and Social Welfare, and the World Health Organisation (WHO), she said effective treatment has transformed HIV from an infection of certain death into a manageable condition.
“Early diagnosis and treatment can prevent HIV from progressing to AIDS, people who remain on effective treatment can maintain healthy immune systems, but feeling healthy after stopping medication does not mean the virus has disappeared,” she stated.
Expressing concern over people who abandon ARV therapy after told they have been cured and advised to stop taking their drugs, she said “There is no cure for HIV, as of today; some people have proposed that they have cures, but science says otherwise, those claims have not been tested.
“To the best of my knowledge, it has not been documented scientifically that somebody was cured. If you are living with HIV and someone tells you that you have been healed, don’t stop your medication.,” she asserted.
Further, Ilori said consistent treatment can reduce the amount of HIV in the blood to undetectable levels.
“While ARV therapy can suppress HIV effectively, there is no cure for HIV as of today. An HIV diagnosis is no longer a death sentence, but it is not the same thing as being cured.
“For now, science offers something highly effective but different from a cure – treatment that can suppress HIV to undetectable levels, protect the immune system and prevent sexual transmission,” she noted.
“People on treatment are not supposed to stop their medication, the drugs are effective and, when taken consistently, can suppress the virus to undetectable levels. Suppressed such that by the time you go for your six month appointment, many times the virus is almost undetected, and that’s where the expression “undetectable equals untransmittable” comes from.
“Undetectable equals untransmittable,” she said, explaining that people living with HIV who achieve and maintain an undetectable viral load through effective treatment do not sexually transmit the virus.
She said the development has also made it possible for HIV-positive and HIV-negative couples to have normal relationships and biological children without transmitting HIV, provided the partner living with HIV remains on effective treatment and maintains viral suppression.
L- R: Dr. Taiwo Olakunle; Deputy Director; Prevention Component; National AIDS, Viral Hepatitis and STI Control Programme (NASCP), Pharm. Halima Momodu; National Consultant, World Health Organization (WHO), Dr. Temitope Ilori, Director General, National Agency for the Control of AIDS (NACA); Dr. Oluwafunke Odunlade, Technical Officer, HIV, Viral Hepatitis & STIs, World Health Organisation (WHO); Mrs. Toyin Aderibigbe, Head Public Relations and Protocol, National Agency for the Control of AIDS (NACA) and Dr. Ayoola Abiodun, Director, Health and Social Care, National Orientation Agency (NOA) at the training of media personnel on Pre-exposure Prophylaxis (PrEP) in Lagos.
The NACA boss said people should not abandon medically prescribed treatment based on unverified claims of healing even as she admonished the media to help tackle misinformation and stigma surrounding HIV, particularly false claims about cures and misconceptions about how the virus is transmitted.
Highlighting the growing role of HIV prevention technologies, Ilori stressed said “Pre-exposure prophylaxis (PrEP) provides HIV-negative people at substantial risk of infection with an additional layer of protection. Options include daily oral PrEP and long-acting injectable PrEP. Nigeria has introduced newer long-acting prevention options, including cabotevir and Lenacapavir, a twice-yearly injectable HIV prevention option.
She also urged Nigerians to use condoms, know their HIV status, get tested and seek immediate treatment where necessary.
The NACA boss said misinformation remains a major obstacle to HIV control, with some people still believing that HIV can be transmitted through hugging, shaking hands, sharing food or drinks, or mosquito bites. She said such misconceptions fuel stigma and discrimination against people living with HIV.
Ilori said Nigeria’s HIV response had made significant progress but warned that the country must sustain prevention, testing and treatment efforts if it is to achieve epidemic control.
She said the focus must now be on ensuring that people know their HIV status, those who test positive commence treatment and remain on it, while those at substantial risk have access to appropriate prevention tools.
The challenge, Ilori said, is ensuring that Nigerians have accurate information and continue treatment long enough to benefit from those advances.
Three PrEP options used for HIV prevention in the country include, the daily oral PrEP which is a tablet taken every day, the “Event driven” or “2+1+1” PrEP taken around sexual activity rather than every day, and the long acting injectable PrEP, Cabotegravir (CAB-LA) given at two month intervals, and the recently introduced long acting injectable Lenacapavir (LEN) administered twice a year.

items.author: Nwafor
items.content:
By Folashade Ajayi, Co-Founder, CareStrong
When a person’s heart stops, every second suddenly matters.
The heart’s job is remarkably simple. It pumps oxygen-rich blood around the body, supplying the brain and vital organs with what they need to function. When that pumping action stops, the consequences begin almost immediately.
Without a constant supply of blood, the brain starts to suffer damage. The longer the interruption continues, the greater the risk of permanent injury or death.
This is where CPR comes in.
CPR stands for Cardiopulmonary Resuscitation. It is one of the most widely taught emergency skills in the world and one of the most important interventions available during a cardiac emergency.
Despite its familiarity, CPR is often misunderstood.
Many people imagine it as a complex medical procedure performed only by doctors or paramedics. Others know the term but have little understanding of what it actually does.
In reality, CPR is designed to help maintain blood circulation when the heart is no longer pumping effectively. By applying rhythmic chest compressions, blood can continue moving through the body while further medical care is being arranged.
CPR does not restart the heart. It is not a miracle cure. It does not guarantee survival.
What it does is help sustain life during a critical period when every minute matters.
One of the most common misconceptions about CPR comes from television and films, where a person receives a few chest compressions and immediately opens their eyes. Real emergencies are rarely so dramatic.
CPR is physically demanding. It requires persistence and effort. Its purpose is not to provide an instant recovery but to keep vital organs supplied with blood for as long as possible.
Over the years, millions of people around the world have learned CPR. Most are not healthcare professionals.
They are ordinary members of the public who understand that emergencies do not always happen in hospitals.
Cardiac emergencies can occur in offices, airports, homes, places of worship, restaurants, meeting rooms, and countless other everyday environments.
When they do, the people nearby are often the first witnesses.
Understanding CPR does not turn someone into a medical professional. It simply helps people understand one of the most important actions available during a cardiac emergency.
For a skill that requires no medical degree, CPR has helped save countless lives around the world. That is why it continues to be taught, practised, and promoted across so many countries and communities.
Next Week: The Machine That Can Restart a Heart – understanding the automated device designed to work alongside CPR during a cardiac emergency.
THE FIRST 5 MINUTES Preparedness Saves Lives.

The Peoples Democratic Party (PDP) governorship candidate in Cross River, Arthur Archibong, has accepted Gov. Bassey Otu’s challenge to an open debate.
Archibong said he was ready to debate Otu at any time and venue the governor chose, provided Otu attended personally.
The candidate spoke with journalists in Calabar on Tuesday, responding to a challenge issued by the state Commissioner for Information, Ekpenyong Cobham.
“I am willing to honour the challenge to a debate, on one condition: that Gov. Bassey Otu will be there in person.
“The people deserve to hear directly from those seeking to lead them, not from proxies,” he said.
Archibong said he would not engage Cobham in a war of words, describing the commissioner as his brother and stressing he was not on the ballot.
“Pastor Cobham is my brother. But he is not on the ballot, so I will not join issues with him,” he said.
Cobham had earlier challenged Archibong to publicly debate the Otu administration’s policies, programmes and performance ahead of the 2027 election.
Archibong also defended Arthur Jarvis University (AJU), which he founded in Akpabuyo Local Government Area, against recent criticisms.
He described the allegations against the institution as politically motivated, saying AJU was established to contribute to Cross River’s development.
He urged critics to focus instead on environmental sanitation, blocked drainages and emergency response, particularly the condition of Watt Market.
He said: “Instead of chasing imaginary bedbugs in Akpabuyo, they should come and see the real crisis in Watt Market.
“Go there today and see the filth, the stench, the blocked drainages, and traders selling beside refuse.”
Archibong also alleged that inadequate resources were undermining emergency response, particularly the state fire service.
“Our firefighters have no diesel. Our fire trucks have no water. And when infernos like the one at SPAR Mall happened, we are left helpless,” he said.
The PDP candidate expressed sympathy for traders, workers and families affected by the recent fire at SPAR Shopping Mall in Calabar.
He promised that his administration, if elected, would strengthen emergency response and provide firefighters with water, diesel and essential equipment.
Archibong also questioned the economic benefits of the administration’s foreign investment trips and Memoranda of Understanding (MoUs).
“After so many MoUs, show me how many have translated to successful projects that are addressing the pitiful situation of this state.
“Where are the factories? Where are the jobs? Where is the relief for the ordinary man?” he asked.
The candidate criticised what he described as Otu’s absence during crises, citing recent landslides and the SPAR Mall fire.
“When landslides claimed lives and destroyed properties, and when fire swept through our businesses like the recent SPAR Mall crisis, the presence of our governor is nowhere to be found,” he said.
On scholarships, Archibong said educational support remained a personal commitment rather than an instrument for political advantage.
“Scholarships are a personal act of service. I will not bring charity to the marketplace just to score cheap political points,” he said.
He urged voters to make the 2027 election a contest based on ideas, records, competence and service rather than money, intimidation or violence.
Archibong said: “Cross River deserves a governor who will not govern from a distance or by proxy.
“Our people deserve leadership that shows up, listens and delivers. Let this contest be about ideas, about track records, and about who is ready to serve.”

items.content:
…Says poll not about money bags, but scorecard , performance
By Ike Uchechukwu, CALABAR
The Peoples Democratic Party (PDP) governorship candidate in Cross River, Sir Arthur Javis-Archibong, has accepted a challenge to engage Gov. Bassey Otu in an open debate ahead of the 2027 governorship election.
Archibong, who spoke with journalists in Calabar on Tuesday, said he was ready to participate in the debate at any time and venue chosen by the governor, provided Otu would attend personally.
His response followed a challenge issued by the state Commissioner for Information, Pst Ekpenyong Cobham.
“I am willing to honour the challenge to a debate, on one condition: that Governor Bassey Otu will be there in person.
“The people deserve to hear directly from those seeking to lead them, not from proxies,” he said.
Archibong said he would not engage in a verbal exchange with Cobham, describing the commissioner as his brother.
“Pastor Cobham is my brother. But he is not on the ballot, so I will not join issues with him,” he said.
The PDP candidate also defended Arthur Jarvis University (AJU), the private university he established in Akpabuyo Local Government Area, against recent criticisms.
Archibong said the institution was established to contribute to the development of Cross River and would not be distracted by what he described as false allegations.
“All sorts of things have been said about AJU. Funnily enough, the last I heard of bed bugs was in my childhood when we slept on straw beds,” he said.
He challenged those criticising the university to demonstrate their own contributions to the state, particularly through employment and business development.
“Before pointing fingers at AJU, they should first point to one business they own where they have employed at least 15 people from this state,” he said.
Archibong said attention should instead be directed at pressing challenges confronting the state, including environmental sanitation, drainage and emergency response.
“Instead of chasing imaginary bedbugs in Akpabuyo, they should come and see the real crisis in Watt Market.
“Go there today and see the filth, the stench, the blocked drainages, and traders selling beside refuse. That is the environmental emergency staring us in the face.
“Our firefighters have no diesel. Our fire trucks have no water. And when infernos like the one at SPAR Mall happened, we are left helpless.
“That is where government attention should be, not in spreading lies about a university that is trying to add value,” he said.
On scholarships, Archibong said supporting education had always been a personal commitment and should not be reduced to political propaganda.
“Scholarships are a personal act of service. I will not bring charity to the marketplace just to score cheap political points,” he said.
He urged Cobham to conduct proper research before making public statements, particularly by consulting residents of Akpabuyo, Bakassi and other communities who, he said, had benefited from his interventions over the years.
Archibong also criticised what he described as attacks on his character, urging the commissioner to uphold the values associated with the Christian faith.
“Barefaced lying is alien to the calling of a pastor. If he is truly a pastor and not self-acclaimed, then he should be wary of the God who sees and knows all things,” he said.
He added that the 2027 election should be determined by the electorate rather than money, intimidation or violence.
According to him, This election will not be won by attacking institutions that should be supported by government. Arthur Jarvis University is a thriving institution that employs our people and trains our children.
“Instead of support, it is being subjected to unprovoked attacks simply because of politics. That is not how you build a state.”
Archibong further criticised the Otu administration over what he described as the governor’s absence during moments of crisis, citing landslides and the recent fire incident at SPAR Shopping Mall in Calabar.
“When landslides claimed lives and destroyed properties, and when fire swept through our businesses like the recent SPAR Mall crisis, the presence of our governor is nowhere to be found,” he said.
He questioned the economic impact of the administration’s foreign investment trips and memoranda of understanding (MoUs), saying Cross Riverians were yet to see sufficient tangible outcomes.
“Government keeps going out for MoUs, but Cross Riverians are yet to see the dividends.
“After so many MoUs, show me how many have translated to successful projects that are addressing the pitiful situation of this state.
“Where are the factories? Where are the jobs? Where is the relief for the ordinary man? You cannot be absent at home in the name of chasing investors abroad, while the house is on fire and there is no water to put it out,” he said.
The PDP candidate expressed sympathy for traders, workers and families affected by the early Saturday fire at SPAR Shopping Mall.
“My heart bleeds for every trader, every young worker, and every family whose livelihood went up in flames that morning.
“As a businessman myself, I know the pain of watching years of sweat and sacrifice turn to ashes overnight,” he said.
Archibong promised that, if elected, his administration would strengthen emergency response and equip the state fire service with the necessary resources.
“Under my watch, we will never be caught unprepared again. Emergency response will be fast, equipped, and present.
“We will ensure our fire service has water, has diesel, and has the tools to protect lives and properties within the time of need. No Cross Riverian should ever have to face disaster alone,” he said.
Archibong said leadership was ultimately about presence, service and accountability.
“Cross River deserves a governor who will not govern from a distance or by proxy.
“Our people deserve leadership that shows up, listens, and delivers. That is the covenant I offer the people of Cross River in 2027.
“Let this contest be about ideas, about track records, and about who is ready to serve and nothing less,” he added.

By Juliet Umeh
Security analyst and lawyer, Dr Bulama Bukarti, has said that terrorist groups operating in Nigeria are exploiting social media, international remittance services to raise and move funds into the country.
Bukarti, who spoke on Channels Television on Tuesday, said terrorism financing was becoming more sophisticated, warning that unsuspecting Nigerians at home and abroad could unknowingly fund terrorist activities.
He said the Nigerian Financial Intelligence Unit, NFIU, report revealed how foreign-based individuals solicit donations through Telegram and Instagram, disguising appeals as humanitarian or educational support.
According to him, donations ranging from $50 to $500 are accumulated in a master account before being broken into smaller amounts and transferred to different recipients in Nigeria through international remittance platforms.
“These people are doing all of this in order to evade Nigeria’s tightening financial regulations,” he said.
Bukarti urged Nigerians to conduct checks before donating online, stressing that the warning was not against genuine humanitarian assistance.
“It is not a call for us to stop supporting humanitarian or educational appeals. It is a call for us to do our due diligence, know the person you are donating to and make sure you trust them,” he said.
He also called for stronger linkage of Bank Verification Numbers, BVN, with SIM cards, saying deceased persons’ accounts and accounts controlled by third parties had allegedly been exploited for terrorism financing.
“We need to strengthen the linkage between Bank Verification Numbers and SIM cards. The NFIU and the Nigerian Communications Commission must work together to ensure that only properly registered and verified SIM cards are linked to bank accounts and used for financial transactions.
“The only way to defeat terrorism is to follow the money,” he said.
He also warned: “People need to be careful. If someone says, ‘carry this for me’, trust them first and make sure you know what you are carrying,” he said.
On jungle justice, Bukarti said, “Jungle justice is not justice. It is injustice, and it is cruel, and it only sends a country into anarchy.”
He called for prompt investigations and prosecutions, saying law-enforcement failures did not justify mob action.
“The failure by government or security and law enforcement agencies doesn’t justify jungle justice,” he said.
Bukarti also called for a multinational security pact between Nigeria, Niger and Benin to tackle emerging terrorist corridors.
“Nigeria needs to do more,” he said, adding that cutting terrorists’ financial lifelines was crucial.

items.author: Emmanuel Okogba
items.content:
. Project to gulp 𝗡548.98𝗯𝗻, ready within 24 months
By Olasunkanmi Akoni
The Federal Government has commenced the demolition of the dilapidated Carter Bridge in Lagos, with an estimated N548.98 billion set for reconstruction.
The rehabilitation project is expected to be completed within 24 months instead of the 36 months initially scheduled for the project.
Minister of Works, Sen. Dave Umahi, disclosed this while inspecting the reconstruction of the Carter Bridge and the Iddo Bridge in Lagos.
The minister was accompanied by the Minister of State for Works, Sen. Mohammed Goronyo, and some members of the National Assembly, including the Chairman of the House of Representatives Committee on Works, Mr Akin Alabi.
Umahi said the Federal Government was accelerating work on the bridge because of its importance to vehicle movement in Lagos.
He said the bridge, which is about 1.58km long, had remained in use for more than 60 years with inadequate maintenance, leading to serious structural problems.
“Carter Bridge has stayed for over 60 to 70 years with no maintenance.
“The lifespan of every bridge is about 50 years, and what we found out from the underwater survey is that a lot of the piles had detached from the pile caps.
“It is like having the leg removed from the hip. There was also a lot of rust within the piles, while scouring and illegal sand mining contributed to the failure of the bridge,” he said.
The minister said the government had completed the new design for the bridge and introduced features that would improve traffic flow and protect the structure from future damage.
According to Umahi, the new bridge will have additional ramps to reduce congestion, with one carriageway built above the other.
He said a cable-stayed section would also be introduced to provide adequate clearance for navigation.
“We are going to be flying one carriageway over the other, increasing the number of ramps to decongest traffic towards the ramp sections.
“We are also having a cable bridge to contain the 105 spans for navigational activities. It is going to be beautiful,” Umahi said.
He said the contractor, China Civil Engineering Construction Company (CCECC), had completed about 15 per cent of preparatory work, including acquiring the project yard and constructing access roads.
According to the minister, piling is expected to commence before the end of the week.
The minister said the government was also introducing additional protective measures, including gabions, to protect the bridge foundations from erosion and scouring.
Umahi said that Carter Bridge could not be closed completely during the reconstruction because of its importance to vehicular movement.
He said the Federal Government would therefore carry out regular monitoring and maintenance of the existing structure until the new bridge is completed.
“If we close Carter Bridge, Lagos will go into katakata (chaos). That is why we are maintaining it while the reconstruction is going on,” he said.
Umahi also said the Federal Government was applying similar measures on the Third Mainland Bridge, adding that the intervention was designed to extend its lifespan by another 50 years.
He expressed confidence that the new Carter Bridge would last for more than 100 years because of the additional engineering features being introduced.
The minister commended the contractor for progress made so far, and thanked members of the National Assembly for their support.
Earlier, the Federal Controller of Works in Lagos, Mr Olufemi Dare, told the minister that the contractor had mobilised to site and was constructing access roads.
He said the contractor’s yard had also been established, while piling work was expected to begin soon.
Dare also briefed the minister on progress on the Iddo Bridge.
He said three spans of the bridge — spans 13, 14 and 15 — had failed completely and had been replaced.
“Three days ago, we completed the casting, and the bridge has also been elevated, giving us very good headroom underneath.
“In another 10 days, after the concrete has cured, we will open this section to traffic and close the other section, after which demolition will start immediately,” he said.
Dare said that other components of the Iddo Bridge project were also progressing, with drainage and Continuously Reinforced Concrete Pavement (CRCP) works about 90 per cent completed.
He expressed confidence that the Iddo Bridge intervention would be completed within two months.
Sen. Allwell Onyesoh, who was in the minister’s entourage, described the reconstruction of Carter Bridge as timely, noting that Lagos had experienced significant population growth since the bridge was originally constructed.
Onyesoh said the National Assembly would support measures necessary to complete the project successfully.
The Chairman of the House of Representatives Committee on Works, Mr Akin Alabi, said the reconstruction was long overdue.
He said that the bridge ought to have been rehabilitated and expanded many years ago.
He commended Umahi for his commitment to the project, and expressed confidence that its completion would benefit Lagos residents and Nigerians generally.
The post 𝗙𝗚 commences reconstruction of Carter Bridge appeared first on Vanguard News.

items.content:
United States singer, actress, businesswoman and philanthropist, Dolly Parton, has died at the age of 80.
Parton, who was known for hit songs including “Jolene” and “Coat of Many Colors,” died on Tuesday, August 25, 2026.
Her death was announced by her nephew, Bryan Seaver, in a video shared on social media.
“Dolly has lived in the light and is in the arms of Jesus,” Seaver said.
He described Parton as a multiple award-winning singer who had “opened doors for generations of singers, songwriters, musicians, and dreamers from every walk of life.”
The family did not disclose the cause of her death.
However, Parton had spoken publicly in recent months about her health, including her decision to cancel a series of planned Las Vegas concerts in May because of ongoing health concerns.
In videos shared on her social media accounts, Parton said that treatment for an unspecified illness was going well, but that she was not ready to return to the stage.
Parton’s death comes a year after the death of her husband, Carl Dean.
United States President Donald Trump ordered American flags to be lowered to half-staff across the United States for a week in honour of Parton, describing her death as a “true loss for millions of people.”
“There has never been anyone like her, and never will,” Trump posted on Truth Social.
Parton spent her entire adult life at the centre of Americana, folk and country music, building a career that spanned six decades.
The day after graduating from high school, she moved to Nashville, the country music capital, to pursue a career in music.
By 1967, at the age of 21, Parton had become one of the most recognised figures in American music after joining Porter Wagoner’s syndicated country music television show.
The programme helped take her voice and image into millions of homes across the United States and marked a major stage in the development of her career.
Over the course of her six-decade career, Parton was prolific as a songwriter, penning about 3,000 songs.
Among her best-known works were the soundtrack hit “9 to 5,” “Islands In the Stream” and the iconic ballad “I Will Always Love You,” which later became an international success for Whitney Houston.
Parton released 49 studio albums as well as more than 100 compilation and collaboration albums during her career, earning her the title of the “queen of country music.”
Her influence extended beyond her own recordings, with her songs being covered by several prominent artists, including Shania Twain, Sinead O’Connor and the White Stripes.
Through her music and career, Parton became one of the most enduring figures in American popular culture, establishing herself as an American treasure whose work influenced generations of singers, songwriters and musicians.

Alhaji Bello Matawalle, Minister of State for Defence, has urged Muslims in Nigeria to use the Maulud period to pray for peace ahead of the 2027 general elections.
Matawalle made the call in a statement issued in Gusau on Tuesday by the Publicity Secretary, Matawalle Political Movement, Malam Yusuf Idris.
Felicitating the Muslim Ummah on the occasion of 1448AH/2026 Maulud celebration, the minister urged them to use the period for prayer and supplication for the return of peace in the state and country at large.
“The Prophet Muhammad’s teachings cover every aspect of human life and should be emulated by every Muslim.
“Eid-el-Maulud offers the Muslim Ummah an opportunity for reflection on the teachings of the noble Prophet Muhammad (SAW), which are anchored on peace, unity, and love for humanity,” he said.
According to the minister, the Prophet’s teachings encompass every facet of human life and remain worthy of emulation by all Muslims.
Matawalle, therefore, urged Muslims to emulate the virtues of love, peace, tolerance, and compassion exemplified by the Holy Prophet Muhammad (SAW).

items.author: Emmanuel Okogba
items.content:
By Samuel Oyadongha, Yenagoa
The National Chairman of the Pan Niger Delta Forum (PANDEF), Ambassador Godknows Igali, has decried the deteriorating condition of roads across the South-South region, declaring that the oil-rich area has been reduced to a state of “crisis” despite being the nation’s economic backbone.
Speaking against the backdrop of the horrific state of the Benin-Agbor-Asaba Road, where motorists have been stranded for days amid severe gridlock, Igali said the Federal Government’s continued neglect of the region’s infrastructure was breeding bitterness and alienation among its people.
He said’ “We are the goose that lays the golden egg, but that goose has almost been starved.”
The PANDEF chairman recalled that about a month ago, he had held a press conference in Abuja to lament the Federal Executive Council’s approval of N3.9 trillion for 27 major road projects across the country, none of which were in the South-South.
He noted that of the 26 projects covering 15 states, the only one remotely connected to the region was the road linking Cross River and Benue states, which received just N86 billion out of the nearly N4 trillion allocation.
“I never said the President should only concentrate on one part of the country, even if we are the revenue base of the nation,” Igali said. “We only demand, and rightly so, to be treated with fairness and equity.”
Painting a grim picture of the region’s road network, Igali detailed the ordeal facing travellers daily. On the Benin-Sapele-Warri corridor, he said motorists at Mosogar can spend up to three or four hours navigating a single stretch. The once 40-minute journey from Warri to Sapele now takes two to three hours, if travellers can find passable routes at all.
The East-West Road, he said, “has become a metaphor for failed projects.” On the Port Harcourt axis towards Eleme Junction, the road is terribly bad, with commuters spending hours in traffic, especially at peak periods.
Travelling from the University of Port Harcourt towards Bayelsa State presents its own nightmare, Igali said. “After Elele, you begin to connect. You pass two kilometres, cross to the other side, go 500 metres, cross back to this side, go one kilometre. It’s like a zigzag. There is no straight five-to-ten-kilometre stretch.”
Contractors are present on many sections, he acknowledged, but work has slowed to a crawl due to payment issues and logistical challenges. On the Calabar route, about 60 per cent of the road has been completed, but the remaining portion is in such bad shape that even the finished sections are deteriorating because contractors are not on site to properly complete the work.
“It is becoming almost impossible to connect within the South-South,” Igali lamented. “From Benin to Auchi, there are so many bad sections. Going from Auchi to Okene, which is an entrance into the South-South, is almost impossible. On the other side, from Benin, once you pass towards Akure, it is also very bad. So, we are in an almost crisis situation.”
The PANDEF chairman cited the recent fifth coronation of the Olu of Warri as a stark example of the crisis. Many guests were stuck for hours on the road; some turned back at Sapele, while others abandoned their journey at Oghara because they could not reach Mosogar.
“Our people are not happy. They may not say it out of respect, but people are very bitter and sad,” Igali said.
He pointed to the case, where fish and other goods were left to rot because the roads were impassable. The situation is compounded by the fact that the South-South is a major transit route for trailers, which block roads as they navigate failed sections, causing gridlocks everywhere.
Igali, who said his position as PANDEF chairman keeps him constantly on the road attending events across Delta, Akwa Ibom, and other states, noted that he sees construction equipment stationed at various points but no workers.
“My inquiry, and my people’s inquiry, shows that many contractors have slowed down the pace, not just because of the rainy season, but due to payment and other logistical issues,” he said.
He called on President Bola Tinubu and the Federal Government to take immediate remedial action. He also urged the Minister of Works to personally assess the situation on the ground.
“How do we feel when the money from our area is what sustains the national economy? Every day I see on television the Minister commissioning new roads in other places. Naturally, we don’t feel happy, and something should be done,” Igali said.
“We feel neglected and not fairly treated as a part of the country that contributes so significantly to the national economy. This is an emergency situation. It is not a matter of blindly criticising the government.”

items.author: efosataiwo@vanguardngr.com
items.content:
A player opening a card game on a smartphone is rarely thinking about the design behind the screen. They are not analyzing button placement, menu structure, or visual elements. They simply want to enter a table, understand what is happening, and make decisions without unnecessary interruptions.
This is something I have noticed while following mobile gaming experiences over the years: the best interfaces are often the ones users barely notice. When a design works well, it disappears into the background and allows the player to focus entirely on the activity itself.
For card games, this matters even more. Players already understand the excitement of reading situations, making choices, and waiting for the right moment. A digital platform does not need to replace that feeling. It needs to create an environment where that feeling can happen naturally.
The difference between a frustrating experience and an enjoyable one often comes down to small design decisions that most users never consciously think about.
A Smooth Interface Reduces Mental Effort
One of the biggest mistakes I see in mobile entertainment is the assumption that more features automatically create more value.
A crowded interface may look impressive during development meetings, but real users often prefer simplicity. When someone opens a card game, they are not looking for a complicated system that requires constant adjustment. They want clear information, easy navigation, and a direct path to the game.
The best interfaces reduce the amount of thinking required outside the actual gameplay.
A player should not have to wonder where to find a specific option or spend time understanding basic functions. Every unnecessary step creates a small amount of friction, and those small frustrations can eventually affect whether someone decides to return.
This is one reason platforms such as teen patti master attract attention from mobile card enthusiasts. The value of a well-designed experience is not only about appearance. It comes from helping players spend less time managing the platform and more time enjoying the game.
Real Players Notice Small Details During Every Session
When discussing interface design, conversations often focus on major features or visual presentation. However, regular users usually remember much smaller details.
A player who joins a quick session after work notices whether actions respond smoothly. They notice whether information is easy to understand. They notice whether the screen feels organized when important decisions need to be made.
These details may seem insignificant individually, but together they shape the entire experience.
Imagine a player entering a competitive round. They do not want to search for basic controls or deal with confusing layouts at a moment when concentration matters. The interface should support the decision-making process rather than interrupt it.
Experienced players understand that confidence comes from familiarity. When every interaction feels predictable, the platform becomes easier to trust.
Mobile Design Must Match Real-Life Playing Habits
One interesting change in mobile entertainment is that people rarely sit down with the same mindset they had when playing traditional games.
A physical card session usually requires preparation. Friends need to gather, time needs to be arranged, and everyone needs to commit to the activity. Mobile gaming creates a different situation.
A player may open a card game while waiting for someone, during a short break, or while relaxing at home in the evening. These moments are often spontaneous.
Because of this, mobile interfaces need to respect limited attention. Users do not want unnecessary steps between opening an application and reaching the experience they came for.
A well-designed platform understands these everyday situations. It does not force players to adapt to the technology. Instead, the technology adapts to the way people naturally use their time.
Good Design Protects the Original Feeling of the Game
There is always a challenge when traditional games move into digital environments. Developers need to improve accessibility without removing the elements that made the original experience enjoyable.
For Teen Patti, much of the appeal comes from decision-making, timing, and reading the situation. The interface should support those elements rather than distract from them.
A common mistake is adding too many unnecessary features in an attempt to make a game feel more advanced. However, complexity does not always create a better experience. Sometimes it creates distance between the player and the game.
The strongest designs understand what should remain untouched.
Players do not open a card game because they want to explore menus. They open it because they enjoy the competition, the anticipation, and the choices that happen during each round.
A good interface protects that connection.
Performance Creates Confidence Before Players Even Realize It
Visual design alone cannot create a smooth experience. Performance plays an equally important role.
A delayed response, unclear loading process, or inconsistent interaction can immediately affect how players feel about a platform. Most users do not think about technical details, but they quickly notice when something feels unreliable.
This is especially important for mobile card games because timing influences the entire rhythm of a session. Players expect actions to happen naturally, without distractions breaking their concentration.
A reliable experience builds confidence over time. When users know what to expect every time they return, the platform becomes easier to integrate into their routines.
The connection between design and performance is simple: a beautiful interface means little if the experience behind it does not feel stable.
The Best Interfaces Become Invisible
The most successful mobile experiences are not always the ones with the largest number of features. They are usually the ones that understand human behavior.
Players appreciate platforms that respect their time, reduce unnecessary effort, and allow them to focus on what they enjoy. This is why interface design has become such an important part of digital card gaming.
A platform like teenpatti master represents this idea by focusing on the relationship between player expectations and digital convenience. The goal of a strong interface is not to impress users with complexity. It is to create a smooth environment where every action feels natural.
In the end, great mobile design is not about making players notice the interface. It is about making them forget it exists. When the technology quietly supports the experience, players can focus on what has always made card games enjoyable: strategy, decisions, and the excitement of every hand.

items.content:
The Minister of Works, David Umahi, has apologised to commuters and residents of Edo and Delta states over the deplorable condition of the Benin-Sapele Road, which has caused untold hardship to the people.
The minister also ordered the arrest of the contractor and concessionaire, as well as others found removing asphalt from federal roads without authorisation.
Umahi offered the apology and issued the directive on Tuesday in Benin during an inspection tour of some major roads in Edo.
The minister thanked Edo youths for remaining calm despite the hardship caused by the road’s condition, noting that their restraint helped prevent a possible breakdown of law and order.
He expressed disappointment with the concessionaire handling the road, accusing the company of lacking the technical competence required to execute the project.
Umahi said he had personally observed the removal of asphalt from the road during an earlier inspection with the state Governor, Monday Okpebholo, and directed the contractor to stop the practice.
According to him, the Ministry of Works does not permit contractors to remove asphalt from federal roads without authorisation, describing such acts as “destruction of public infrastructure.”
He therefore directed all ministry controllers to arrest any contractor or concessionaire found removing asphalt from federal roads without approval.
The minister criticised the concessionaire’s handling of the project, alleging that its lack of technical capacity had subjected commuters and residents to untold hardship.
He said the Federal Government had a responsibility to ensure that concessionaires possessed the necessary technical competence before being awarded road projects.
Umahi maintained that the concessionaire lacked a reputation for competence and integrity before taking over construction of the Benin-Agbor Road.
The minister further stated that President Bola Tinubu had taken note of the suffering of road users and directed the Ministry of Works to do everything necessary to restore the road and ameliorate the suffering of the people.
He explained that although concession agreements were governed by law, the government could invoke overriding public interest where necessary to protect citizens and critical infrastructure.
The minister reiterated his apology to commuters, residents of Edo and Delta, and other road users affected by the poor condition of the road.
He assured them of the road’s immediate rehabilitation to bring relief to the people, in line with Tinubu’s directive.
Umahi added that the government would prioritise the welfare and safety of the people.
He thanked Okpebholo for his commitment to infrastructure development and for intervening in the rehabilitation of federal roads in Edo.
Responding,  Okpebholo appealed to residents and youths in the affected areas to remain patient and exercise restraint over the deplorable condition of the road.
The governor recalled the poor state of the Benin-Ekpoma road, saying President Tinubu had promised to reconstruct it after their meeting and had fulfilled the promise.
He said Edo’s strategic location made it a gateway to several regions, warning that unrest in the state could have consequences for the entire country.
The Chief Executive Officer (CEO) of the concessionaire, Mr Samuel Daramola, blamed the slow pace of work on heavy rains, saying the company had resorted to palliative works to allow traffic to move.
Daramola maintained that one of the first things the company did after taking over construction of the Benin-Agbor Road was to expand the road.
He said the company started with palliative works because of the numerous potholes on the road, to create easier access for commuters.

By Juliet Umeh
An aggrieved governorship aspirant of the All Progressives Congress (APC) in Ogun State, Abayomi Hunye, has said his challenge to the outcome of the party’s governorship primary is not aimed at undermining the party but at seeking justice.
Hunye, who spoke during an interview on Channels Television, said he remained committed to the APC despite the crisis generated by the emergence of Senator Solomon Yayi as the party’s governorship candidate.
“I am not fighting the party. I am fighting for justice. I have suffered for this party, and I have been with the progressives for about 20 years,” he said.
He stated:  “How can I have an open election and my name will be allocated zero? I participated, I voted, and my people were there. So I am challenging that result,” he said.
According to him, he obtained the party’s nomination and expression-of-interest forms for N50 million, underwent screening, and was cleared to contest.
“I bought the form. I have the receipt. I was invited for screening, and I was cleared. On the screening list, my number was 52, while Yayi’s number was 53,” he said.
Hunye also faulted the consensus arrangement that produced Yayi, alleging that the aspirants were not properly consulted before the decision was reached.
“Nobody called me. All the aspirants ought to have been invited to a meeting where the consensus would be explained. They should agree and put it in black and white,” he said.
He denied allegations that he was falsely parading himself as the party’s candidate, saying, “I have never said I am the candidate. I am challenging the result in court.”
Hunye said he was prepared to abide by the court’s decision, stressing that his objective was to ensure fairness within the party.
“I want justice. Let the court decide. Whatever the outcome, I will accept it,” he said.
He warned that unresolved grievances could deepen the crisis within the APC ahead of the 2027 election, urging party leaders to address the issues and prevent division.

By Peter Duru, Makurdi
A team of engineers from Al Wadi Al Akhdar Oil Mills, Asher, Cairo, Egypt, has inspected the long abandoned Taraku Mills in Benue State and rated the facility 75 percent ready for full-scale production following ongoing rehabilitation of the plant.
The team, led by Saleh Mansury, carried out an on-site assessment of the factory alongside officials of the Corporate Communications and Information Technology Unit (CCIT) of the Benue Investment and Property Company Limited (BIPC).
The inspection covered key sections of the factory, with the engineers assessing its equipment, operational processes and production systems to determine its preparedness for the resumption of full-scale operations.
Speaking after the assessment, Mansury said the facility was in good condition, noting that only about 25 percent of work remained to get it fully operational.
“The factory is about 75 percent ready for full production. What is remaining is basically some minor upgrades in certain sections to bring the facility in line with modern technology,” he said.
Mansury identified the boiler and solvent machine as major areas requiring attention, explaining that upgrading the equipment would improve operational efficiency and reduce energy consumption.
He said the Egyptian team was prepared to commence full-scale production once the identified upgrades were completed, adding that plans were also underway to introduce additional production lines, particularly for cake production.
The engineer also called on farmers in Benue State to increase the cultivation of soybeans, groundnuts and maize, stressing that the crops were critical raw materials required to sustain the factory’s operations.
Also speaking, James Emmanuel of BIPC corroborated the assessment, saying the factory was in good condition and capable of operating effectively.
Emmanuel said the completion of the required upgrades, particularly in the boiler and solvent sections, would position the factory to operate at full production capacity.
He stated that inspection formed part of ongoing efforts to revitalise Taraku Mills, optimise its production capacity and establish a clear timeline for the commencement of full-scale production.

items.author: Emmanuel Okogba
items.content:
The US government plans to revoke the visas of foreigners who came to the country for tourism or business but sought to stay longer by applying for asylum, the State Department said Tuesday.
The crackdown marks another step in the Trump administration’s signature drive to reduce immigration into the United States.
The administration said it is now working with the Department of Homeland Security to identify and revoke the visas of people who, it said, came to America billing themselves as temporary visitors but then applied for asylum so they could stay permanently.
“Obtaining a visa in order to seek asylum is fraud — which is grounds for visa revocation,” State Department spokesman Tommy Pigott said in a statement that confirmed press reports about the new policy.
The White House, in a post on X, suggested “up to two hundred thousand visas” would be affected and claimed it would be the “largest mass visa revocation in history.”
The State Department neither confirmed nor denied that number. Pigott said, “The number of revocations remains dynamic and will be done on a rolling basis.”
Early this month the department said that since President Donald Trump returned to power in January 2025, some 175,000 foreigners had seen their US visas revoked on grounds ranging from criminal offenses, including driving under the influence, to praising the killing of the right-wing activist Charlie Kirk.
The administration also recently revoked the visas of Mexican officials, including the son of the former president Andres Manuel Lopez Obrador. This prompted a complaint from the current president, Claudia Sheinbaum.
Trump, who won reelection in large part on his promise to fight illegal immigration, has expelled huge numbers of people who were in the country without proper residence papers.
But he has also worked to restrict the entry of foreigners who do go by the rules and has gone after those who overstay their visas after they expire.
Some of these measures have been challenged and curtailed by the courts.
Last Friday a federal judge struck down a government ban on visas to nationals from 75 countries who wish to settle in the country indefinitely. These countries included Afghanistan, Brazil, Egypt, Iran, Iraq, Nigeria, Somalia, Thailand and Yemen.
The Trump administration is also planning to expand vetting of the social media accounts of visa applicants.
“We are making clear that a visa is a privilege — not a right,” Pigott said Tuesday.
